By "the city" is meant Makkah, and He singled it out from among all other cities because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the city most beloved to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." Al-Jumhur read it this way. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read "which He has made sacred" so that the relative clause is an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made it sacred" is that He made it a sanctuary, secure, in which no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, possession, and disposal, that is: everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to the command of God, surrender to Him in obedience, carry out His orders, and avoid His prohibitions. By His saying "that I be" is meant that I remain steadfast upon what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾, that is: that I continue its recitation and persist in it.

It is said: the intended meaning of reciting the Qur'an here is none other than reciting the call to faith, though the first (view) is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith; and the first (view) is preferable. "Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self" because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in Allah and acting upon His laws.

The majority (of readers) recited "wa-an atluwa" (وأنْ أتْلُوَ) with the waw affirmed after the lam, as being from tilawa (تِلاوَة), which is recitation, or from talw (تِلْو), which is following.

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited "wa-ani itlu" (وأنِ اتْلُ) with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (the Prophet, ﷺ). Thus al-Farra' explained it.

Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know of anyone who recited this reading, and it contradicts all the codices (mashahif)." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾, i.e., and whoever goes astray into disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have indeed fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing upon me other than that.

It is also said: the answer is omitted, i.e., "then the consequence of his going astray falls upon him," and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its stead, because it serves as the cause for it.

﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge, and other things. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, i.e., Allah will show you His signs in yourselves and in others, so you will recognize them, i.e., you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham, and Hafs from ʿAsim read taʿmalun (تَعْمَلُونَ) with the second-person form (the feminine ending of direct address, "you"), while the rest read it with the third-person form (yaʿmalun).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "dakhirin" (داخِرِينَ), that he said: "ṣaghirin" (صاغِرِينَ), i.e., humbled.

They also transmitted from him, regarding His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, that he said: "qaʾima" (قائِمَةً), i.e., standing; ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "aḥkama", i.e., made firm.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, in His saying: ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, that he said: "He made beautiful everything He created and made it secure."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but Allah'; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." And if this is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then recourse to it in interpreting the speech of Allah, glorified is He, is required, and it is understood that what is meant is: "There is no god but Allah" with its true meaning and what is due to it, so that every act of obedience is included under that. Supporting this is what al-Hakim recorded in al-Kuna from Safwan ibn ʿAssal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Faith and Shirk will come kneeling before Allah, glorified is He. Allah will say to Faith: 'Go, you and your people, to Paradise,' and He will say to Shirk: 'Go, you and your people, to the Fire.'"

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, meaning his saying: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Anas, and similar, in a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) form.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but Allah, ﴿then for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq transmitted from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted regarding ﴿then for him is better than it﴾ that he said: "For him, there is better than it, meaning from its direction (source)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "﴿then for him is better than it﴾, he said: reward." He also transmitted from him: "The city is Makkah."

(p-1090) Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned briefly some of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿And on the day when We gather from every nation a company﴾. The word governing the adverbial phrase "on the day" is a verb that is omitted, and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-hashr means gathering.

It has been said that the intended gathering here is the gathering of punishment, after the general gathering that includes all of creation. Min (from) indicates the starting point. Al-fawj means a group, like a band. The min in ﴿of those who deny Our signs﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyya). ﴿Then they are marshalled﴾ means that the first of them is held back until the last of them joins them. Its full analysis has already been discussed in this surah. It has also been said that it means they are driven back or pushed. From this is the line of al-Shammakh:

*And how many a host, a mighty army, have we repelled*

The meaning of the verse is: Mention, O Muhammad, a day when We gather from every nation of the nations a company of those who deny Our signs. At that gathering they are turned back, the first of them against the last, or they are pushed. That is: recount this to them, or make it clear to them, as a warning and a frightening.

﴿Until, when they arrive﴾ at the place of reckoning, God says to them, as rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did you deny My signs?﴾ which I sent down upon My messengers and commanded them to convey to you, ﴿while you did not encompass them in knowledge?﴾ Rather, you denied them at the very outset, ignorant of them, not examining them, nor reasoning about whether they were true or false, out of defiance, stubbornness, and audacity toward God and His messengers. In this there is further rebuke and reproach, because whoever denies something without having encompassed it in knowledge has erred in his denial. He has announced his own ignorance, unfairness, poor understanding, and deficient perception. Of this kind is whoever undertakes to disparage one of the religious sciences, or a science that is a prerequisite of them and a means by which one reaches them, and which increases insight into them and understanding of their meanings, such as all the sciences of the Arabic language, which are twelve sciences, and the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), by which the legal rulings are deduced from their detailed evidences, together with its explanation of the general rules of the language. Likewise every science that is of great benefit in understanding the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Such a person has announced with the loudest voice that he is ignorant, a disputer using falsehood, a critic of the religious sciences, deserving that some calamity of the calamities of punishment should strike him, which would restrain him from his ignorance, his error, and his criticism of what he does not know, nor has knowledge of, nor encompasses its reality, until he becomes a lesson to others and an admonition by which those like him are admonished: the weak-minded, the frail of religion, the rabble who clothe themselves with knowledge falsely and deceitfully.

The "am" in His saying ﴿Or what were you doing?﴾ is the disjunctive (munqati'a) "am," and the meaning is: "Or what were you doing that kept you occupied from considering them and reflecting on their meanings?" This question is posed as a means of reproach to them.

﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾ has already been explained shortly before. The ba' in ﴿because of what they did wrong﴾ indicates cause: that is, the word becomes due against them because of the wrongdoing, the greatest kind of which is associating partners with God. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ at the time the word falls upon them, meaning they have no excuse to speak with, or they are unable to speak because of the great terror they witness.

Most of the exegetes said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak. Then, after He had warned them with the terrors of the Resurrection, He, glory be to Him, mentioned what may serve as evidence for monotheism, for the gathering, and for prophethood, in order to intensify guidance and to complete the proof.

So He said: ﴿Do they not see that We made the night for them to rest in, and the day to give sight?﴾ That is: We made the night for rest, settledness, and sleep, because of the darkness in it, for they do not strive in it for livelihood. And the day to give sight, so that they may see in it what they strive for of livelihood, which they cannot do without. The description of the day as "giving sight," though sight is an attribute of people, is an intensification of its brightness, as if it sees what is in it.

It has been said that there is an omission in the speech, and the sense is: "And We made the night dark so that they may rest." He omitted "dark" because "giving sight" indicates it. Its full verification has already been discussed in al-Isra' and in Yunus. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ meaning indications and evidences ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glory be to Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another sign of the Hour, saying: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿the day We gather﴾ and is in the accusative governed by the same governing element mentioned earlier.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "And that is the day the Trumpet is blown." But the first is preferable.

Al-sur is a horn into which Israfil blows, and the discussion of it has already been fully treated in al-An'am.

The blasts of the Trumpet are three: the first is the blast of terror, the second is the blast of swooning, and the third is the blast of resurrection.

It has been said that there are two blasts, and that the blast of terror is either referred to the blast of swooning or to the blast of resurrection. This view was preferred by al-Qushayri, al-Qurtubi, and others.

Al-Mawardi said: the blast mentioned here is the blast of the rising from the graves. ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾, meaning they fear and are alarmed because of the intensity of what they hear. It has also been said that "fazi'a" here means hastening and responding to a call, from the expression "fazi'tu ilayka fi kadha," meaning I hurried to answer you. But the first is preferable to the meaning of the verse.

He used the past tense although it is coordinated with a present-tense verb, to indicate that the event is certain to occur, as the scholars of rhetoric (al-bayan) have explained.

Al-Farra' said: it is to be understood in terms of meaning, because the meaning is: when it is blown, except whom God wills, that is, except those whom God wills not to be terrified at that blast.

There has been disagreement about who is the object of the exception. It has been said: they are the martyrs and the prophets. It has been said: the angels. It has been said: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It has been said: the dark-eyed houris. It has been said: all the believers, as evidenced by His later saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from terror that day﴾. It is possible that the exception includes all of those mentioned, and there is no obstacle to that.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled.﴾ Al-Jumhur read "atuhu" with the form of the active participle, with the pronoun referring back to God, glory be to Him.

Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Hafs from 'Asim read "atawhu" as a past-tense verb. Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

Qatada read "wa kullun ataahu."

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it as a past-tense verb has made it singular according to the wording of "kull," and whoever reads it as an active participle has made it plural according to its meaning. This is a clear error, for neither reading is singular in form. The singular is only in Qatada's reading. The meaning of "dakhirin" is humbled and abased. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Jumhur read "dakhirin," and al-A'raj read "dakhirin" without the alif. This has already been explained in Surat al-Nahl.

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed﴾ is coordinated with "is blown."

The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. ﴿You think them fixed﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state either of the subject of "you see" or of its object, because the seeing is visual. It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first sentence, but this is weak. This is the third sign of the Hour. The meaning of ﴿You think them fixed﴾ is that they are standing still. The clause ﴿while they pass by like clouds﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, meaning they move swiftly, like the passing of clouds driven by winds.

Al-Qutaybi said: that is because the mountains will be gathered and set in motion, while in the eye's sight they appear stationary although they are moving.

Al-Qushayri said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [al-Naba' 20]. The people of Kufa read "tahsabuha" with a fatha on the sin, and the rest read it with a kasra.

﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. The accusative of "sun'a" is as a verbal noun (masdar) according to al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others. That is, God has done that as a work. It has been said that it is a verbal noun emphasizing His saying ﴿and the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (ighra'), meaning: look at the handiwork of God. The meaning of ﴿who perfected everything﴾ is who made it firm. One says: "a man is tiqn," meaning skilled in things. The clause ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, namely His doing what He did and perfecting everything.

Khabir means one who is informed of outward things and inward secrets.

Al-Jumhur read with the second-person ta' (addressing you). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hisham read with the third-person ya' (speaking of them).

﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it﴾. The alif and lam are generic, meaning whoever brings a good deed of its kind will have from reward and recompense with God something better than it, that is, better and greater. It has been said: "better" means good that comes from it. The first is preferable.

It has been said that the good deed here means: "There is no god but God." It has been said: sincerity. It has been said: performing the obligations. The generalization is preferable, and there is no basis for restriction, even though some of the early scholars held it.

It has been said that this clause explains His saying ﴿He is Aware of what you do﴾. It has also been said that it explains His saying ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾.

'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and they from terror﴾ with tanwin and a fatha on the mim of "yawma'idhin." Nafi' read it with a fatha on the mim without tanwin. The rest read "fazi'" as an annexed construct to "yawma'idhin."

Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations, for its meaning is safety from the terror of that entire day. With tanwin, safety would be from a terror, not from all terror.

It has been said: it is a verbal noun that covers the many, so the preference based on what was mentioned is not complete, and the two readings have one meaning.

It has been said: the terror meant here is the greatest terror mentioned in His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya' 103]. The basis of Nafi''s reading is that he put "yawm" in the accusative as a time adverb, because its grammatical case is not fully declinable. Since the annexation of "terror" to a non-declinable time-word, it was indeclinable. A full discussion of this was given before in Surat Hud.

﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire.﴾

A group of the Companions and those after them, to the point that it has been said to be a consensus among the interpreters, held that the evil deed here means polytheism. The basis for this restriction is His saying: ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾, for this retribution is only for an evil like the evil of polytheism. The meaning of ﴿their faces were overturned into the Fire﴾ is that they were thrown into it upon their faces and cast down into it. One says: "kababtu al-rajul," meaning I threw the man on his face, so he fell on his face (inkabba and akabba). The clause ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ is spoken with an implied speech, meaning it is said, and the speaker is the keepers of Hell, that is: you are only repaid for the reward of your deeds.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. When He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the states of the beginning and the return, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them this statement, that is: Say, O Muhammad, "I have only been commanded to single out God for worship alone, with no partner." By "the city" is meant Makkah, and He singled it out from among all other cities because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the city most beloved to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." Al-Jumhur read it this way. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read "which He has made sacred" so that the relative clause is an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made it sacred" is that He made it a sanctuary, secure, in which no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, possession, and disposal, that is: everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to the command of God, surrender to Him in obedience, carry out His orders, and avoid His prohibitions. By His saying "that I be" is meant that I remain steadfast upon what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾, that is: that I continue its recitation and persist in it.

It is said: the intended meaning of reciting the Qur'an here is none other than reciting the call to faith, though the first (view) is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith; and the first (view) is preferable. "Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self" because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in Allah and acting upon His laws.

The majority (of readers) recited "wa-an atluwa" (وأنْ أتْلُوَ) with the waw affirmed after the lam, as being from tilawa (تِلاوَة), which is recitation, or from talw (تِلْو), which is following.

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited "wa-ani itlu" (وأنِ اتْلُ) with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (the Prophet, ﷺ). Thus al-Farra' explained it.

Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know of anyone who recited this reading, and it contradicts all the codices (mashahif)." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾, i.e., and whoever goes astray into disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have indeed fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing upon me other than that.

It is also said: the answer is omitted, i.e., "then the consequence of his going astray falls upon him," and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its stead, because it serves as the cause for it.

﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge, and other things. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, i.e., Allah will show you His signs in yourselves and in others, so you will recognize them, i.e., you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is a severe warning and a great threat.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but Allah'; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." Allah will say to Faith: 'Go, you and your people, to Paradise,' and He will say to Shirk: 'Go, you and your people, to the Fire.'"

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Anas, and similar, in a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) form.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but Allah, ﴿then for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq transmitted from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted regarding ﴿then for him is better than it﴾ that he said: "For him, there is better than it, meaning from its direction (source)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "﴿then for him is better than it﴾, he said: reward." He also transmitted from him: "The city is Makkah."

﴿Until, when they arrive﴾ at the place of reckoning, God says to them, as rebuke and reproach: ﴿Did you deny My signs?﴾ which I sent down upon My messengers and commanded them to convey to you, ﴿while you did not encompass them in knowledge?﴾ Rather, you denied them at the very outset, ignorant of them, not examining them, nor reasoning about whether they were true or false, out of defiance, stubbornness, and audacity toward God and His messengers. In this there is further rebuke and reproach, because whoever denies something without having encompassed it in knowledge has erred in his denial. He has announced his own ignorance, unfairness, poor understanding, and deficient perception. Of this kind is whoever undertakes to disparage one of the religious sciences, or a science that is a prerequisite of them and a means by which one reaches them, and which increases insight into them and understanding of their meanings, such as all the sciences of the Arabic language, which are twelve sciences, and the science of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), by which the legal rulings are deduced from their detailed evidences, together with its explanation of the general rules of the language. Likewise every science that is of great benefit in understanding the Book of God and the Sunnah of His Messenger. Such a person has announced with the loudest voice that he is ignorant, a disputer using falsehood, a critic of the religious sciences, deserving that some calamity of the calamities of punishment should strike him, which would restrain him from his ignorance, his error, and his criticism of what he does not know, nor has knowledge of, nor encompasses its reality, until he becomes a lesson to others and an admonition by which those like him are admonished: the weak-minded, the frail of religion, the rabble who clothe themselves with knowledge falsely and deceitfully.

The "am" in His saying ﴿Or what were you doing?﴾ is the disjunctive (munqati'a) "am," and the meaning is: "Or what were you doing that kept you occupied from considering them and reflecting on their meanings?" This question is posed as a means of reproach to them.

﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾ has already been explained shortly before. The ba' in ﴿because of what they did wrong﴾ indicates cause: that is, the word becomes due against them because of the wrongdoing, the greatest kind of which is associating partners with God. ﴿So they will not speak﴾ at the time the word falls upon them, meaning they have no excuse to speak with, or they are unable to speak because of the great terror they witness.

Most of the exegetes said: their mouths will be sealed, so they will not speak. Then, after He had warned them with the terrors of the Resurrection, He, glory be to Him, mentioned what may serve as evidence for monotheism, for the gathering, and for prophethood, in order to intensify guidance and to complete the proof.

So He said: ﴿Do they not see that We made the night for them to rest in, and the day to give sight?﴾ That is: We made the night for rest, settledness, and sleep, because of the darkness in it, for they do not strive in it for livelihood. And the day to give sight, so that they may see in it what they strive for of livelihood, which they cannot do without. The description of the day as "giving sight," though sight is an attribute of people, is an intensification of its brightness, as if it sees what is in it.

It has been said that there is an omission in the speech, and the sense is: "And We made the night dark so that they may rest." He omitted "dark" because "giving sight" indicates it. Its full verification has already been discussed in al-Isra' and in Yunus. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ meaning indications and evidences ﴿for a people who believe﴾ in God, glory be to Him.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned another sign of the Hour, saying: ﴿And the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. This is coordinated with ﴿the day We gather﴾ and is in the accusative governed by the same governing element mentioned earlier.

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "And that is the day the Trumpet is blown." But the first is preferable.

Al-sur is a horn into which Israfil blows, and the discussion of it has already been fully treated in al-An'am.

The blasts of the Trumpet are three: the first is the blast of terror, the second is the blast of swooning, and the third is the blast of resurrection.

It has been said that there are two blasts, and that the blast of terror is either referred to the blast of swooning or to the blast of resurrection. This view was preferred by al-Qushayri, al-Qurtubi, and others.

Al-Mawardi said: the blast mentioned here is the blast of the rising from the graves. ﴿So whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified﴾, meaning they fear and are alarmed because of the intensity of what they hear. It has also been said that "fazi'a" here means hastening and responding to a call, from the expression "fazi'tu ilayka fi kadha," meaning I hurried to answer you. But the first is preferable to the meaning of the verse.

He used the past tense although it is coordinated with a present-tense verb, to indicate that the event is certain to occur, as the scholars of rhetoric (al-bayan) have explained.

Al-Farra' said: it is to be understood in terms of meaning, because the meaning is: when it is blown, except whom God wills, that is, except those whom God wills not to be terrified at that blast.

There has been disagreement about who is the object of the exception. It has been said: they are the martyrs and the prophets. It has been said: the angels. It has been said: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death. It has been said: the dark-eyed houris. It has been said: all the believers, as evidenced by His later saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it, and they will be secure from terror that day﴾. It is possible that the exception includes all of those mentioned, and there is no obstacle to that.

﴿And all will come to Him, humbled.﴾ Al-Jumhur read "atuhu" with the form of the active participle, with the pronoun referring back to God, glory be to Him.

Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamza, and Hafs from 'Asim read "atawhu" as a past-tense verb. Ibn Mas'ud also read it this way.

Qatada read "wa kullun ataahu."

Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads it as a past-tense verb has made it singular according to the wording of "kull," and whoever reads it as an active participle has made it plural according to its meaning. This is a clear error, for neither reading is singular in form. The singular is only in Qatada's reading. The meaning of "dakhirin" is humbled and abased. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). Al-Jumhur read "dakhirin," and al-A'raj read "dakhirin" without the alif. This has already been explained in Surat al-Nahl.

﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed﴾ is coordinated with "is blown."

The address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or to everyone who is fit to see. ﴿You think them fixed﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state either of the subject of "you see" or of its object, because the seeing is visual. It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first sentence, but this is weak. This is the third sign of the Hour. The meaning of ﴿You think them fixed﴾ is that they are standing still. The clause ﴿while they pass by like clouds﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, meaning they move swiftly, like the passing of clouds driven by winds.

Al-Qutaybi said: that is because the mountains will be gathered and set in motion, while in the eye's sight they appear stationary although they are moving.

Al-Qushayri said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and similar to it is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, and they will become a mirage﴾ [al-Naba' 20]. The people of Kufa read "tahsabuha" with a fatha on the sin, and the rest read it with a kasra.

﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. The accusative of "sun'a" is as a verbal noun (masdar) according to al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and others. That is, God has done that as a work. It has been said that it is a verbal noun emphasizing His saying ﴿and the day the Trumpet is blown﴾. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (ighra'), meaning: look at the handiwork of God. The meaning of ﴿who perfected everything﴾ is who made it firm. One says: "a man is tiqn," meaning skilled in things. The clause ﴿Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ is a reason for what precedes it, namely His doing what He did and perfecting everything.

Khabir means one who is informed of outward things and inward secrets.

Al-Jumhur read with the second-person ta' (addressing you). Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Hisham read with the third-person ya' (speaking of them).

﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have better than it﴾. The alif and lam are generic, meaning whoever brings a good deed of its kind will have from reward and recompense with God something better than it, that is, better and greater. It has been said: "better" means good that comes from it. The first is preferable.

It has been said that the good deed here means: "There is no god but God." It has been said: sincerity. It has been said: performing the obligations. The generalization is preferable, and there is no basis for restriction, even though some of the early scholars held it.

It has been said that this clause explains His saying ﴿He is Aware of what you do﴾. It has also been said that it explains His saying ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾.

'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and they from terror﴾ with tanwin and a fatha on the mim of "yawma'idhin." Nafi' read it with a fatha on the mim without tanwin. The rest read "fazi'" as an annexed construct to "yawma'idhin."

Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations, for its meaning is safety from the terror of that entire day. With tanwin, safety would be from a terror, not from all terror.

It has been said: it is a verbal noun that covers the many, so the preference based on what was mentioned is not complete, and the two readings have one meaning.

It has been said: the terror meant here is the greatest terror mentioned in His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya' 103]. The basis of Nafi''s reading is that he put "yawm" in the accusative as a time adverb, because its grammatical case is not fully declinable. Since the annexation of "terror" to a non-declinable time-word, it was indeclinable. A full discussion of this was given before in Surat Hud.

﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire.﴾

A group of the Companions and those after them, to the point that it has been said to be a consensus among the interpreters, held that the evil deed here means polytheism. The basis for this restriction is His saying: ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾, for this retribution is only for an evil like the evil of polytheism. The meaning of ﴿their faces were overturned into the Fire﴾ is that they were thrown into it upon their faces and cast down into it. One says: "kababtu al-rajul," meaning I threw the man on his face, so he fell on his face (inkabba and akabba). The clause ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ is spoken with an implied speech, meaning it is said, and the speaker is the keepers of Hell, that is: you are only repaid for the reward of your deeds.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. When He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the states of the beginning and the return, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them this statement, that is: Say, O Muhammad, "I have only been commanded to single out God for worship alone, with no partner." By "the city" is meant Makkah, and He singled it out from among all other cities because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the city most beloved to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." Al-Jumhur read it this way. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read "which He has made sacred" so that the relative clause is an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made it sacred" is that He made it a sanctuary, secure, in which no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, possession, and disposal, that is: everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to the command of God, surrender to Him in obedience, carry out His orders, and avoid His prohibitions. By His saying "that I be" is meant that I remain steadfast upon what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾, that is: that I continue its recitation and persist in it.

It is said: the intended meaning of reciting the Qur'an here is none other than reciting the call to faith, though the first (view) is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith; and the first (view) is preferable. "Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self" because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in Allah and acting upon His laws.

The majority (of readers) recited "wa-an atluwa" (وأنْ أتْلُوَ) with the waw affirmed after the lam, as being from tilawa (تِلاوَة), which is recitation, or from talw (تِلْو), which is following.

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited "wa-ani itlu" (وأنِ اتْلُ) with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (the Prophet, ﷺ). Thus al-Farra' explained it.

Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know of anyone who recited this reading, and it contradicts all the codices (mashahif)." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾, i.e., and whoever goes astray into disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have indeed fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing upon me other than that.

It is also said: the answer is omitted, i.e., "then the consequence of his going astray falls upon him," and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its stead, because it serves as the cause for it.

﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge, and other things. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, i.e., Allah will show you His signs in yourselves and in others, so you will recognize them, i.e., you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham, and Hafs from ʿAsim read taʿmalun (تَعْمَلُونَ) with the second-person form (the feminine ending of direct address, "you"), while the rest read it with the third-person form (yaʿmalun).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "dakhirin" (داخِرِينَ), that he said: "ṣaghirin" (صاغِرِينَ), i.e., humbled.

They also transmitted from him, regarding His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, that he said: "qaʾima" (قائِمَةً), i.e., standing; ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "aḥkama", i.e., made firm.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, in His saying: ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, that he said: "He made beautiful everything He created and made it secure."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but Allah'; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." And if this is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then recourse to it in interpreting the speech of Allah, glorified is He, is required, and it is understood that what is meant is: "There is no god but Allah" with its true meaning and what is due to it, so that every act of obedience is included under that. Supporting this is what al-Hakim recorded in al-Kuna from Safwan ibn ʿAssal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Faith and Shirk will come kneeling before Allah, glorified is He. Allah will say to Faith: 'Go, you and your people, to Paradise,' and He will say to Shirk: 'Go, you and your people, to the Fire.'"

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, meaning his saying: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Anas, and similar, in a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) form.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but Allah, ﴿then for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq transmitted from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted regarding ﴿then for him is better than it﴾ that he said: "For him, there is better than it, meaning from its direction (source)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "﴿then for him is better than it﴾, he said: reward." He also transmitted from him: "The city is Makkah."

(p-1090) Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned briefly some of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, saying: ﴿And on the day when We gather from every nation a company﴾. The word governing the adverbial phrase "on the day" is a verb that is omitted, and it is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-hashr means gathering.

It has been said that the intended gathering here is the gathering of punishment, after the general gathering that includes all of creation. Min (from) indicates the starting point. Al-fawj means a group, like a band. The min in ﴿of those who deny Our signs﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyya). ﴿Then they are marshalled﴾ means that the first of them is held back until the last of them joins them. Its full analysis has already been discussed in this surah. It has also been said that it means they are driven back or pushed. From this is the line of al-Shammakh:

*And how many a host, a mighty army, have we repelled*

The meaning of the verse is: Mention, O Muhammad, a day when We gather from every nation of the nations a company of those who deny Our signs. At that gathering they are turned back, the first of them against the last, or they are pushed. That is: recount this to them, or make it clear to them, as a warning and a frightening.

It has been said that the good deed here means: "There is no god but God." It has been said: sincerity. It has been said: performing the obligations. The generalization is preferable, and there is no basis for restriction, even though some of the early scholars held it.

It has been said that this clause explains His saying ﴿He is Aware of what you do﴾. It has also been said that it explains His saying ﴿And all will come to Him, humbled﴾.

'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and they from terror﴾ with tanwin and a fatha on the mim of "yawma'idhin." Nafi' read it with a fatha on the mim without tanwin. The rest read "fazi'" as an annexed construct to "yawma'idhin."

Abu 'Ubayd said: this is more pleasing to me, because it is more general in the two interpretations, for its meaning is safety from the terror of that entire day. With tanwin, safety would be from a terror, not from all terror.

It has been said: it is a verbal noun that covers the many, so the preference based on what was mentioned is not complete, and the two readings have one meaning.

It has been said: the terror meant here is the greatest terror mentioned in His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya' 103]. The basis of Nafi''s reading is that he put "yawm" in the accusative as a time adverb, because its grammatical case is not fully declinable. Since the annexation of "terror" to a non-declinable time-word, it was indeclinable. A full discussion of this was given before in Surat Hud.

﴿And whoever brings an evil deed, their faces will be overturned into the Fire.﴾

A group of the Companions and those after them, to the point that it has been said to be a consensus among the interpreters, held that the evil deed here means polytheism. The basis for this restriction is His saying: ﴿their faces will be overturned into the Fire﴾, for this retribution is only for an evil like the evil of polytheism. The meaning of ﴿their faces were overturned into the Fire﴾ is that they were thrown into it upon their faces and cast down into it. One says: "kababtu al-rajul," meaning I threw the man on his face, so he fell on his face (inkabba and akabba). The clause ﴿Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ is spoken with an implied speech, meaning it is said, and the speaker is the keepers of Hell, that is: you are only repaid for the reward of your deeds.

﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city, who has made it sacred﴾. When He, glory be to Him, finished explaining the states of the beginning and the return, He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them this statement, that is: Say, O Muhammad, "I have only been commanded to single out God for worship alone, with no partner." By "the city" is meant Makkah, and He singled it out from among all other cities because the Sacred House of God is in it, and because it is the city most beloved to His Messenger. The relative clause is an attribute of "the Lord." Al-Jumhur read it this way. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud read "which He has made sacred" so that the relative clause is an attribute of "the city." The meaning of "made it sacred" is that He made it a sanctuary, secure, in which no blood is shed, no one is wronged, its game is not hunted, and its grass is not cut. ﴿And to Him belongs everything﴾ among things, in creation, possession, and disposal, that is: everything belongs to God. ﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, that is, those who submit to the command of God, surrender to Him in obedience, carry out His orders, and avoid His prohibitions. By His saying "that I be" is meant that I remain steadfast upon what I am upon.

﴿And to recite the Qur'an﴾, that is: that I continue its recitation and persist in it.

It is said: the intended meaning of reciting the Qur'an here is none other than reciting the call to faith, though the first (view) is preferable. ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self﴾, because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith; and the first (view) is preferable. "Whoever is guided, he is only guided for his own self" because the benefit of that returns to him, i.e., whoever is guided in general, or whoever is guided by what I recite to him and acts upon what it contains of faith in Allah and acting upon His laws.

The majority (of readers) recited "wa-an atluwa" (وأنْ أتْلُوَ) with the waw affirmed after the lam, as being from tilawa (تِلاوَة), which is recitation, or from talw (تِلْو), which is following.

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) recited "wa-ani itlu" (وأنِ اتْلُ) with the waw omitted, as an imperative addressed to him (the Prophet, ﷺ). Thus al-Farra' explained it.

Al-Nahhas said: "We do not know of anyone who recited this reading, and it contradicts all the codices (mashahif)." ﴿And whoever goes astray, say: I am only one of the warners﴾, i.e., and whoever goes astray into disbelief and turns away from guidance, say to him: I am only one of the warners, and I have indeed fulfilled that by conveying it to you, and there is nothing upon me other than that.

It is also said: the answer is omitted, i.e., "then the consequence of his going astray falls upon him," and "I am only one of the warners" has been placed in its stead, because it serves as the cause for it.

﴿And say: All praise is for Allah﴾ for His blessings which He has bestowed upon me, of prophethood, knowledge, and other things. His saying: ﴿He will show you His signs﴾ is among what the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to say, i.e., Allah will show you His signs in yourselves and in others, so you will recognize them, i.e., you will recognize His signs and the proofs of His power and His oneness. This recognition does not benefit the disbelievers, because they recognized them at a time when faith is no longer accepted from them, and that is at the moment of the presence of death.

Then He concluded the surah with His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a statement from Him, glorified is He, not included within the speech which He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to say, and in it is a severe warning and a great threat.

Ahl al-Madina, al-Sham, and Hafs from ʿAsim read taʿmalun (تَعْمَلُونَ) with the second-person form (the feminine ending of direct address, "you"), while the rest read it with the third-person form (yaʿmalun).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "dakhirin" (داخِرِينَ), that he said: "ṣaghirin" (صاغِرِينَ), i.e., humbled.

They also transmitted from him, regarding His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed﴾, that he said: "qaʾima" (قائِمَةً), i.e., standing; ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, he said: "aḥkama", i.e., made firm.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, in His saying: ﴿the handiwork of Allah, who perfected everything﴾, that he said: "He made beautiful everything He created and made it secure."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, he said: it is 'There is no god but Allah'; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾, he said: it is shirk (associating partners with Allah)." And if this is authentically related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then recourse to it in interpreting the speech of Allah, glorified is He, is required, and it is understood that what is meant is: "There is no god but Allah" with its true meaning and what is due to it, so that every act of obedience is included under that. Supporting this is what al-Hakim recorded in al-Kuna from Safwan ibn ʿAssal, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Faith and Shirk will come kneeling before Allah, glorified is He. Allah will say to Faith: 'Go, you and your people, to Paradise,' and He will say to Shirk: 'Go, you and your people, to the Fire.'"

﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it﴾, meaning his saying: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and Anas, and similar, in a marfuʿ (traced to the Prophet) form.

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami transmitted from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever comes with a good deed, meaning the testimony that there is no god but Allah, ﴿then for him is better than it﴾, meaning by the good, Paradise; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, meaning shirk; ﴿their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾." And he said: "This one saves, and this one destroys."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and al-Kharaʾiti in Makarim al-Akhlaq transmitted from Ibn Masʿud: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾, he said: "There is no god but Allah"; ﴿and whoever comes with an evil deed﴾, he said: "with shirk."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted regarding ﴿then for him is better than it﴾ that he said: "For him, there is better than it, meaning from its direction (source)."

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him: "﴿then for him is better than it﴾, he said: reward." He also transmitted from him: "The city is Makkah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 13 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn al-Durays, Ibn al-Najjar, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Qasas was revealed at Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: it was revealed between Makkah and Madinah.

Ibn Sallam said: at al-Juhfah, at the time of the Messenger of Allah's (ﷺ) migration, and it is His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, He who has imposed upon you the Qur'an will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ [al-Qasas: 85]. Muqatil said: among it, from the Madani part, is ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ up to His saying: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ [al-Qasas: 52–55].

Ahmad, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated, and al-Suyuti said: its chain is good, from Ma'd Yakrib, who said: "We came to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and asked him to recite to us ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ of the two hundred, and he said: 'It is not with me, but upon you is to go to the one who took it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Khabbab ibn al-Aratt.' So I came to Khabbab and said: 'How did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾, or Ta-Sin?' He said: 'All of them, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it.'"

In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion of the opening of the surah has already passed in the opening of al-Shu'ara' and elsewhere, so we do not repeat it.

Likewise, the discussion of His saying: ﴿These are the verses of the clear Book﴾ has passed. The demonstrative "tilka" is a subject whose predicate is what follows it, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject; "ayat" is a substitute (badal) for the demonstrative. It is permissible that "tilka" be in the accusative position governed by "natlu" (we recite). Al-Mubin is that which contains the explanation of truth from falsehood.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Mubin" means that it distinguishes the truth from falsehood, and the lawful from the unlawful, and it is from abana, meaning "to make manifest."

﴿We recite to you from the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth for a people who believe﴾: that is, We reveal to you from their account, accompanied by truth. He specified the believers because recitation benefits only the believer.

It has been said that the object of "natlu" is omitted, and the estimate is: "We recite to you something of their news." It is permissible that "min" be extra according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, meaning: "We recite to you the news of Musa and Fir'awn." The preferable view is that it is for explanation, given the omitted object as mentioned, or for partitiveness, and there is no compelling reason to judge it extra. "Al-Haqq" means the truth.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn exalted himself in the land﴾ and what follows it is a resumptive clause, brought to explain what was summarized of the news.

The exegetes said: the meaning of "ala" is that he became arrogant and tyrannical through his authority, and "al-ard" here means the land of Egypt.

It has also been said: the meaning of "ala" is that he claimed lordship; and it has been said: he exalted himself above the worship of his Lord. ﴿And made its people into sects﴾: that is, factions and categories in his service, who support him in what he wills and obey him. The clause ﴿He oppresses a group of them﴾ is a resumptive clause, brought to explain the condition of the people whom he made into factions and categories. It is permissible that it be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "ja'ala": that is, he made them sects while a group of them was oppressed. It is also permissible that it be a qualifier of "ta'ifah" (group). The group are the Children of Israel. The clause ﴿He slaughters their sons and spares their women﴾ is a substitute for the first clause; it is also permissible that it be a resumptive explanatory clause, or a circumstantial clause, or a qualifier like the one before it, on the assumption that it is not a substitute for it. Fir'awn slaughtered their sons and left the women because the astrologers of that era had informed him that his kingdom would perish at the hands of a boy from the Children of Israel.

Al-Zajjaj said: "And how strange is the foolishness of Fir'awn: if the soothsayer who told him this was truthful in his view, then killing is of no benefit; and if he was lying, then there is no sense in killing." ﴿Indeed, he was among the corrupters﴾ in the land through sins and tyranny, and in this is a clarification that killing is the act of the people of corruption.

﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ came in the present tense to narrate a past situation and to bring its images before the mind: that is, We wished to show grace to them after their oppression. By "these" are meant the Children of Israel. The "wa" in "wa nurid" is for coordination with the clause ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn exalted himself﴾, although the coordinated clause is nominal, because there is a correspondence between them in that each of them serves as explanation and clarification. It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yastad'if," with an omitted subject: that is, "while We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land," as in the words of the poet:

"I escaped and left them as pledge, Malik..."

The first (view) is preferable. ﴿And We would make them leaders﴾: that is, guides in good and callers to it, rulers over the people, and kings among them. ﴿And We would make them the inheritors﴾ of Fir'awn's kingdom and the dwellings and possessions of the Copts, so that Fir'awn's kingdom would be theirs, they would dwell in his dwellings and the dwellings of his people, and they would benefit from his possessions and their possessions.

﴿And We would establish them in the land﴾: that is, We would make them empowered over it and over its people, given authority to dispose of it as they wished.

The majority read "numakkina" without a lam; al-A'mash read "linumakkina" with the lam of cause. ﴿And We would show Fir'awn and Haman and their hosts﴾: the majority read "nuriya" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the ra', with Allah, glorified is He, as the agent. Al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-yara" with a fath on the ya' and the ra', with Fir'awn as the agent.

The first reading is more fitting to the context, because before it are "nurid," "naj'alu," and "numakkinu," all with the nun. Al-Farra' permitted "wa-yuri Fir'awna" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ra', meaning "and Allah shows Fir'awn." The meaning of "minhum" is "from among those oppressed." ﴿That which they feared﴾: the relative pronoun is the second object in the first reading, and the first object in the second reading. The meaning: Allah shows them, or they see, that which they feared and strove to repel, namely the loss of their kingdom and their destruction at the hands of the boy from the oppressed Children of Israel.

﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa: suckle him﴾: that is, We inspired her, and cast into her heart. This was not the revelation given to the messengers. It has been said that it was a dream in her sleep; it has been said that it was by an angel whom Allah sent to inform her of it.

The scholars have agreed that she was not a prophetess. The sending of the angel to her, according to those who held it, was like the angel's speaking to the leper, the bald man and the blind man, as in the established hadith in the two Sahihs and elsewhere; and the angels greeted 'Imran ibn Husayn, as in the established hadith in the Sahih, but he was not thereby a prophet. The "an" in ﴿an arditihi﴾ is interpretive, because revelation contains the meaning of speech. It is also permissible that it be verbal (masdariyyah), meaning "that you suckle him." 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-‘Aziz read "an" with a kasra on the nun, and with the hamzah of "arditihi" connected; the kasra is due to the meeting of two quiescent letters, and the elision of the hamzah of connection is contrary to analogy.

﴿And when you fear for him﴾ from Fir'awn, that his news reaches him, ﴿then cast him into the river﴾, which is the Nile. The manner in which she cast him into the river has been explained earlier in Surat Ta-Ha. ﴿And do not fear and do not grieve﴾: that is, do not fear for him drowning or being lost, and do not grieve over his separation. ﴿We will surely return him to you﴾ soon, in a way by which he is saved. ﴿And make him one of the messengers﴾ whom We send to the servants. The "fa" in His saying ﴿So the family of Fir'awn picked him up﴾ is the explanatory fa. "Iltiqat" is coming upon a thing without seeking it. The "family of Fir'awn" are those who took the chest in which Musa was from the river. There is an omission in the speech, and the estimate is: she placed him in the river after she had put him in the chest, and so whoever found him from the family of Fir'awn picked him up. The lam in ﴿that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ is the lam of consequence: they took him in order that he might be for them a son and a comfort to the eye, not that he be an enemy; so the outcome of that was that he became for them an enemy and a grief. Since this enmity was a result of their act and its fruit, it was likened to the motive for which an agent performs an action; and from this is the saying of the poet:

"They are born for death and build for ruin."

And the saying of another:

"Every nursing mother rears for death, and our homes we build for the ruin of time."

The majority read "wa-hazanan" with a fatha on the ha' and the za'; al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read "wa-huznan" with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the za'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, and both are dialects, like "al-'adam" and "al-'udm," "al-rashad" and "al-rushd," "al-saqam" and "al-suqm." The clause ﴿Indeed, Fir'awn and Haman and their hosts were sinners﴾ is either a causal explanation of what precedes it, or an interjected clause for emphasis. The meaning of "khati'in" is: sinful, guilty in all their deeds and sayings, and it is derived from "khata'," the opposite of "sawab" (correctness). It was read "khatin" with a ya' without a hamzah; this reading may have the same meaning as the majority reading but with the hamzah dropped for lightness, or it may derive from "khata-ya yakhtu," meaning he exceeded the correct course.

﴿And the wife of Fir'awn said: "A comfort of the eye for me and for you"﴾: that is, the wife of Fir'awn said to Fir'awn. "Qurratu" is in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, as al-Kisa'i and others said. It was also said that it is the subject with the predicate ﴿Do not kill him﴾, as al-Zajjaj said, but the first is preferable.

She said this when she saw him after he reached her and she took him out of the chest, and she addressed Fir'awn and those around him of his people with her words ﴿Do not kill him﴾, or Fir'awn alone in the manner of honouring him.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "And the wife of Fir'awn said: 'Do not kill him; a comfort of the eye for me and for you.'" It is permissible to put "qurrata" in the accusative governed by "la taqtuluhu" (do not kill him) by the construction of preoccupation (ishtighal).

It has also been said that she said: "Do not kill him, for Allah has brought him from a distant land and he is not of the Children of Israel."

Then she gave a reason for what she said by hoping for benefit from him for them, or by adoption of him, so she said: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾, so that we obtain good from him, ﴿or we may take him as a son﴾. She could not bear children, so she asked Fir'awn to grant him to her, and he granted him to her. The clause ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause: that is, ﴿while they did not perceive﴾ that they were in error in picking him up, and did not perceive that their destruction would be at his hand; so it is a circumstantial clause from the family of Fir'awn, and it is part of the speech of Allah, glorified is He.

It has been said that it is part of the woman's speech, meaning: "and the Children of Israel do not know that we picked him up, ﴿and they do not perceive﴾." This was said by al-Kalbi, and it is very far-fetched.

Al-Farra' related from al-Suddi, from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿Do not kill him﴾ is part of Fir'awn's speech, and he raised an objection to it with a statement that refers to the wording. Its weakness of chain suffices in refuting it.

﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾. The exegetes said: the meaning of that is that she was empty of everything except the matter of Musa, as though she cared for nothing other than him.

Abu 'Ubayda said: empty of the mention of everything in the world except the mention of Musa. Al-Hasan, Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd said: empty of what had been revealed to her, His saying ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve﴾, because of what Satan had suggested to her about his drowning and destruction.

Al-Akhfash said: empty of fear and sorrow, since she knew that he had not drowned, by reason of the revelation previously given to her. The same was related from Abu 'Ubayda also.

Al-Kisa'i said: forgetful, dazed. Al-'Ala' ibn Ziyad said: fleeing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: bewildered, she almost said "O my son!" from the intensity of her anguish.

Muqatil said: she almost cried out out of compassion for him from drowning.

It has been said that the meaning is: when she heard of his falling into the hand of Fir'awn, her reason flew away from the excess of her anguish and bewilderment.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 13 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Nahhas said: The most sound of these opinions is the first, and those who held it have greater knowledge of the Book of Allah. If her heart was empty of everything except the remembrance of Musa, then it was empty of revelation. The view of the one who said "empty of grief" is a gross error, because what follows is ﴿Had We not strengthened her heart, she would have almost revealed it.﴾ Fadala ibn Ubayd al-Ansari, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa', Abu al-Aliya and Ibn Muhaysin recited *fazi'an* (فَزِعًا) with the *fa'*, *zay* and unpointed *ayn*, from *al-faza'* (fear), meaning frightened and anxious.

Ibn Abbas recited *qari'an* (قَرِعًا) with an open *qaf*, a kasra on the unpointed *ra'*, and an unpointed *ayn*, from *qari'a ra'suhu*, meaning when his hair had receded. The meaning of *wa-asbaha* (وأصْبَحَ) here is "and became," as the poet said:

*Gone are the caliphs in a rightly guided matter,*
*and Medina has become the (domain) of al-Walid.*

﴿Had We not strengthened her heart, she would have almost revealed it.﴾ Here *an* (أنْ) is the lightened form of the heavy *inna*, and its noun is a deleted *dhamir al-sha'n* (pronoun of the matter, a dummy pronoun). The meaning is: indeed she almost revealed the matter of Musa and that he was her son, because of the extreme alarm, fear and grief that overwhelmed her. From *badā yabdū* means "to appear," and *abdā yubdī* means "to make appear." It was also said that the pronoun in *bihi* refers to the revelation that had been sent to her, but the first view is preferable.

Al-Farra' said: "Indeed she almost would have revealed it by his name, due to the tightness of her chest, had We not strengthened her heart."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of "strengthening the heart" is inspiring patience and reinforcing it. The answer to *law la* (لَوْلا, "had it not been") is deleted, meaning: had We not strengthened her heart, she would have revealed it. The *lam* in ﴿so that she might be among the believers﴾ is connected to *rabatna* (We strengthened). The meaning is: We strengthened her heart so that she would be among those who affirm the promise of Allah, which is His saying ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you.﴾ It was said that the *ba'* in ﴿she would have revealed it﴾ is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: she would have revealed it, as you say, "I took the rope with the rope." It was also said that the meaning is: she would have revealed the speech about him.

﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him."﴾ That is, the mother of Musa said to the sister of Musa, who was Maryam: "Follow him," meaning: trace his trail, learn his news, and watch where he has gone and to whom he has come. It is said: *qasastu al-shay'* (I followed the thing), when you follow its trail to learn its condition.

﴿So she watched him from afar﴾ means she saw him from a distance. Its origin is "from a place at a side," and from it comes *al-ajnabi* (the stranger). The poet said:

*So do not deprive me of a gift from afar,*
*for I am a man, a stranger amid the dwellings.*

It was also said that the meaning of ﴿from afar﴾ is "from the side," so the meaning is that she looked at him sidelong, furtively. This is supported by the recitation of al-Nu'man ibn Salim, "*'an jani*b" (from the side). The place of *'an janbin* (عَنْ جَنْبٍ) is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative), either from the subject, meaning she watched him while hidden, being from the side, or from the object, meaning distant from her.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *basurat* (بَصُرَتْ) with an open *ba'* and a damma on the *sad*. Qatada read it with an open *sad*, and Isa ibn Umar read it with a kasra on it. Al-Mubarrad said: *absarathu* and *basurat bihi* have the same meaning. The majority read *'an junubin* (عَنْ جُنُبٍ) with two dammas. Qatada, al-Hasan, al-A'raj and Zayd ibn Ali read it with an open *jim* and a sukun on the *nun*. It is also reported from Qatada that he read it with both open, and it is reported from al-Hasan that he read it with a damma on the *jim* and a sukun on the *nun*. Abu Amr ibn al-Ala' said: the meaning of ﴿from the side﴾ is "out of longing," and he said: this is the dialect of Juzam, who say *jannabtu ilayka*, meaning "I longed for you."

﴿And they did not perceive﴾ that she was following him, tracing his news, and that she was his sister.

﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾. *Al-maradi'* (المَراضِعُ) is the plural of *murdi'* (a nursing woman), meaning We prevented him from suckling from the nursing women. It was also said that *al-maradi'* is the plural of *marda'* with an open *dad*, which means the act of suckling or its place, namely the breast. The meaning of ﴿before﴾ is: before We returned him to his mother, or before his mother came to him, or before she followed his trail. The wife of Pharaoh had sought wet-nurses for Musa so that they might nurse him, but he would not suckle from any of them. At that point, when she saw his refusal to suckle, his sister said ﴿Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you?﴾ meaning: who will guarantee to you that they will care for him and nurse him, ﴿and they will be sincere toward him﴾, meaning: they will be compassionate toward him and will not fall short in nursing and raising him.

There is an omission in the speech, and the implied meaning is: they said to her, "Who are they?" She said, "My mother." It was then said to her, "Does your mother have milk?" She said, "Yes, the milk of my brother Harun." So she guided them to the mother of Musa, and they handed him to her, and he accepted her breast and suckled from it.

That is the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So We returned him to his mother that her eye might be cooled﴾ by her child, ﴿and that she would not grieve﴾ over his separation, ﴿and that she might know that the promise of Allah﴾ meaning all of His promise, of which is what He promised her by His saying ﴿Indeed, We will return him to you﴾, which is a truth without any breach, certain to occur without doubt. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, meaning most of the people of Pharaoh did not know of this, rather they were heedless of the decree and the secret of the divine decree. Or most people do not know this, or do not know that Allah promised her that He would return him to her.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding ﴿and made its people into factions﴾ that he said: He divided them.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Qatada regarding ﴿and made its people into factions﴾ that he said: He enslaves a group of them and leaves a group, kills a group and spares a group.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding His saying ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land and to make them leaders﴾ that he said: they are Yusuf and his descendants. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ that he said: they are the Children of Israel. ﴿And make them leaders﴾, meaning rulers of affairs. ﴿And make them the inheritors﴾, meaning those who inherit the land after Pharaoh and his people. ﴿And show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts from them what they were fearing﴾. He said: what the people had feared.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Musa﴾ that it means: We inspired her to do what she did with Musa.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-A'mash who said: Ibn Abbas said regarding His saying ﴿And if you fear for him﴾: that the neighbours would hear his voice.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud regarding His saying ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾ that he said: it became empty of remembering everything of worldly matters except the remembrance of Musa.

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported through several chains from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾ that he said: empty of everything except the remembrance of Musa.

Regarding His saying ﴿Had she almost revealed it﴾ he said: she would say, "O my son!"

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from him regarding His saying ﴿And she said to his sister, "Follow him"﴾, that is, follow his trail, ﴿so she watched him from afar﴾, he said: from the side.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Asakir reported from Abu Umama that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Khadija: "Did you not perceive that Allah married me to Maryam bint Imran, Kulthum the sister of Musa, and the wife of Pharaoh?" She said: "Congratulations to you, Messenger of Allah."

Ibn Asakir reported it from Ibn Abi Rawwad as a raised (marfu') report, longer than this, and at its end it says that she said: "With ease and sons."

Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses before﴾ that he said: a nursing woman would not be brought to him, and he would accept her.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 14–24 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And when he reached his maturity (ashudd)﴾ The discussion of reaching maturity (bulugh al-ashudd) was already given in surah al-An'am. Rabi'ah and Malik said: it is the age of puberty (al-hulum), based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them maturity (rushd)﴾ [an-Nisa': 6], and its upper limit is thirty-four years, as Mujahid, Sufyan al-Thawri and others said.

It was also said: al-ashudd is between eighteen and thirty years, and al-istiwa' (full maturity) is from thirty to forty. It was said: al-istiwa' is reaching forty. It was said: al-istiwa' is an indication of the completion of physical form. It was said: the two mean one thing, but this is weak, because the conjunction (al-'atf) implies difference.

﴿We gave him judgement (hukm) and knowledge (ilm)﴾ Hukm here means wisdom in general. It was said: it means prophethood. It was said: it means understanding of the religion (al-fiqh fi al-din). Ilm means understanding, as said by al-Suddi. Mujahid said: it means fiqh. Ibn Ishaq said: it means knowledge of his religion and the religion of his forefathers. It was said: this was before prophethood. The explanation of this meaning has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ That is: like that reward with which We rewarded the mother of Musa when she submitted to God's command, cast her child into the sea, and believed in God's promise. "We reward the good-doers" for their good deeds, and the intended meaning is general.

﴿And he entered the city﴾ That is, Musa entered the great city of Egypt. It was said: it was another city among the cities of Egypt. The position of His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), either from the subject, meaning: while concealing himself, or from the object.
