﴿Musa said to him: Indeed, you are clearly a person of error (laghiyy mubin)﴾ That is: clearly in error, because you fight one whom you cannot contend with and cannot withstand. It was said: he said this to him only because he had caused the killing of a man the previous day, and now he wanted to cause the killing of another.

﴿Then when he wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾ That is: to seize the Copt who was an enemy of Musa and of the Israelite, since he was not of their religion. The meaning of "yabtishu" and the variation of the readers concerning it has already been mentioned.

﴿He said: O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ The speaker was the Israelite. When he heard Musa say to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly in error﴾ and saw him wanting to seize the Copt, he thought he wanted to seize him, so he said to Musa: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ When the Copt heard that, he disclosed it. None of Pharaoh's companions had known that Musa was the one who had killed the Copt the previous day, until the Israelite exposed him. This is what the majority of the exegetes said.

It was said: the speaker of "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" was the Copt, who had learned the news from the Israelite. This is the apparent meaning, and the Copt was mentioned just before this without interruption, because he is the one meant by "an enemy to both of them." There is no reason to contradict the apparent meaning, so as to imply that the one who sought his help the first time, and the one who exposed him the second time, were the same person. Also, His saying: ﴿You intend only to be a tyrant in the land﴾ is not befitting to come from anyone but a disbeliever, and the "in" of "you intend" is negation, meaning: you intend only to be a tyrant in the land.

Al-Zajjaj said: the tyrant (jabbar) in the language is one who does not humble himself before the command of God, and one who kills without right is a tyrant.

It was said: the tyrant is one who does whatever he wills of striking and killing, does not consider consequences, and does not repel with what is better.

﴿And you do not intend to be of the reformers (muslihin)﴾ That is: those who make peace among people.

﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾ It was said: the intended man is Hizqil, the believer of Pharaoh's family, who was a cousin of Musa. It was said: his name was Sham'un, and it was said: Talut, and it was said: Sham'an.

"The farthest part of the city" means its end and its most distant part. "Yas'a" may be in the nominative position as a qualifier of "rajul", and it may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, because although the word "rajul" is indefinite, it has been specified by His saying ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾.

﴿He said: O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ That is: they are consulting about killing you and plotting because of you.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them are urging others to kill you.

Abu 'Ubayd said: they consult about you to kill you, meaning the notables of Pharaoh's people.

Al-Azhari said: "ta'amara al-qawm" and "ta'amaru" mean that they urged one another. A parallel is His saying ﴿and consult among yourselves in kindness﴾ [at-Talaq: 6]. An-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"I see that people have invented a custom, and in every new event they consult."

﴿So leave; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers﴾ regarding the command to leave. The lam is for specification (li'l-bayan), because the complement of the preposition does not precede it.

﴿So he left it, fearful and watchful﴾ So Musa went out of the city, while fearful of the wrongdoers and awaiting their pursuit and overtaking of him. Then he called upon his Lord to save him from what he feared, saying: ﴿My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people﴾ That is: rescue me from the disbelieving people, repel them from me, and come between me and them.

﴿And when he turned toward Madyan (tilqa' Madyan)﴾ That is: toward Madyan, intending to reach it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, he took the road which faces Madyan and goes to it. It is said: "his house is opposite (tilqa') the house of so-and-so," and its root is from "liqa'" (meeting). This town was not under Pharaoh's authority, and for this reason he went out to it. ﴿He said: Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way (sawa' al-sabil)﴾ That is: will guide me toward the level road to Madyan.

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ That is: reached it, and it is the water from which they draw. ﴿He found upon it a community of people watering (yasqun)﴾ That is: he found at the water a large group of people watering their livestock. The term "wurud" is sometimes applied to entering the watering place, and sometimes to reaching it without entering. The latter is what is meant here, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So when we reached the water, its waves blue..."

Al-Shawkani's commentary on surah 28, verses 14–24 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of *al-wurud* (coming to a water source) has already been verified in His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71]. It was said that Madyan is the name of a tribe, and it is not declined (*ghayr munsarifah*) under either interpretation. ﴿And he found, besides them﴾, that is, besides the people who were watering their animals, between them and the direction from which he had come. It was also said that the meaning is: at a place lower than them. ﴿Two women driving back﴾, that is, holding back their sheep from the water until the people finish and the water is clear for them. The meaning of *al-dawd* is pushing away and holding back. From it is the poet's saying:

*I spend the night at the door of the rhymes, as if I were driving away from them a herd of wild beasts, scattered*

That is: I hold back and prevent. *Al-dawd* also occurs with the meaning of driving away. From it is the poet's saying:

*The Banu Tamim have seized your staff, so you no longer know with which staff you drive away*

That is: you drive away. ﴿He said: What is your business?﴾ That is, Musa said to the two women: What is your situation, that you do not water your flock with the people? *Al-khatb* means matter or affair. It was said: "What is your *khatb*?" is said to one who is afflicted, or oppressed, or to one who commits something objectionable.

﴿They said: We cannot water until the shepherds take their flocks away.﴾ That is: our custom is to wait until the people have left the water and departed from it, out of caution against mixing with them, or out of inability to water alongside them.

The majority (*al-jumhur*) read *yusdiru* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *dal*, the present tense of *asdara*, which is transitive with the *hamza*. On this reading the object is elided, meaning: they return their livestock. Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *dal*, from *sadara yasduru*, which is intransitive. *Al-ri'a'* is the plural of *ra'in* (shepherd).

The majority read *al-ri'a'* with a *kasra* on the *ra'*. Abu 'Amr, in one transmission from him, read it with a *fatha*. Abu al-Fadl said: it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of an adjective, which is why the singular and plural are the same in it. *Al-ru'a'* with a *damma* was also read, as a collective noun (*ism jam'*).

Talhah ibn Musarrif read *nusqi* with a *damma* on the *nun*, from *asqa*.

﴿And our father is a very old man.﴾ He is advanced in years. This is part of their speech: that is, he cannot water his flock because of his old age, so we have been compelled, though we are two weak women, to water the sheep, since there is no man to do this for us. When Musa heard their speech, he watered for them out of mercy toward them, that is, he watered their sheep for their sake. Then, when he had finished watering for them, ﴿he turned back to the shade﴾, that is, he withdrew toward it and sat in it. It was said: this shade was the shade of a *samurah* tree there.

Then, when hardship and fatigue had befallen him, he called out to his Lord: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, whatever good it was. ﴿Faqir﴾ means in need of that. It was said he meant food. The *lam* in ﴿li-ma anzalta﴾ carries the sense of *ila* (toward).

Al-Akhfash said: it is said, "he is *faqir* to him and to it."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Mahamili in his *Amali* related, through Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And when he reached his maturity﴾, that he said: thirty-three years. ﴿And attained full strength﴾, he said: forty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related in *Kitab al-Mu'ammarin*, through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from him, that he said: *al-ashudd* is the period between eighteen and thirty years, and *al-istiwa'* is the period between thirty and forty. When one exceeds forty, he begins to decline.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through several chains from him also, regarding His saying ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾, that he said: midday.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from him also regarding the verse, that he said: between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also ﴿This one is of his faction﴾, that he said: an Israelite. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾, he said: a Copt. ﴿The one from his faction sought his help against the one from his enemy﴾, the Israelite against the Copt, ﴿so Musa struck him and finished him off﴾, he said: so he died. He said: this weighed heavily upon Musa.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying ﴿Behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help﴾ [p. 1098], that he said: he is the companion of Musa who had sought his help the day before.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah, who said: the one who sought his help is the one who cried out to him for help.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Sha'bi, who said: whoever kills two men is a tyrant (*jabbar*). Then he recited this verse: ﴿You want only to be a tyrant in the land﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah, who said: a man is not a tyrant until he kills two souls.

al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Musa went out fearful, watchful, hungry, with no provision, until he reached the water of Madyan. ﴿Upon it he found a group of people watering﴾, and two women sitting with their sheep. He asked them: ﴿What is your business?﴾ They said: ﴿We cannot water until the shepherds take their flocks away, and our father is a very old man.﴾ He said: Is there water near you? They said: No, except a well over which there is a rock that has been placed on it, which a company of men cannot lift. He said: Go and show it to me. So they went with him, and he pushed the rock with his hand and moved it aside. Then he drew a single bucket for them, and watered the sheep. Then he returned the rock to its place. ﴿Then he turned back to the shade and said: My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾. They heard him. He said: So they returned to their father, who was surprised at how quickly they had come. He asked them and they told him. He said to one of them: Go and call him. She came and said: ﴿Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for watering [the flocks] for us﴾. She walked ahead of him, and he said to her: Walk behind me, for I am a man of the lineage of Ibrahim; it is not lawful for me to look at what God has forbidden me, and guide me on the way. ﴿When he came to him and related to him the narrative, he said: Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾. ﴿One of them said: O father, hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾.

Her father said to her: What did you see of his strength and trustworthiness? She told him the matter that had happened. She said: As for his strength, he lifted the rock alone, when only a company of men could lift it. As for his trustworthiness, he said to me: Walk behind me and guide me on the way; for I am a man of the lineage of Ibrahim, and it is not lawful for me to have from you what God has forbidden.

It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil? He said: the more righteous and the more complete of them.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: When Musa came to the water of Madyan, he found upon it a group of people watering. When they had finished, they replaced the rock over the well, and no one could lift it except ten men. Then he found two women. He said: What is your business? They told him. So he went to the rock, lifted it alone, then drew water, and drew only one bucket until the sheep were satisfied. The two women returned to their father and told him. Musa turned back to the shade and said: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾.

He said: ﴿Then one of them came to him walking shyly﴾ [al-Qasas: 25], placing her garment over her face, not a bold woman, going out and coming in. ﴿She said: Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for watering [the flocks] for us﴾. So Musa rose and went with her. He said to her: Walk behind me and direct me on the way, for I dislike that the wind should strike your garments and reveal your body to me. When he reached her father, he related the story to him. One of the two said: O father, hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy. He said: My daughter, what is your knowledge of his trustworthiness and strength? She said: As for his strength, his lifting the rock, which only ten men could lift. As for his trustworthiness, he said to me: Walk behind me and direct me on the way, for I dislike that the wind should strike your garments and reveal your body to me. This increased his desire for him.

He said: ﴿I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾, up to His saying ﴿you will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas: 27], that is: in good companionship and in fulfilling what I have said. He said: Musa said: ﴿That is between me and you; whichever term I fulfil, there shall be no injustice against me﴾ [al-Qasas: 28]. He said: Yes. He said: ﴿God is a witness over what we say﴾ [al-Qasas: 28]. So he married him to her, and he stayed with him, serving him and working in the tending of his flock and whatever else he needed. He married him to Safura and her sister Sharfa, and they were the two who used to drive back their flocks.

Ibn Kathir said, after citing several chains for this hadith: its chain is sound (*sahih*).

*Al-salfa'* among women is the bold and sharp-tongued one.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, that he said: he arrived at the water where it was, and the greenness of the herbs could be seen in his belly from emaciation.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, who said: Musa left Egypt for Madyan, between him and it being eight nights, and he had no food except the leaves of trees, and he left barefoot, so that by the time he reached it, the soles of his feet had worn away.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, who said: ﴿Driving back﴾ means holding back their sheep until the people have finished and the well is clear for them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* related from him also, who said: Musa said: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, and he was the most honoured of His creation before Him. He was in need of half a date, and his belly clung to his back from the severity of hunger.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, who said: He asked only for food.

'Abdullah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, who said: He asked for pieces of bread with which he might hold up his back from hunger.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 14–24 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And when he reached his maturity (ashudd)﴾ The discussion of reaching maturity (bulugh al-ashudd) was already given in surah al-An'am. Rabi'ah and Malik said: it is the age of puberty (al-hulum), based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach marriageable age, if you perceive in them maturity (rushd)﴾ [an-Nisa': 6], and its upper limit is thirty-four years, as Mujahid, Sufyan al-Thawri and others said.

It was also said: al-ashudd is between eighteen and thirty years, and al-istiwa' (full maturity) is from thirty to forty. It was said: al-istiwa' is reaching forty. It was said: al-istiwa' is an indication of the completion of physical form. It was said: the two mean one thing, but this is weak, because the conjunction (al-'atf) implies difference.

﴿We gave him judgement (hukm) and knowledge (ilm)﴾ Hukm here means wisdom in general. It was said: it means prophethood. It was said: it means understanding of the religion (al-fiqh fi al-din). Ilm means understanding, as said by al-Suddi. Mujahid said: it means fiqh. Ibn Ishaq said: it means knowledge of his religion and the religion of his forefathers. It was said: this was before prophethood. The explanation of this meaning has already been given in al-Baqarah.

﴿Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾ That is: like that reward with which We rewarded the mother of Musa when she submitted to God's command, cast her child into the sea, and believed in God's promise. "We reward the good-doers" for their good deeds, and the intended meaning is general.

﴿And he entered the city﴾ That is, Musa entered the great city of Egypt. It was said: it was another city among the cities of Egypt. The position of His saying ﴿at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾ is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), either from the subject, meaning: while concealing himself, or from the object.

It was said: when Musa recognised the truth in his religion, he criticised what the people of Pharaoh were upon, and this spread from him, so they threatened him and he feared them. Thus he did not enter the city except secretly.

It was said: his entry was between the evening (al-'isha') and the late night ('atamah). It was said: it was at the time of midday rest (al-qa'ilah).

Al-Dahhak said: he sought to enter the city at the time of its people's heedlessness, but he entered when they had knowledge of him. So there happened what God related in His saying: ﴿and he found therein two men fighting, one of his party (shi'ah) and the other of his enemy﴾ That is: one of those who supported him in his religion, and they were the Children of Israel. ﴿And this one was of his enemy﴾ That is: of those who were hostile to him in his religion, and they were the people of Pharaoh. ﴿So the one of his party sought his help against the one of his enemy﴾ That is: he asked him to help him and aid him against his opponent. ﴿So Musa helped him, because helping the oppressed is obligatory in all religious communities.

It was said: the Copt wanted to conscript the Israelite to carry firewood for Pharaoh's kitchen, so he refused and sought help from Musa. ﴿Then Musa struck him (fawakazahu)﴾ (p-1096) al-wakz means striking with the joined palm; likewise al-lakz and al-lahz. It was said: al-lakz is on the jaw, and al-wakz is on the heart. It was said: he struck him with his staff.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "falakazahu" (فلكزه), and al-Tha'labi related that in the codex of Uthman it was "fanakazahu" (فنكزه) with a nun.

Al-Asma'i said: nakazahu with a nun means he struck him and pushed him.

Al-Jawhari said: al-lakz is striking on the chest.

Abu Zayd said: it is on the whole body, meaning that it is said of it "lakz". Al-lahz is striking with both hands on the chest, and similarly from Abu 'Ubaydah.

﴿And he finished him off (faqada 'alayhi)﴾ That is: he killed him. Whatever you reach and finish, you have "qadayta 'alayhi" (finished him), and from this is the poet's saying:

"He bit him, and the bravest one finished him off."

It was said: Musa did not intend to kill the Copt; he only intended to repel him, but it resulted in his death. This is why he said: ﴿This is of the work of Satan﴾. He said this although the slain was a disbeliever deserving of killing, because at that time he had not been commanded to kill the unbelievers.

It was also said: that situation was one of restraint from fighting, since he was secure among them, so it was not permitted for him to ambush them.

Then he described Satan with His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is a clear, misleading enemy﴾ That is: an enemy to mankind who strives to mislead them, manifestly hostile and misleading.

It was said: the indication in His saying "this" refers to the deed of the slain man, because he was a disbeliever opposing what God wills.

It was said: it refers to the slain man himself, meaning that he was of the soldiers of Satan and his party.

Then he asked God, glorified is He, to forgive him what had occurred from him.

﴿He said: My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ So God forgave him that. ﴿Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ The aspect of his seeking forgiveness is that it was not permitted for a prophet to kill until he is commanded. It was said: he sought forgiveness for leaving what is better (tark al-awla), as is the practice of the messengers; or he meant: I have wronged myself by killing this disbeliever, because if Pharaoh knew of it he would have killed me for it. The meaning of ﴿so forgive me﴾ is: conceal this from me, do not let Pharaoh know of it. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, for Musa, peace be upon him, remained regretful for that and fearful of punishment because of it, to the extent that on the Day of Resurrection, when people ask him for intercession, he says: "I killed a soul which I was not commanded to kill," as is established in the authentic hadith of intercession.

It has been said that this was before prophethood. It was also said that it occurred before he reached the age of legal responsibility, and that he was then twelve years old. All these remote interpretations uphold what is established regarding the infallibility of prophets. There is no doubt that they are protected from major sins, and the killing that occurred from him was not intentional, so it is not a major sin, since a single blow usually does not kill.

Then, when God answered his request and forgave him what he asked forgiveness for:

﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾ This preposition (ba') may be the oath particle, with the answer omitted, meaning: I swear by Your bestowal upon me that I will repent, and the clause ﴿so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ serves as an explanation of the answer, as if he swore by what God bestowed on him that he would not support a criminal.

It may also be the causal ba', attached to an omitted element, meaning: protect me because of what You have bestowed upon me. Then His saying ﴿so I will never be a supporter﴾ is consequent upon it, and in this there is an appeal to God, exalted is He, and a means of seeking further favour through His favour. And what is in His saying ﴿by what You have bestowed﴾ is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-infinitive (masdariyyah). The intended bestowal is either what He gave him of judgement and knowledge, or forgiveness, or all of these. By supporting the criminals he meant either companionship with Pharaoh and being counted among his entourage in outward appearance, or supporting him in what is sinful.

Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: His saying ﴿so I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ is not a report but a supplication, meaning: "So do not make me, O Lord, a supporter for them."

Al-Kisa'i said: in the recitation of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) it is "So do not make me, O Lord, a supporter for the criminals." Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "O God, so I will never be a supporter of the criminals."

Al-Nahhas said: taking it as a report is more complete and more fitting to the flow of the discourse.

﴿So he became in the city, fearful and watchful (khaifan yataraqqabu)﴾ That is: he entered the city at morning time, the city in which he had killed the Copt. "Fearful" is the predicate of "asbaha" and it may be a circumstantial clause, with the predicate being "in the city". "Yataraqqabu" may be a second predicate, or a second circumstantial clause, or a substitute for "fearful". The object of "yataraqqabu" is omitted, and the meaning is: he watches for what is disliked, or he watches for what is pleasing.

﴿Then suddenly the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him (yastasrikhuhu)﴾ "Idha" here is the sudden (fuja'iyyah) particle, the relative pronoun is the subject, and its predicate is "yastasrikhuhu", meaning: suddenly his companion, the Israelite who had sought his help the previous day, was fighting another Copt whom he wanted to conscript and oppress, just as the Copt whom Musa had killed the previous day had wanted to. "Istisrakh" means seeking help, and it derives from "sarakh" (shout), because the one seeking help raises his voice and cries out to request aid. From this is the poet's saying:

"Whenever a frightened crier came to us, the answer to him was the striking of the bellies (of the horses)."

﴿Musa said to him: Indeed, you are clearly a person of error (laghiyy mubin)﴾ That is: clearly in error, because you fight one whom you cannot contend with and cannot withstand. It was said: he said this to him only because he had caused the killing of a man the previous day, and now he wanted to cause the killing of another.

﴿Then when he wanted to seize the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾ That is: to seize the Copt who was an enemy of Musa and of the Israelite, since he was not of their religion. The meaning of "yabtishu" and the variation of the readers concerning it has already been mentioned.

﴿He said: O Musa, do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ The speaker was the Israelite. When he heard Musa say to him: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly in error﴾ and saw him wanting to seize the Copt, he thought he wanted to seize him, so he said to Musa: ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?﴾ When the Copt heard that, he disclosed it. None of Pharaoh's companions had known that Musa was the one who had killed the Copt the previous day, until the Israelite exposed him. This is what the majority of the exegetes said.

It was said: the speaker of "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a soul yesterday?" was the Copt, who had learned the news from the Israelite. This is the apparent meaning, and the Copt was mentioned just before this without interruption, because he is the one meant by "an enemy to both of them." There is no reason to contradict the apparent meaning, so as to imply that the one who sought his help the first time, and the one who exposed him the second time, were the same person. Also, His saying: ﴿You intend only to be a tyrant in the land﴾ is not befitting to come from anyone but a disbeliever, and the "in" of "you intend" is negation, meaning: you intend only to be a tyrant in the land.

Al-Zajjaj said: the tyrant (jabbar) in the language is one who does not humble himself before the command of God, and one who kills without right is a tyrant.

It was said: the tyrant is one who does whatever he wills of striking and killing, does not consider consequences, and does not repel with what is better.

﴿And you do not intend to be of the reformers (muslihin)﴾ That is: those who make peace among people.

﴿And there came a man from the farthest part of the city, running﴾ It was said: the intended man is Hizqil, the believer of Pharaoh's family, who was a cousin of Musa. It was said: his name was Sham'un, and it was said: Talut, and it was said: Sham'an.

"The farthest part of the city" means its end and its most distant part. "Yas'a" may be in the nominative position as a qualifier of "rajul", and it may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, because although the word "rajul" is indefinite, it has been specified by His saying ﴿from the farthest part of the city﴾.

﴿He said: O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you﴾ That is: they are consulting about killing you and plotting because of you.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them are urging others to kill you.

Abu 'Ubayd said: they consult about you to kill you, meaning the notables of Pharaoh's people.

Al-Azhari said: "ta'amara al-qawm" and "ta'amaru" mean that they urged one another. A parallel is His saying ﴿and consult among yourselves in kindness﴾ [at-Talaq: 6]. An-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"I see that people have invented a custom, and in every new event they consult."

﴿So leave; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers﴾ regarding the command to leave. The lam is for specification (li'l-bayan), because the complement of the preposition does not precede it.

﴿So he left it, fearful and watchful﴾ So Musa went out of the city, while fearful of the wrongdoers and awaiting their pursuit and overtaking of him. Then he called upon his Lord to save him from what he feared, saying: ﴿My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people﴾ That is: rescue me from the disbelieving people, repel them from me, and come between me and them.

﴿And when he turned toward Madyan (tilqa' Madyan)﴾ That is: toward Madyan, intending to reach it.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, he took the road which faces Madyan and goes to it. It is said: "his house is opposite (tilqa') the house of so-and-so," and its root is from "liqa'" (meeting). This town was not under Pharaoh's authority, and for this reason he went out to it. ﴿He said: Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way (sawa' al-sabil)﴾ That is: will guide me toward the level road to Madyan.

﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ That is: reached it, and it is the water from which they draw. ﴿He found upon it a community of people watering (yasqun)﴾ That is: he found at the water a large group of people watering their livestock. The term "wurud" is sometimes applied to entering the watering place, and sometimes to reaching it without entering. The latter is what is meant here, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"So when we reached the water, its waves blue..."

Al-Shawkani's commentary on surah 28, verses 14–24 (part 2 of 2):

The meaning of *al-wurud* (coming to a water source) has already been verified in His saying: ﴿And there is none of you but will come to it﴾ [Maryam: 71]. It was said that Madyan is the name of a tribe, and it is not declined (*ghayr munsarifah*) under either interpretation. ﴿And he found, besides them﴾, that is, besides the people who were watering their animals, between them and the direction from which he had come. It was also said that the meaning is: at a place lower than them. ﴿Two women driving back﴾, that is, holding back their sheep from the water until the people finish and the water is clear for them. The meaning of *al-dawd* is pushing away and holding back. From it is the poet's saying:

*I spend the night at the door of the rhymes, as if I were driving away from them a herd of wild beasts, scattered*

That is: I hold back and prevent. *Al-dawd* also occurs with the meaning of driving away. From it is the poet's saying:

*The Banu Tamim have seized your staff, so you no longer know with which staff you drive away*

That is: you drive away. ﴿He said: What is your business?﴾ That is, Musa said to the two women: What is your situation, that you do not water your flock with the people? *Al-khatb* means matter or affair. It was said: "What is your *khatb*?" is said to one who is afflicted, or oppressed, or to one who commits something objectionable.

﴿They said: We cannot water until the shepherds take their flocks away.﴾ That is: our custom is to wait until the people have left the water and departed from it, out of caution against mixing with them, or out of inability to water alongside them.

The majority (*al-jumhur*) read *yusdiru* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *dal*, the present tense of *asdara*, which is transitive with the *hamza*. On this reading the object is elided, meaning: they return their livestock. Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read it with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *dal*, from *sadara yasduru*, which is intransitive. *Al-ri'a'* is the plural of *ra'in* (shepherd).

The majority read *al-ri'a'* with a *kasra* on the *ra'*. Abu 'Amr, in one transmission from him, read it with a *fatha*. Abu al-Fadl said: it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) placed in the position of an adjective, which is why the singular and plural are the same in it. *Al-ru'a'* with a *damma* was also read, as a collective noun (*ism jam'*).

Talhah ibn Musarrif read *nusqi* with a *damma* on the *nun*, from *asqa*.

﴿And our father is a very old man.﴾ He is advanced in years. This is part of their speech: that is, he cannot water his flock because of his old age, so we have been compelled, though we are two weak women, to water the sheep, since there is no man to do this for us. When Musa heard their speech, he watered for them out of mercy toward them, that is, he watered their sheep for their sake. Then, when he had finished watering for them, ﴿he turned back to the shade﴾, that is, he withdrew toward it and sat in it. It was said: this shade was the shade of a *samurah* tree there.

Then, when hardship and fatigue had befallen him, he called out to his Lord: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, whatever good it was. ﴿Faqir﴾ means in need of that. It was said he meant food. The *lam* in ﴿li-ma anzalta﴾ carries the sense of *ila* (toward).

Al-Akhfash said: it is said, "he is *faqir* to him and to it."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh and al-Mahamili in his *Amali* related, through Mujahid from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And when he reached his maturity﴾, that he said: thirty-three years. ﴿And attained full strength﴾, he said: forty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related in *Kitab al-Mu'ammarin*, through al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from him, that he said: *al-ashudd* is the period between eighteen and thirty years, and *al-istiwa'* is the period between thirty and forty. When one exceeds forty, he begins to decline.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through several chains from him also, regarding His saying ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾, that he said: midday.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, through Ibn Jurayj from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, from him also regarding the verse, that he said: between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also ﴿This one is of his faction﴾, that he said: an Israelite. ﴿And this one is of his enemy﴾, he said: a Copt. ﴿The one from his faction sought his help against the one from his enemy﴾, the Israelite against the Copt, ﴿so Musa struck him and finished him off﴾, he said: so he died. He said: this weighed heavily upon Musa.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying ﴿Behold, the one who had sought his help the day before was crying out to him for help﴾ [p. 1098], that he said: he is the companion of Musa who had sought his help the day before.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah, who said: the one who sought his help is the one who cried out to him for help.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Sha'bi, who said: whoever kills two men is a tyrant (*jabbar*). Then he recited this verse: ﴿You want only to be a tyrant in the land﴾.

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Ikrimah, who said: a man is not a tyrant until he kills two souls.

al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Musa went out fearful, watchful, hungry, with no provision, until he reached the water of Madyan. ﴿Upon it he found a group of people watering﴾, and two women sitting with their sheep. He asked them: ﴿What is your business?﴾ They said: ﴿We cannot water until the shepherds take their flocks away, and our father is a very old man.﴾ He said: Is there water near you? They said: No, except a well over which there is a rock that has been placed on it, which a company of men cannot lift. He said: Go and show it to me. So they went with him, and he pushed the rock with his hand and moved it aside. Then he drew a single bucket for them, and watered the sheep. Then he returned the rock to its place. ﴿Then he turned back to the shade and said: My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾. They heard him. He said: So they returned to their father, who was surprised at how quickly they had come. He asked them and they told him. He said to one of them: Go and call him. She came and said: ﴿Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for watering [the flocks] for us﴾. She walked ahead of him, and he said to her: Walk behind me, for I am a man of the lineage of Ibrahim; it is not lawful for me to look at what God has forbidden me, and guide me on the way. ﴿When he came to him and related to him the narrative, he said: Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾. ﴿One of them said: O father, hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy﴾.

Her father said to her: What did you see of his strength and trustworthiness? She told him the matter that had happened. She said: As for his strength, he lifted the rock alone, when only a company of men could lift it. As for his trustworthiness, he said to me: Walk behind me and guide me on the way; for I am a man of the lineage of Ibrahim, and it is not lawful for me to have from you what God has forbidden.

It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: Which of the two terms did Musa fulfil? He said: the more righteous and the more complete of them.

al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah in *al-Musannaf*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who declared it authentic, related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: When Musa came to the water of Madyan, he found upon it a group of people watering. When they had finished, they replaced the rock over the well, and no one could lift it except ten men. Then he found two women. He said: What is your business? They told him. So he went to the rock, lifted it alone, then drew water, and drew only one bucket until the sheep were satisfied. The two women returned to their father and told him. Musa turned back to the shade and said: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾.

He said: ﴿Then one of them came to him walking shyly﴾ [al-Qasas: 25], placing her garment over her face, not a bold woman, going out and coming in. ﴿She said: Indeed my father invites you so that he may reward you for watering [the flocks] for us﴾. So Musa rose and went with her. He said to her: Walk behind me and direct me on the way, for I dislike that the wind should strike your garments and reveal your body to me. When he reached her father, he related the story to him. One of the two said: O father, hire him; the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy. He said: My daughter, what is your knowledge of his trustworthiness and strength? She said: As for his strength, his lifting the rock, which only ten men could lift. As for his trustworthiness, he said to me: Walk behind me and direct me on the way, for I dislike that the wind should strike your garments and reveal your body to me. This increased his desire for him.

He said: ﴿I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾, up to His saying ﴿you will find me, God willing, among the righteous﴾ [al-Qasas: 27], that is: in good companionship and in fulfilling what I have said. He said: Musa said: ﴿That is between me and you; whichever term I fulfil, there shall be no injustice against me﴾ [al-Qasas: 28]. He said: Yes. He said: ﴿God is a witness over what we say﴾ [al-Qasas: 28]. So he married him to her, and he stayed with him, serving him and working in the tending of his flock and whatever else he needed. He married him to Safura and her sister Sharfa, and they were the two who used to drive back their flocks.

Ibn Kathir said, after citing several chains for this hadith: its chain is sound (*sahih*).

*Al-salfa'* among women is the bold and sharp-tongued one.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾, that he said: he arrived at the water where it was, and the greenness of the herbs could be seen in his belly from emaciation.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, who said: Musa left Egypt for Madyan, between him and it being eight nights, and he had no food except the leaves of trees, and he left barefoot, so that by the time he reached it, the soles of his feet had worn away.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also, who said: ﴿Driving back﴾ means holding back their sheep until the people have finished and the well is clear for them.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* related from him also, who said: Musa said: ﴿My Lord, I am truly in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾, and he was the most honoured of His creation before Him. He was in need of half a date, and his belly clung to his back from the severity of hunger.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, who said: He asked only for food.

'Abdullah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also, who said: He asked for pieces of bread with which he might hold up his back from hunger.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 28, verses 25–37 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1099) His saying: ﴿Then there came to him one of the two women, walking shyly﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, indicated by the context.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its implied meaning is: "So the two of them went to their father quickly, and their habit had been to delay in watering. They told him about the man who had watered for them. So he ordered the elder of his two daughters, and it was said the younger, to call him for him, and she came to him."

Most of the exegetes held that they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb. It was said that they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb's brother, and that Shu'ayb had died. The first view is more likely, and it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

The place of ﴿walking﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the subject of ﹙came﹚. ﴿Shyly﴾ is another circumstantial state, meaning: being shy in both states, of walking and of coming, only. The clause ﴿She said: Indeed my father invites you﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did she say to him when she came to him?" ﴿So that he may reward you the wage for what you gave us to drink﴾, i.e., as a recompense for your watering for us.

﴿So when he came to him and related to him the narrative﴾: "the narrative" (al-qaṣaṣ) is a verbal noun used as the passive participle, i.e., "what was narrated." That is, he informed him of everything that had befallen him from the time of his killing of the Copt until his arrival at the water of Madyan. Shu'ayb said: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., Pharaoh and his companions, because Pharaoh has no authority over Madyan.

Al-Razi has in this place some extremely cold objections, which do not deserve to be mentioned in the explanation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The answer to them is apparent even to the deficient, let alone the perfect. The most refined thing said in this regard is: how did Musa accept an invitation justified by a reward for his watering?

It may be answered that he followed the practice of Allah in responding to the invitation of a prophet from the prophets of Allah, and that response was not for the sake of taking a wage for this deed. For this reason it is reported that when he (Shu'ayb) presented food to him, he said: "We are a household that does not sell our religion for the filling of the earth with gold."

﴿One of the two said: O my father, hire him﴾. The one who spoke was the one who had come to him, i.e., hire him to herd our sheep for us. In this there is evidence that hiring (ijara, a contract of hire) was lawful among them.

All the scholars of Islam have agreed on its permissibility and legitimacy, except al-Asamm, for he was deaf to the hearing of its proofs. The clause ﴿Indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is an explanation (taʿlil) of what she had done by guiding her father to hire Musa, i.e., he is deserving of your hiring him because he combines the two qualities of strength and trustworthiness.

It has already been mentioned in what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Umar that her father asked her about her description of him as strong and trustworthy, and she answered him with what has been mentioned shortly before.

﴿He said: Indeed I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾. In this is the legitimacy of a woman's guardian offering her to a man. This is an established practice in Islam, as established by the offer of 'Umar of his daughter Hafsa to Abu Bakr and 'Uthman. The story is well known, and other things that occurred in the days of the Companions and in the days of prophethood. Likewise, what occurred of a woman offering herself to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿On condition that you serve me for eight years﴾, i.e., on condition that you be a hired worker for me for eight years.

Al-Farra' said: He says, "on condition that you make your reward that you herd my sheep for eight years." The place of ﴿on condition that you serve me﴾ is the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is the present form of ajartuhu (I hired him), and its second object is omitted, i.e., yourself, and ﴿eight years﴾ is an adverb of time.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is said: ajartu dārī and mamlūkī (I rented my house and my slave), without the madd (long vowel) and with it, and the first is more common.

﴿And if you complete ten, then it is from you﴾, i.e., if you complete what I hired you for of herding for ten years, then it is from you, meaning as a favour from you, not an obligation from me upon you. He made what exceeded the eight years up to the completion of ten years dependent on his generosity.

The place of ﴿then it is from you﴾ is the nominative, on the assumption of an implied subject (mubtada'), i.e., "then it is from you."

﴿And I do not want to cause you hardship﴾ by obligating you to complete the ten years. The derivation of "hardship" (mashaqqa) is from splitting (shaqq), i.e., he split his thought in two halves: at times he says, "I am able," and at times he says, "I am not able."

Then he encouraged him to accept the hire, saying: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the righteous﴾, in good companionship and fidelity. It was said: He meant righteousness in general, so the righteousness of dealing in that hire enters under the verse by primary inclusion. He restricted that by the will (of Allah), committing the matter to the success and help of Allah.

Then, when Shu'ayb finished his speech, Musa affirmed it, saying: ﴿That is between me and you﴾. The demonstrative (ism al-ishāra) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows it. The demonstrative refers to what the two had agreed upon. The clause ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ is conditional, and its answer is ﴿then there is no transgression against me﴾. By "the two terms" are meant the eight years and the ten years. The meaning of "fulfil" (qaḍaytu) is "I carried it out and completed it." "The two terms" is in the genitive by the annexation of ayy to it, and mā is redundant (zā'ida).

Ibn Kaysan said: "mā" is in the genitive position, by the annexation of "ayy" to it, and "the two terms" is an apposition (badal) to it. Al-Hasan read "ayma" with the ya' vowelless. Ibn Mas'ud read "ayyamā al-ajalayni qaḍaytu." The meaning of ﴿then there is no transgression against me﴾ is: no injustice against me by seeking an increase over what I fulfilled of the two terms, i.e., just as I do not claim an increase over the eight years, I do not claim a reduction from the ten.

It was said: The meaning is that, just as I do not claim an increase over the ten years, I do not claim an increase over the eight years. This is more apparent.

The root of transgression (ʿudwān) is exceeding the limit in what is not required.

Al-Mubarrad said: Musa knew that there would be no transgression against him if he completed both, but he combined them so that the first would be as complete as the second in fulfilment.

The majority read ʿudwān with a ḍamma on the ʿayn. Abu Haywa read it with a kasra.

﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾, i.e., over what we say of these conditions that are between us, a witness and a guardian, so there is no way for either of us to depart from any of that.

It was said: this is the speech of Musa. It was said: it is the speech of Shu'ayb. The first is preferable, because it occurs within the words of Musa.

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: it is the most complete and fullest of the two, which is the ten years, as will come at the end of the discussion. The fa' is eloquent (faṣīḥa). ﴿And he journeyed with his family﴾ toward Egypt. In this is evidence that a man may take his family wherever he wishes. ﴿He perceived from the side of the mountain a fire﴾, i.e., he saw from the direction adjacent to the mountain a fire. The explanation of this has already been given fully in Surah Ta-Ha. ﴿He said to his family: Remain, indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you from it news, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves.﴾ The explanation of this has also been given in Surah Ta-Ha and in Surah al-Naml.

(p-1100) ﴿Or a burning brand﴾. The majority read jidhwa with a kasra on the jīm. Hamza and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a ḍamma. ʿAsim, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with a fatḥa.

Al-Jawhari said: jadhwa, judhwa and jidhwa are all "a live coal" (jamra). The plural is jadhan, judhan and jidhan.

Mujahid said: The verse indicates that a jadhwa is a piece of live coal in the language of all the Arabs.

Abu 'Ubayda said: It is a thick piece of wood, as if there were fire at its end though there was none. What supports that the jadhwa is a live coal is the saying of al-Sulami:

"And after musk and ben-trees, misery was exchanged for smoke from the embers, on the head of a grey, pale old man."

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾, i.e., that you may warm yourselves by the fire.

﴿When he came to it﴾, i.e., he came to the fire that he had perceived. It was said: he came to the tree. The first is preferable because there is no prior mention of a tree. ﴿He was called from the right side of the valley﴾: "from" (min) is for the beginning of the extent. "The right" (al-ayman) is an adjective of "the side (shāṭi')", and it is from yumn, which is blessing; or it is from the direction of the right, opposite the left, with respect to Musa, i.e., the one next to his right rather than his left. The side of a valley is its edge, and likewise its bank.

Al-Raghib said: The plural of shāṭi' is ashṭā'. His saying ﴿in the blessed place﴾ is connected to "was called", or to an omitted element as a circumstantial state of "the side". ﴿From the tree﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the side of the valley", because the tree was growing on the side.

Al-Jawhari said: One says "shāṭi' al-awdiya" (the side of the valleys) and it is not pluralised.

The majority read ﴿in the place﴾ (al-buqʿa) with a ḍamma on the bā'. Abu Salama and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli read it with a fatḥa, and this is a dialect related by Abu Zayd.

﴿That: O Musa, indeed I am Allah﴾. "That" (an) is explanatory (mufassira), and it is possible that it is the lightened form of the heavy (an) whose subject is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause of the calling explains it. The first is preferable.

The majority read the hamza of ﴿indeed I﴾ with a kasra, on the assumption of an implied "saying," or as the calling is taken to include its meaning. It was read with a fatḥa, but that is a weak reading.

His saying ﴿and that: throw down your staff﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that: O Musa﴾. The explanation of this and what follows has already been given in Surah Ta-Ha and al-Naml. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: he threw it, and it became a serpent and moved.

﴿So when he saw it moving as if it were a snake﴾, in the swiftness of its movement together with the greatness of its body, ﴿he turned back fleeing﴾, i.e., routed. The accusative of "fleeing" is as a circumstantial state. His saying ﴿and did not return﴾ is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, i.e., he did not turn back. ﴿O Musa, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are of the secure.﴾ The explanation of all that is mentioned here has already been given fully, so we will not repeat it.

Likewise His saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without defect, and draw in to yourself your wing﴾. The wing (janāḥ) of a person is his upper arm, and the whole hand is also called a wing, i.e., draw in to yourself your two outstretched hands so that you may protect yourself with them from the serpent, like one who is fearful and frightened. This meaning has been expressed in three phrasings: the first, "insert your hand into your pocket"; the second, "draw in to yourself your wing"; the third, "put your hand into your pocket."

It is possible that by the drawing-in is meant steadfastness and firmness at the reversal of the staff into a serpent. The meaning of ﴿from the fear﴾ is "because of the fear", and fear is the dread (rahb).

The majority read al-rahab with a fatḥa on the rā' and the hā'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Hafs, al-Sulami, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatḥa on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'.

Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans, except Hafs, read it with a ḍamma on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'.

Al-Farra' said: By "the wing" he meant his staff. Some of the people of meanings said: al-rahab is "the sleeve" in the dialect of Himyar and Bani Hanifa.

Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin say to another, "Give me what is in your rahab," so I asked him about al-rahab, and he said: "the sleeve."

According to this, the meaning would be: draw your hand in to yourself and bring it out of the sleeve.

﴿Those two﴾ is a reference to the staff and the hand. ﴿Are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, i.e., two shining arguments and two clear signs. The majority read fa-dhānika with a lightened nūn. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a doubled nūn. It was said: the doubling is the dialect of Quraysh.

Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Shibl and Abu Nawfal read it with a yā' after a kasra-ed nūn, and the yā' is a substitution for one of the two nūns. This is the dialect of Hudhayl, and it was said: the dialect of Tamim.

His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to an implied element, i.e., "existing from Him." Likewise His saying ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is connected to an implied element, i.e., "sent," or "reaching them." ﴿Indeed they were a people who were defiant﴾, exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and departing from obedience in the most extreme way. The clause is an explanation (taʿlīl) of what precedes it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, by way of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying ﴿walking shyly﴾ that he said: "She came concealed, with the sleeve of her garment over her face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related it from Abu al-Hudhayl as a statement attributed to him (mawqūf).

Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Hazim who said: When Musa entered upon Shu'ayb, he found dinner ready, and Shu'ayb said to him, "Eat." Musa said, "I seek refuge in Allah." He said, "Why? Are you not hungry?" He said, "Yes, but I fear that this is a return for what I gave them to drink, and I am from a household that does not sell any of the works of the Hereafter for the filling of the earth with gold." He said, "No, by Allah, but it is my custom and the custom of my forefathers to host guests and feed the food." So Musa sat and ate.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Malik ibn Anas that it had reached him that Shu'ayb was the one who related the narrative to him.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verses 25–37 (part 2 of 2):

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The companion of Musa was Athrun, the nephew of Shu'ayb the Prophet."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The one who hired Musa was Yathrib, the companion of Madyan."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: "The name of Musa's khatan (father-in-law) was Yathribi."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "Some people say that he was Shu'ayb, but he was not Shu'ayb; rather, he was the chief of the water on that day."

Ibn Majah, al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Utbah ibn al-Mundhir al-Sulami, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he recited Surah Ta-Sin-Mim, until he reached the story of Musa, and he said: 'Musa hired himself out for eight or ten years in exchange for the chastity of his private parts and the food of his stomach. When he fulfilled the term, it was said: "O Messenger of Allah, which of the two terms did Musa fulfil?" He said: "The best and most complete of them. When he wished to part from Shu'ayb, he commanded his wife to ask her father to give her some of his sheep on which they could live, so he gave her whatever his sheep had borne."'" The hadith continues in full.

In its chain is Maslamah ibn 'Ali al-Hasani al-Dimashqi al-Balati, whom the imams declared weak.

It has also been narrated by another route, but there is scrutiny (nazar) concerning it.

Its chain in Ibn Abi Hatim is as follows: Abu Zur'ah narrated to us from Yahya ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Bukayr, who said: Ibn Lahi'ah told me, from al-Harith ibn Yazid al-Hadrami, from 'Ali ibn Rabah al-Lakhmi, who said: "I heard 'Utbah ibn al-Mundhir al-Sulami, companion of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," and he mentioned it. Ibn Lahi'ah is weak, and the rest of the men of the chain should be examined.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Anas a portion of it as a mawquf (a report ending with a companion).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah in his Musannaf, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated by several routes from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, and he said: "He fulfilled the greater of them and the better of them, for when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said something, he did it." Al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him something similar. His statement "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said something, he did it" is open to scrutiny, for Musa did not say that he would fulfil the greater of the two terms; rather he said: ﴿Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me﴾.

It has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by several routes that Musa fulfilled the more complete of the two terms.

Al-Khatib narrated in his Tarikh from Abu Dharr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "If you are asked which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, say: the better and the more righteous of them. And if you are asked which of the two women he married, say: the younger of them, the one who came and said: 'O my father, hire him.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Jibril said to me: 'O Muhammad, if the Jews ask you which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, say: the most complete of them. And if they ask you which of the two he married, say: the younger of them.'"

Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated...

Al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Abu Dharr: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked which of the two terms Musa fulfilled. He said: 'The most righteous and the most complete of them.' He said: 'And if you are asked which of the two women he married, say: the younger of them.'" Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know of it being narrated from Abu Dharr except by this chain." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from the hadith of 'Uwayd ibn Abi 'Imran, and he is weak.

As for the reports that he fulfilled the more complete of the two terms, they have several routes which strengthen one another.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated by way of al-Suddi, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "When Musa had fulfilled the term, he set out with his family, and he lost the way. It was winter, and a fire appeared to him. When he saw it, he thought it was a fire, but it was from the light of Allah. ﴿He said to his family: 'Wait here; indeed I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you news from it.﴾ If I do not find news, I will bring you a burning brand (qabas) ﴿so that you may warm yourselves﴾ against the cold."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿perhaps I will bring you news from it﴾: "Perhaps I will find someone who will show me the way, for they had lost their way."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also regarding ﴿or a brand﴾, that it means a shihab (flaming brand).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, also regarding ﴿he was called from the right side of the valley﴾, that the call came from the lowest heaven. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an contradicts what he said, may Allah be pleased with him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim, who declared it sahih, narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was told about the tree under which Musa took shelter, so I travelled towards it all day and night until I reached it in the morning. It was a green sumrah tree (a kind of acacia) trembling. I prayed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and greeted him, and my camel bent towards it, being hungry, and took a mouthful of it, but could not swallow it, so it spat it out. I prayed upon the Prophet and greeted him, then I turned back."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His statement ﴿and draw your arm close to your side﴾, that it means: "your hand."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 28, verses 25–37 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1099) His saying: ﴿Then there came to him one of the two women, walking shyly﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, indicated by the context.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its implied meaning is: "So the two of them went to their father quickly, and their habit had been to delay in watering. They told him about the man who had watered for them. So he ordered the elder of his two daughters, and it was said the younger, to call him for him, and she came to him."

Most of the exegetes held that they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb. It was said that they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb's brother, and that Shu'ayb had died. The first view is more likely, and it is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an.

The place of ﴿walking﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the subject of ﹙came﹚. ﴿Shyly﴾ is another circumstantial state, meaning: being shy in both states, of walking and of coming, only. The clause ﴿She said: Indeed my father invites you﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa), an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did she say to him when she came to him?" ﴿So that he may reward you the wage for what you gave us to drink﴾, i.e., as a recompense for your watering for us.

﴿So when he came to him and related to him the narrative﴾: "the narrative" (al-qaṣaṣ) is a verbal noun used as the passive participle, i.e., "what was narrated." That is, he informed him of everything that had befallen him from the time of his killing of the Copt until his arrival at the water of Madyan. Shu'ayb said: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾, i.e., Pharaoh and his companions, because Pharaoh has no authority over Madyan.

Al-Razi has in this place some extremely cold objections, which do not deserve to be mentioned in the explanation of the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The answer to them is apparent even to the deficient, let alone the perfect. The most refined thing said in this regard is: how did Musa accept an invitation justified by a reward for his watering?

It may be answered that he followed the practice of Allah in responding to the invitation of a prophet from the prophets of Allah, and that response was not for the sake of taking a wage for this deed. For this reason it is reported that when he (Shu'ayb) presented food to him, he said: "We are a household that does not sell our religion for the filling of the earth with gold."

﴿One of the two said: O my father, hire him﴾. The one who spoke was the one who had come to him, i.e., hire him to herd our sheep for us. In this there is evidence that hiring (ijara, a contract of hire) was lawful among them.

All the scholars of Islam have agreed on its permissibility and legitimacy, except al-Asamm, for he was deaf to the hearing of its proofs. The clause ﴿Indeed the best one you can hire is the strong, the trustworthy﴾ is an explanation (taʿlil) of what she had done by guiding her father to hire Musa, i.e., he is deserving of your hiring him because he combines the two qualities of strength and trustworthiness.

It has already been mentioned in what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Umar that her father asked her about her description of him as strong and trustworthy, and she answered him with what has been mentioned shortly before.

﴿He said: Indeed I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine﴾. In this is the legitimacy of a woman's guardian offering her to a man. This is an established practice in Islam, as established by the offer of 'Umar of his daughter Hafsa to Abu Bakr and 'Uthman. The story is well known, and other things that occurred in the days of the Companions and in the days of prophethood. Likewise, what occurred of a woman offering herself to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿On condition that you serve me for eight years﴾, i.e., on condition that you be a hired worker for me for eight years.

Al-Farra' said: He says, "on condition that you make your reward that you herd my sheep for eight years." The place of ﴿on condition that you serve me﴾ is the accusative as a circumstantial state. It is the present form of ajartuhu (I hired him), and its second object is omitted, i.e., yourself, and ﴿eight years﴾ is an adverb of time.

Al-Mubarrad said: It is said: ajartu dārī and mamlūkī (I rented my house and my slave), without the madd (long vowel) and with it, and the first is more common.

﴿And if you complete ten, then it is from you﴾, i.e., if you complete what I hired you for of herding for ten years, then it is from you, meaning as a favour from you, not an obligation from me upon you. He made what exceeded the eight years up to the completion of ten years dependent on his generosity.

The place of ﴿then it is from you﴾ is the nominative, on the assumption of an implied subject (mubtada'), i.e., "then it is from you."

﴿And I do not want to cause you hardship﴾ by obligating you to complete the ten years. The derivation of "hardship" (mashaqqa) is from splitting (shaqq), i.e., he split his thought in two halves: at times he says, "I am able," and at times he says, "I am not able."

Then he encouraged him to accept the hire, saying: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, of the righteous﴾, in good companionship and fidelity. It was said: He meant righteousness in general, so the righteousness of dealing in that hire enters under the verse by primary inclusion. He restricted that by the will (of Allah), committing the matter to the success and help of Allah.

Then, when Shu'ayb finished his speech, Musa affirmed it, saying: ﴿That is between me and you﴾. The demonstrative (ism al-ishāra) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is what follows it. The demonstrative refers to what the two had agreed upon. The clause ﴿whichever of the two terms I fulfil﴾ is conditional, and its answer is ﴿then there is no transgression against me﴾. By "the two terms" are meant the eight years and the ten years. The meaning of "fulfil" (qaḍaytu) is "I carried it out and completed it." "The two terms" is in the genitive by the annexation of ayy to it, and mā is redundant (zā'ida).

Ibn Kaysan said: "mā" is in the genitive position, by the annexation of "ayy" to it, and "the two terms" is an apposition (badal) to it. Al-Hasan read "ayma" with the ya' vowelless. Ibn Mas'ud read "ayyamā al-ajalayni qaḍaytu." The meaning of ﴿then there is no transgression against me﴾ is: no injustice against me by seeking an increase over what I fulfilled of the two terms, i.e., just as I do not claim an increase over the eight years, I do not claim a reduction from the ten.

It was said: The meaning is that, just as I do not claim an increase over the ten years, I do not claim an increase over the eight years. This is more apparent.

The root of transgression (ʿudwān) is exceeding the limit in what is not required.

Al-Mubarrad said: Musa knew that there would be no transgression against him if he completed both, but he combined them so that the first would be as complete as the second in fulfilment.

The majority read ʿudwān with a ḍamma on the ʿayn. Abu Haywa read it with a kasra.

﴿And Allah is Witness over what we say﴾, i.e., over what we say of these conditions that are between us, a witness and a guardian, so there is no way for either of us to depart from any of that.

It was said: this is the speech of Musa. It was said: it is the speech of Shu'ayb. The first is preferable, because it occurs within the words of Musa.

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term﴾: it is the most complete and fullest of the two, which is the ten years, as will come at the end of the discussion. The fa' is eloquent (faṣīḥa). ﴿And he journeyed with his family﴾ toward Egypt. In this is evidence that a man may take his family wherever he wishes. ﴿He perceived from the side of the mountain a fire﴾, i.e., he saw from the direction adjacent to the mountain a fire. The explanation of this has already been given fully in Surah Ta-Ha. ﴿He said to his family: Remain, indeed I have perceived a fire; perhaps I will bring you from it news, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves.﴾ The explanation of this has also been given in Surah Ta-Ha and in Surah al-Naml.

(p-1100) ﴿Or a burning brand﴾. The majority read jidhwa with a kasra on the jīm. Hamza and Yahya ibn Wathhab read it with a ḍamma. ʿAsim, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with a fatḥa.

Al-Jawhari said: jadhwa, judhwa and jidhwa are all "a live coal" (jamra). The plural is jadhan, judhan and jidhan.

Mujahid said: The verse indicates that a jadhwa is a piece of live coal in the language of all the Arabs.

Abu 'Ubayda said: It is a thick piece of wood, as if there were fire at its end though there was none. What supports that the jadhwa is a live coal is the saying of al-Sulami:

"And after musk and ben-trees, misery was exchanged for smoke from the embers, on the head of a grey, pale old man."

﴿So that you may warm yourselves﴾, i.e., that you may warm yourselves by the fire.

﴿When he came to it﴾, i.e., he came to the fire that he had perceived. It was said: he came to the tree. The first is preferable because there is no prior mention of a tree. ﴿He was called from the right side of the valley﴾: "from" (min) is for the beginning of the extent. "The right" (al-ayman) is an adjective of "the side (shāṭi')", and it is from yumn, which is blessing; or it is from the direction of the right, opposite the left, with respect to Musa, i.e., the one next to his right rather than his left. The side of a valley is its edge, and likewise its bank.

Al-Raghib said: The plural of shāṭi' is ashṭā'. His saying ﴿in the blessed place﴾ is connected to "was called", or to an omitted element as a circumstantial state of "the side". ﴿From the tree﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the side of the valley", because the tree was growing on the side.

Al-Jawhari said: One says "shāṭi' al-awdiya" (the side of the valleys) and it is not pluralised.

The majority read ﴿in the place﴾ (al-buqʿa) with a ḍamma on the bā'. Abu Salama and al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli read it with a fatḥa, and this is a dialect related by Abu Zayd.

﴿That: O Musa, indeed I am Allah﴾. "That" (an) is explanatory (mufassira), and it is possible that it is the lightened form of the heavy (an) whose subject is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause of the calling explains it. The first is preferable.

The majority read the hamza of ﴿indeed I﴾ with a kasra, on the assumption of an implied "saying," or as the calling is taken to include its meaning. It was read with a fatḥa, but that is a weak reading.

His saying ﴿and that: throw down your staff﴾ is conjoined to ﴿that: O Musa﴾. The explanation of this and what follows has already been given in Surah Ta-Ha and al-Naml. There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: he threw it, and it became a serpent and moved.

﴿So when he saw it moving as if it were a snake﴾, in the swiftness of its movement together with the greatness of its body, ﴿he turned back fleeing﴾, i.e., routed. The accusative of "fleeing" is as a circumstantial state. His saying ﴿and did not return﴾ is also in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, i.e., he did not turn back. ﴿O Musa, come forward and do not fear; indeed you are of the secure.﴾ The explanation of all that is mentioned here has already been given fully, so we will not repeat it.

Likewise His saying: ﴿Insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without defect, and draw in to yourself your wing﴾. The wing (janāḥ) of a person is his upper arm, and the whole hand is also called a wing, i.e., draw in to yourself your two outstretched hands so that you may protect yourself with them from the serpent, like one who is fearful and frightened. This meaning has been expressed in three phrasings: the first, "insert your hand into your pocket"; the second, "draw in to yourself your wing"; the third, "put your hand into your pocket."

It is possible that by the drawing-in is meant steadfastness and firmness at the reversal of the staff into a serpent. The meaning of ﴿from the fear﴾ is "because of the fear", and fear is the dread (rahb).

The majority read al-rahab with a fatḥa on the rā' and the hā'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Hafs, al-Sulami, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with a fatḥa on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'.

Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans, except Hafs, read it with a ḍamma on the rā' and a sukūn on the hā'.

Al-Farra' said: By "the wing" he meant his staff. Some of the people of meanings said: al-rahab is "the sleeve" in the dialect of Himyar and Bani Hanifa.

Al-Asma'i said: I heard a Bedouin say to another, "Give me what is in your rahab," so I asked him about al-rahab, and he said: "the sleeve."

According to this, the meaning would be: draw your hand in to yourself and bring it out of the sleeve.

﴿Those two﴾ is a reference to the staff and the hand. ﴿Are two proofs from your Lord to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾, i.e., two shining arguments and two clear signs. The majority read fa-dhānika with a lightened nūn. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a doubled nūn. It was said: the doubling is the dialect of Quraysh.

Ibn Mas'ud, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Shibl and Abu Nawfal read it with a yā' after a kasra-ed nūn, and the yā' is a substitution for one of the two nūns. This is the dialect of Hudhayl, and it was said: the dialect of Tamim.

His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to an implied element, i.e., "existing from Him." Likewise His saying ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is connected to an implied element, i.e., "sent," or "reaching them." ﴿Indeed they were a people who were defiant﴾, exceeding the limit in wrongdoing and departing from obedience in the most extreme way. The clause is an explanation (taʿlīl) of what precedes it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, by way of 'Abd Allah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning His saying ﴿walking shyly﴾ that he said: "She came concealed, with the sleeve of her garment over her face."

Ibn al-Mundhir related it from Abu al-Hudhayl as a statement attributed to him (mawqūf).

Ibn 'Asakir related from Abu Hazim who said: When Musa entered upon Shu'ayb, he found dinner ready, and Shu'ayb said to him, "Eat." Musa said, "I seek refuge in Allah." He said, "Why? Are you not hungry?" He said, "Yes, but I fear that this is a return for what I gave them to drink, and I am from a household that does not sell any of the works of the Hereafter for the filling of the earth with gold." He said, "No, by Allah, but it is my custom and the custom of my forefathers to host guests and feed the food." So Musa sat and ate.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Malik ibn Anas that it had reached him that Shu'ayb was the one who related the narrative to him.
