﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ among people, and that is not up to you ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance ﴿and He knows best those who are guided﴾, that is: those who are receptive to guidance and prepared for it. This verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, and this has been mentioned earlier in Bara'a.

Al-Zajjaj said: The commentators agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. It has been established in the principles (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of jurisprudence) that the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specific cause of revelation, so Abu Talib enters into this ruling in the first place.

﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land"﴾, that is: the polytheists of Quraysh and those who followed them said: "If we enter your religion, O Muhammad, we will be snatched away from our land", that is: the Arabs will seize us from our land, meaning Makkah, and we have no power against them. This is among their false excuses and their empty pretexts. Al-takhattuf, in origin, is seizing quickly.

The majority read "natakhattaf" with a jazm (apocopate) as a response to the condition. Al-Minqari read it with a raf' (nominative) as a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

Then Allah refuted them with a refutation introduced by a question of reproach and rebuke, saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾, that is: did We not make for them a sanctuary with security?

Abu al-Baqa said: it takes its object directly because it has the meaning of "ja'ala" (to make), as is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a sanctuary?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 67]. Then He described this sanctuary with His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾, that is: the fruits are gathered to it from its various kinds, from different lands, and carried to it.

The majority read "yujbā" with the yaʾ (third person masculine), considering the masculine form of "kull shay'" (every thing) and the presence of a barrier between the verb and "thamarāt" (fruits), and also because the feminine form of "thamarāt" is not a true feminine. Abu Ubayd chose the majority reading for the reasons we mentioned. Nafi' read it with the taʾ (feminine), considering "thamarāt."

The majority also read "thamarāt" with two fathas. Aban read it with two dammas, the plural of "thumur" with two dammas. It was also read with a fatha on the thaʾ and sukun on the mim. ﴿A provision from Us﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "yujbā" is "We provide them." It may also be accusative as an object of a hidden verb, that is: "We bring it to them as a provision from Us." It may also be accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), that is: providing. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because of their extreme ignorance, their great heedlessness, their lack of reflection on the matter of their return and their right guidance, because they are among those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and placed a covering over their sight.

Al-Firyabi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (all together) narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, that he said: "They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I have answered you before you call upon Me."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another chain from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Asakir narrated it from him through another chain with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah, and al-Daylami narrated from Amr ibn Absah who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾: What was the calling? And what was the mercy?" He said: "Allah wrote it two thousand years before He created His creation, then He placed it upon His Throne, then He called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, My mercy has preceded My wrath. I have given you before you ask Me, and I have forgiven you before you seek My forgiveness. Whoever among you meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is My servant and My messenger, truthfully, I will admit him into Paradise." (p. 1106)

al-Khutalli in al-Dibaj narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Hudhayfah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, traced to the Prophet: "He said: They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, you did not call upon Us when We answered you, nor did you ask Us when We gave you."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet: "Allah called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, respond to your Lord. He said: They responded while they were in the loins of their fathers and the wombs of their mothers until the Day of Resurrection, and they said: 'Labbayka, You are truly our Lord, and we are truly Your servants.' He said: 'You have spoken truly. I am your Lord and you are truly My servants. I have pardoned you before you call upon Me, and I have given you before you ask Me. Whoever meets Me among you with the testimony that there is no god but Allah will enter Paradise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who perishes in the fatrah (the gap between prophets) will say: 'My Lord, no book or messenger came to me.'" Then he recited this verse: ﴿Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger...﴾ (the verse).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿They said: "Two magics supporting each other"﴾ etc.

He said: They are the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). ﴿Indeed we are disbelievers in both﴾, meaning by the two books: the Torah and the Furqan.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Mawardi, and Ibn Qani' (the three in the lexicons of the Companions, al-Ma'ajim al-Sahabah) and al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh with a good chain, narrated from Rifa'ah al-Qurazi who said: The verse ﴿And We have conveyed to them the word that perhaps they will remember﴾ down to His saying ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ was revealed concerning ten men, I being one of them.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ that he said: It means those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in the first Book and the last, a man who had a slave-girl whom he educated well, then freed and married her, and a servant who worshipped his Lord well and gave sincere counsel to his master."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of al-Musayyib, and Muslim and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Talib when he refused to accept Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that some people of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If we follow you, the people will snatch us away," and then the verse ﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you"﴾ was revealed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ that he said: "The fruits of the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 44–57 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾. This begins the explanation of the sending down of the Qur'an. That is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the western side of the mountain, so this is an instance of omitting the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its position. Al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Al-Kalbi said: "On the western side of the valley," that is, the place where Musa spoke with his Lord. ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾, that is, We entrusted him and firmly settled the matter with him concerning the message to Pharaoh and his people. ﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ to that, so that you would stand upon its reality and relate it from your own knowledge.

Since it has been established that knowledge of the details of those circumstances cannot be obtained by being present there, by our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) witnessing them, and since it has been established by sound evidences that he did not receive that from any other human being, nor did any human teacher instruct him, as we have already set out, it becomes clear that it is from Allah, the Exalted, by revelation from Him to His Messenger through the angel sent down with it. So this statement is in the manner of ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would undertake the care of Maryam﴾ (Aal 'Imran 3:44). It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾ is: when We charged him and obligated him. And it has been said: We informed him that the nation of Muhammad is the best of nations. The negation of his being on the western side does not entail the negation of his being among the witnesses, because it is possible for him to be present without witnessing.

It has been said: the witnesses are the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time.

﴿But We brought into being generations﴾, that is, We created nations between your time, O Muhammad, and the time of Musa. ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾: the respite lengthened for them and the duration extended over them, so the laws and rulings changed, the religions were forgotten, and they abandoned the command of Allah and forgot His covenant. Similar to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the term grew long for them and their hearts became hard﴾ (al-Hadid 57:16). This statement has been cited as evidence that Allah, the Exalted, had made covenants with Musa concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and belief in him; then, when the lifetime grew long for them and generations passed after generations, they forgot those covenants and abandoned fulfilling them.

﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, that is, residing among them as Musa resided, so that you would recite to the people of Makkah their news and relate it to them from your own knowledge. It is said: thawa yathwi thawa'an wa thuwiyyan, fa huwa thawin (he dwelt, so he is a dweller).

Dhu al-Rummah said:
"Indeed there was in a year of dwelling that I dwelt, its lubanat being decided, and the weary traveler grows weary."

And al-‘Ajjaj said:
"So he spent the night where the dweller enters,"
meaning the guest who stays. Another said:
"The dwelling was prolonged over the messenger of the abode."

﴿Reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, reciting to the people of Madyan Our verses and learning from them. It has been said: reminding them of the promise and the threat. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or as a second predicate. It is also permissible that this clause be the predicate and "dweller" be a circumstantial state.

Al-Farra' made it a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "And here you are reciting to your nation." ﴿But We were ever sending [messengers]﴾, that is, We sent you to the people of Makkah and sent down upon you these reports, and had that not been so, you would not have known them.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We revealed them to you and related them to you.

﴿Nor were you on the side of the Tur when We called﴾, that is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the mountain called the Tur when We called Musa, when he came to the appointed time together with the seventy.

It has been said: the one called was the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Wahb said: That is because when Allah mentioned to Musa the virtue of Muhammad and his nation, (p-1104) he said: "O Lord, show them to me." Allah said: "You will not reach them, but if you wish, I will call them and make you hear their voice." He said: "Yes, O Lord." So Allah said: "O nation of Muhammad!" and they answered from the loins of their fathers.

So the meaning of the verse according to this is: you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the Tur when We spoke to Musa, and We called your nation. What indicates this and strengthens and supports it will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills. ﴿But it was a mercy from your Lord﴾, that is: but We did that as a mercy from Us to you. It has been said: We sent the Qur'an as a mercy to you. It has been said: We taught you. It has been said: We made you know.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative: meaning as a mercy, as an infinitive of the verb: "But We had mercy on you with a mercy."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose: that is, We did that for you for the sake of mercy.

Al-Nahhas said: that is, you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We sent you and revealed them to you as a mercy.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is the predicate of an implied kana: that is, "but that was a mercy." ‘Isa ibn ‘Umar and Abu Haywah read "rahmatun" with the nominative, on the estimate: "but you are a mercy." Al-Kisa'i said: the nominative is because it is the subject of an implied kana, but this is remote unless it is taken that kana is complete.

The lam in ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ is connected to the verb implied, according to the disagreement over its estimate. The people are the people of Makkah, for no warner had come to them before him (ﷺ). The clause "mā atāhum" is conjoined and is an attribute of "qawman" (a people). ﴿Perhaps they will remember﴾, that is: they will take warning by your warning.

﴿And [so] that they would not say, if disaster struck them for what their hands had sent forth: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses and be among the believers?"﴾ The "law" here is the one of prohibition, and "an" with what is in its scope is in the position of a nominative as the subject. Its response is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is: "We did not send messengers to them." That is, the motive for sending messengers is the removal of their excuses. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:165). Ibn ‘Atiyyah estimated it as: "We would have hastened the punishment for them," and al-Wahidi agreed with him on this estimate, saying: the meaning is: had it not been that they would argue by the abandonment of sending to them, We would have hastened the punishment upon them for their disbelief. His saying "fa-yaqūlū" is conjoined to "tuṣībahum" and is among what is within the scope of "law": that is, "fa-yaqūlū, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger...'" The second "law" here is the one of urging: that is, "Why did You not send to us a messenger from You?" Its response is ﴿so we would follow Your verses﴾, and it is in the accusative by the implied "an" because it is a response to the urging. The "verses" are the verses of revelation, manifest and clear. The reason the saying was conjoined to "tuṣībahum" is that it is the cause of the sending; but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, and its existence came with its existence, it is as if the punishment itself were the cause of sending the messengers through the saying. ﴿And [so] that we would be among the believers﴾ in these verses.

The meaning of the verse is: were We to punish them, they would say, "The time has been long since the messengers, and Allah did not send to us a messenger," and they would think that this is an excuse for them. But there is no excuse for them after the reports of the messengers reached them. Rather, We have completed the proof, removed the pretext, and perfected the clarification by sending you, O Muhammad, to them.

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ That is: when the truth came to the people of Makkah from Allah, which is Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down upon him of the Qur'an, they said, out of obstinacy and contentious falsehood: "Why was this Messenger not given the like of what was given to Musa of the signs, among which is the Torah sent down to him all at once?" Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?﴾ That is: before this saying, or before the appearance of Muhammad. The meaning: they had disbelieved in the signs of Musa just as they disbelieved in the signs of Muhammad. The clause ﴿They said: "Two sorceries supporting each other"﴾ is resumptive, brought to establish their disbelief and obstinacy. The intended meaning of their saying "two sorcerers" is Musa and Muhammad, and "tazahara" means they cooperated, that is: they cooperated in sorcery. The pronoun in His saying ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It has been said: it refers to the Jews.

The first is preferable, for the Jews do not describe Musa as a sorcerer; this is said only by the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like, unless what is meant is one who denied the prophethood of Musa, like Pharaoh and his people, for they described Musa and Harun as sorcerers, but they were not Jews.

It is possible that the pronoun refers to those who disbelieved in Musa and those who disbelieved in Muhammad, for those who disbelieved in Musa described him as a sorcerer, and those who disbelieved in Muhammad also described him as a sorcerer.

It has been said: the meaning is: did the Jews of the age of Muhammad not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before him, by the good tidings of ‘Isa and Muhammad?

The majority of readers read "sāḥirān" (two sorcerers), but the Kufans read "siḥrān" (two sorceries), meaning the Torah and the Qur'an. It has been said: the Gospel and the Qur'an. Al-Farra' spoke in accordance with the first, and Abu Zayd spoke in accordance with the second.

It has been said: the pronoun in "awa lam yakfurū" refers to the Jews, and that by their saying "sāḥirān" they meant ‘Isa and Muhammad. ﴿And they said: "Indeed we are disbelievers in each of them"﴾, that is: in each of Musa and Muhammad, or in Musa and Harun, or in Musa and ‘Isa, according to the differing opinions. This is according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, what is meant is the Torah and the Qur'an, or the Gospel and the Qur'an.

In this clause there is a confirmation of what precedes it, of describing the two prophets as sorcerers, or of describing the two scriptures as such, and an emphasis of that.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet to say to them a statement by which their incapacity would become manifest, so He said: ﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: say to them, O Muhammad: "Then bring a Book which is better guidance than the Torah and the Qur'an." "And I will follow it" is the response to the command, and the majority of readers have put it in the jussive for this reason.

Zayd ibn ‘Ali read "atabi‘uhu" in the nominative, as a resumption: that is, "then I follow it." Al-Farra' said: on this reading it is an attribute of "Book." In this statement there is a mockery of them.

It is also evidence that the reading of the Kufans is stronger than the reading of the majority, because the speech returns to the two books and not to the two messengers. The meaning of "if you are truthful" is: if you are truthful in what you have described the two messengers or the two books with.

﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾, that is: they do not do what you charged them with, of bringing a Book that is better guidance than the two books. The response of the condition is: ﴿then know that they only follow their own desires﴾, that is: their deviant opinions and their false preferences without any proof or evidence. It has been said: the meaning is: if they do not respond to you by believing in what you have brought. Construing "yastajībū" with "lām" is one of the two permissible usages. ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ That is: no one is more astray than him; rather, he is the complete example of error. Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people, who wrong themselves by disbelief, denying the prophets and turning away from the signs of Allah.

﴿And We have certainly made the word continuous for them﴾ (p-1105) The majority read "waṣṣalnā" with a shaddah on the ṣād, and al-Hasan read it without the shaddah. The meaning of the verse: We made some of it follow others, and We sent messenger after messenger.

Abu ‘Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: its meaning is: We completed it.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah and al-Suddi said: We made it clear. Ibn Zayd said: We joined for them the good of this world with the good of the Hereafter, until it was as if they witnessed the Hereafter in this world. The first is preferable, and it is derived from joining ropes, one part to another. Among its usage is the saying of the poet:

"So say to the sons of Marwan: what is the matter with my covenant, bound by a weak rope that is never joined?"

And Imru' al-Qays said:
"Turning his two hands with a joined thread."

The pronoun in "lahum" refers to Quraysh, and it has been said: to the Jews, and it has been said: to all of them, "that perhaps they will remember," so that remembrance would be a cause of their belief, out of fear that what befell those before them might befall them.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾: that is, before the Qur'an. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "they believe in it." Allah, the Exalted, informed that a group of the Children of Israel believed in the Qur'an, such as ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and the rest of the People of the Book who embraced Islam. It has been said: the pronoun in "min qablihi" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is preferable.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an according to the first view, and to Muhammad according to the second view.

﴿When it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it"﴾, that is: when the Qur'an is recited to them, they say, "We affirm it" ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾, that is: the truth that we recognize, sent down from our Lord ﴿Indeed we were Muslims before it﴾, that is: devoted to Allah in monotheism (tawhid), or believers in Muhammad and in what he brought, because of what we know of his mention in the Torah and the Gospel, its good tidings of him, and that he would be sent at the end of time and the Qur'an would be revealed to him.

The reference in His words ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ is to those described with these qualities. The "bi" in ﴿bi-mā ṣabarū﴾ (because they endured) denotes causation, that is: because of their patience and steadfastness in faith in the first Book and the last Book, and in the first Prophet and the last Prophet. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾. Al-darʾ (repelling) means pushing away: they push away, with forbearance and good speech, the harm they encounter.

It is said: they push away disobedience with obedience. It is said: they push away shirk with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It is said: they push away sins with repentance and seeking forgiveness. ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, that is: they spend their wealth in acts of obedience and in what the Shariah has commanded.

Then He praised them, glorified is He, for turning away from vain talk, saying: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾, out of nobility, dignity, and adherence to the etiquette of the Shariah. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. Here, vain talk is what they hear from the polytheists, such as insults to them and their religion and mockery of them. ﴿And they say: "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds"﴾: the harm of your disbelief will not reach us, and the benefit of our faith will not reach you. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾: this peace is not the greeting of salutation; rather, what is meant is the peace of those who abandon (dispute), and its meaning is: security for you from us and safety; we will not join you or respond to you in what you are engaged in.

Al-Zajjaj said: This was before the command to fight. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾, that is: we do not seek their company. Muqatil said: We do not want to be among the people of ignorance and foolishness. Al-Kalbi said: We do not love your religion which you follow.

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ among people, and that is not up to you ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance ﴿and He knows best those who are guided﴾, that is: those who are receptive to guidance and prepared for it. This verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, and this has been mentioned earlier in Bara'a.

Al-Zajjaj said: The commentators agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. It has been established in the principles (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of jurisprudence) that the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specific cause of revelation, so Abu Talib enters into this ruling in the first place.

﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land"﴾, that is: the polytheists of Quraysh and those who followed them said: "If we enter your religion, O Muhammad, we will be snatched away from our land", that is: the Arabs will seize us from our land, meaning Makkah, and we have no power against them. This is among their false excuses and their empty pretexts. Al-takhattuf, in origin, is seizing quickly.

The majority read "natakhattaf" with a jazm (apocopate) as a response to the condition. Al-Minqari read it with a raf' (nominative) as a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

Then Allah refuted them with a refutation introduced by a question of reproach and rebuke, saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾, that is: did We not make for them a sanctuary with security?

Abu al-Baqa said: it takes its object directly because it has the meaning of "ja'ala" (to make), as is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a sanctuary?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 67]. Then He described this sanctuary with His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾, that is: the fruits are gathered to it from its various kinds, from different lands, and carried to it.

The majority read "yujbā" with the yaʾ (third person masculine), considering the masculine form of "kull shay'" (every thing) and the presence of a barrier between the verb and "thamarāt" (fruits), and also because the feminine form of "thamarāt" is not a true feminine. Abu Ubayd chose the majority reading for the reasons we mentioned. Nafi' read it with the taʾ (feminine), considering "thamarāt."

The majority also read "thamarāt" with two fathas. Aban read it with two dammas, the plural of "thumur" with two dammas. It was also read with a fatha on the thaʾ and sukun on the mim. ﴿A provision from Us﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "yujbā" is "We provide them." It may also be accusative as an object of a hidden verb, that is: "We bring it to them as a provision from Us." It may also be accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), that is: providing. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because of their extreme ignorance, their great heedlessness, their lack of reflection on the matter of their return and their right guidance, because they are among those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and placed a covering over their sight.

Al-Firyabi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (all together) narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, that he said: "They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I have answered you before you call upon Me."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another chain from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Asakir narrated it from him through another chain with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah, and al-Daylami narrated from Amr ibn Absah who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾: What was the calling? And what was the mercy?" He said: "Allah wrote it two thousand years before He created His creation, then He placed it upon His Throne, then He called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, My mercy has preceded My wrath. I have given you before you ask Me, and I have forgiven you before you seek My forgiveness. Whoever among you meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is My servant and My messenger, truthfully, I will admit him into Paradise." (p. 1106)

al-Khutalli in al-Dibaj narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Hudhayfah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, traced to the Prophet: "He said: They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, you did not call upon Us when We answered you, nor did you ask Us when We gave you."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet: "Allah called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, respond to your Lord. He said: They responded while they were in the loins of their fathers and the wombs of their mothers until the Day of Resurrection, and they said: 'Labbayka, You are truly our Lord, and we are truly Your servants.' He said: 'You have spoken truly. I am your Lord and you are truly My servants. I have pardoned you before you call upon Me, and I have given you before you ask Me. Whoever meets Me among you with the testimony that there is no god but Allah will enter Paradise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who perishes in the fatrah (the gap between prophets) will say: 'My Lord, no book or messenger came to me.'" Then he recited this verse: ﴿Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger...﴾ (the verse).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿They said: "Two magics supporting each other"﴾ etc.

He said: They are the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). ﴿Indeed we are disbelievers in both﴾, meaning by the two books: the Torah and the Furqan.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Mawardi, and Ibn Qani' (the three in the lexicons of the Companions, al-Ma'ajim al-Sahabah) and al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh with a good chain, narrated from Rifa'ah al-Qurazi who said: The verse ﴿And We have conveyed to them the word that perhaps they will remember﴾ down to His saying ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ was revealed concerning ten men, I being one of them.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ that he said: It means those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in the first Book and the last, a man who had a slave-girl whom he educated well, then freed and married her, and a servant who worshipped his Lord well and gave sincere counsel to his master."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of al-Musayyib, and Muslim and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Talib when he refused to accept Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that some people of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If we follow you, the people will snatch us away," and then the verse ﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you"﴾ was revealed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ that he said: "The fruits of the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 44–57 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾. This begins the explanation of the sending down of the Qur'an. That is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the western side of the mountain, so this is an instance of omitting the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its position. Al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Al-Kalbi said: "On the western side of the valley," that is, the place where Musa spoke with his Lord. ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾, that is, We entrusted him and firmly settled the matter with him concerning the message to Pharaoh and his people. ﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ to that, so that you would stand upon its reality and relate it from your own knowledge.

Since it has been established that knowledge of the details of those circumstances cannot be obtained by being present there, by our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) witnessing them, and since it has been established by sound evidences that he did not receive that from any other human being, nor did any human teacher instruct him, as we have already set out, it becomes clear that it is from Allah, the Exalted, by revelation from Him to His Messenger through the angel sent down with it. So this statement is in the manner of ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would undertake the care of Maryam﴾ (Aal 'Imran 3:44). It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾ is: when We charged him and obligated him. And it has been said: We informed him that the nation of Muhammad is the best of nations. The negation of his being on the western side does not entail the negation of his being among the witnesses, because it is possible for him to be present without witnessing.

It has been said: the witnesses are the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time.

﴿But We brought into being generations﴾, that is, We created nations between your time, O Muhammad, and the time of Musa. ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾: the respite lengthened for them and the duration extended over them, so the laws and rulings changed, the religions were forgotten, and they abandoned the command of Allah and forgot His covenant. Similar to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the term grew long for them and their hearts became hard﴾ (al-Hadid 57:16). This statement has been cited as evidence that Allah, the Exalted, had made covenants with Musa concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and belief in him; then, when the lifetime grew long for them and generations passed after generations, they forgot those covenants and abandoned fulfilling them.

﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, that is, residing among them as Musa resided, so that you would recite to the people of Makkah their news and relate it to them from your own knowledge. It is said: thawa yathwi thawa'an wa thuwiyyan, fa huwa thawin (he dwelt, so he is a dweller).

Dhu al-Rummah said:
"Indeed there was in a year of dwelling that I dwelt, its lubanat being decided, and the weary traveler grows weary."

And al-‘Ajjaj said:
"So he spent the night where the dweller enters,"
meaning the guest who stays. Another said:
"The dwelling was prolonged over the messenger of the abode."

﴿Reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, reciting to the people of Madyan Our verses and learning from them. It has been said: reminding them of the promise and the threat. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or as a second predicate. It is also permissible that this clause be the predicate and "dweller" be a circumstantial state.

Al-Farra' made it a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "And here you are reciting to your nation." ﴿But We were ever sending [messengers]﴾, that is, We sent you to the people of Makkah and sent down upon you these reports, and had that not been so, you would not have known them.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We revealed them to you and related them to you.

﴿Nor were you on the side of the Tur when We called﴾, that is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the mountain called the Tur when We called Musa, when he came to the appointed time together with the seventy.

It has been said: the one called was the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Wahb said: That is because when Allah mentioned to Musa the virtue of Muhammad and his nation, (p-1104) he said: "O Lord, show them to me." Allah said: "You will not reach them, but if you wish, I will call them and make you hear their voice." He said: "Yes, O Lord." So Allah said: "O nation of Muhammad!" and they answered from the loins of their fathers.

So the meaning of the verse according to this is: you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the Tur when We spoke to Musa, and We called your nation. What indicates this and strengthens and supports it will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills. ﴿But it was a mercy from your Lord﴾, that is: but We did that as a mercy from Us to you. It has been said: We sent the Qur'an as a mercy to you. It has been said: We taught you. It has been said: We made you know.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative: meaning as a mercy, as an infinitive of the verb: "But We had mercy on you with a mercy."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose: that is, We did that for you for the sake of mercy.

Al-Nahhas said: that is, you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We sent you and revealed them to you as a mercy.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is the predicate of an implied kana: that is, "but that was a mercy." ‘Isa ibn ‘Umar and Abu Haywah read "rahmatun" with the nominative, on the estimate: "but you are a mercy." Al-Kisa'i said: the nominative is because it is the subject of an implied kana, but this is remote unless it is taken that kana is complete.

The lam in ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ is connected to the verb implied, according to the disagreement over its estimate. The people are the people of Makkah, for no warner had come to them before him (ﷺ). The clause "mā atāhum" is conjoined and is an attribute of "qawman" (a people). ﴿Perhaps they will remember﴾, that is: they will take warning by your warning.

﴿And [so] that they would not say, if disaster struck them for what their hands had sent forth: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses and be among the believers?"﴾ The "law" here is the one of prohibition, and "an" with what is in its scope is in the position of a nominative as the subject. Its response is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is: "We did not send messengers to them." That is, the motive for sending messengers is the removal of their excuses. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:165). Ibn ‘Atiyyah estimated it as: "We would have hastened the punishment for them," and al-Wahidi agreed with him on this estimate, saying: the meaning is: had it not been that they would argue by the abandonment of sending to them, We would have hastened the punishment upon them for their disbelief. His saying "fa-yaqūlū" is conjoined to "tuṣībahum" and is among what is within the scope of "law": that is, "fa-yaqūlū, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger...'" The second "law" here is the one of urging: that is, "Why did You not send to us a messenger from You?" Its response is ﴿so we would follow Your verses﴾, and it is in the accusative by the implied "an" because it is a response to the urging. The "verses" are the verses of revelation, manifest and clear. The reason the saying was conjoined to "tuṣībahum" is that it is the cause of the sending; but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, and its existence came with its existence, it is as if the punishment itself were the cause of sending the messengers through the saying. ﴿And [so] that we would be among the believers﴾ in these verses.

The meaning of the verse is: were We to punish them, they would say, "The time has been long since the messengers, and Allah did not send to us a messenger," and they would think that this is an excuse for them. But there is no excuse for them after the reports of the messengers reached them. Rather, We have completed the proof, removed the pretext, and perfected the clarification by sending you, O Muhammad, to them.

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ That is: when the truth came to the people of Makkah from Allah, which is Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down upon him of the Qur'an, they said, out of obstinacy and contentious falsehood: "Why was this Messenger not given the like of what was given to Musa of the signs, among which is the Torah sent down to him all at once?" Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?﴾ That is: before this saying, or before the appearance of Muhammad. The meaning: they had disbelieved in the signs of Musa just as they disbelieved in the signs of Muhammad. The clause ﴿They said: "Two sorceries supporting each other"﴾ is resumptive, brought to establish their disbelief and obstinacy. The intended meaning of their saying "two sorcerers" is Musa and Muhammad, and "tazahara" means they cooperated, that is: they cooperated in sorcery. The pronoun in His saying ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It has been said: it refers to the Jews.

The first is preferable, for the Jews do not describe Musa as a sorcerer; this is said only by the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like, unless what is meant is one who denied the prophethood of Musa, like Pharaoh and his people, for they described Musa and Harun as sorcerers, but they were not Jews.

It is possible that the pronoun refers to those who disbelieved in Musa and those who disbelieved in Muhammad, for those who disbelieved in Musa described him as a sorcerer, and those who disbelieved in Muhammad also described him as a sorcerer.

It has been said: the meaning is: did the Jews of the age of Muhammad not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before him, by the good tidings of ‘Isa and Muhammad?

The majority of readers read "sāḥirān" (two sorcerers), but the Kufans read "siḥrān" (two sorceries), meaning the Torah and the Qur'an. It has been said: the Gospel and the Qur'an. Al-Farra' spoke in accordance with the first, and Abu Zayd spoke in accordance with the second.

It has been said: the pronoun in "awa lam yakfurū" refers to the Jews, and that by their saying "sāḥirān" they meant ‘Isa and Muhammad. ﴿And they said: "Indeed we are disbelievers in each of them"﴾, that is: in each of Musa and Muhammad, or in Musa and Harun, or in Musa and ‘Isa, according to the differing opinions. This is according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, what is meant is the Torah and the Qur'an, or the Gospel and the Qur'an.

In this clause there is a confirmation of what precedes it, of describing the two prophets as sorcerers, or of describing the two scriptures as such, and an emphasis of that.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet to say to them a statement by which their incapacity would become manifest, so He said: ﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: say to them, O Muhammad: "Then bring a Book which is better guidance than the Torah and the Qur'an." "And I will follow it" is the response to the command, and the majority of readers have put it in the jussive for this reason.

Zayd ibn ‘Ali read "atabi‘uhu" in the nominative, as a resumption: that is, "then I follow it." Al-Farra' said: on this reading it is an attribute of "Book." In this statement there is a mockery of them.

It is also evidence that the reading of the Kufans is stronger than the reading of the majority, because the speech returns to the two books and not to the two messengers. The meaning of "if you are truthful" is: if you are truthful in what you have described the two messengers or the two books with.

﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾, that is: they do not do what you charged them with, of bringing a Book that is better guidance than the two books. The response of the condition is: ﴿then know that they only follow their own desires﴾, that is: their deviant opinions and their false preferences without any proof or evidence. It has been said: the meaning is: if they do not respond to you by believing in what you have brought. Construing "yastajībū" with "lām" is one of the two permissible usages. ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ That is: no one is more astray than him; rather, he is the complete example of error. Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people, who wrong themselves by disbelief, denying the prophets and turning away from the signs of Allah.

﴿And We have certainly made the word continuous for them﴾ (p-1105) The majority read "waṣṣalnā" with a shaddah on the ṣād, and al-Hasan read it without the shaddah. The meaning of the verse: We made some of it follow others, and We sent messenger after messenger.

Abu ‘Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: its meaning is: We completed it.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah and al-Suddi said: We made it clear. Ibn Zayd said: We joined for them the good of this world with the good of the Hereafter, until it was as if they witnessed the Hereafter in this world. The first is preferable, and it is derived from joining ropes, one part to another. Among its usage is the saying of the poet:

"So say to the sons of Marwan: what is the matter with my covenant, bound by a weak rope that is never joined?"

And Imru' al-Qays said:
"Turning his two hands with a joined thread."

The pronoun in "lahum" refers to Quraysh, and it has been said: to the Jews, and it has been said: to all of them, "that perhaps they will remember," so that remembrance would be a cause of their belief, out of fear that what befell those before them might befall them.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾: that is, before the Qur'an. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "they believe in it." Allah, the Exalted, informed that a group of the Children of Israel believed in the Qur'an, such as ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and the rest of the People of the Book who embraced Islam. It has been said: the pronoun in "min qablihi" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is preferable.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an according to the first view, and to Muhammad according to the second view.

﴿When it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it"﴾, that is: when the Qur'an is recited to them, they say, "We affirm it" ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾, that is: the truth that we recognize, sent down from our Lord ﴿Indeed we were Muslims before it﴾, that is: devoted to Allah in monotheism (tawhid), or believers in Muhammad and in what he brought, because of what we know of his mention in the Torah and the Gospel, its good tidings of him, and that he would be sent at the end of time and the Qur'an would be revealed to him.

The reference in His words ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ is to those described with these qualities. The "bi" in ﴿bi-mā ṣabarū﴾ (because they endured) denotes causation, that is: because of their patience and steadfastness in faith in the first Book and the last Book, and in the first Prophet and the last Prophet. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾. Al-darʾ (repelling) means pushing away: they push away, with forbearance and good speech, the harm they encounter.

It is said: they push away disobedience with obedience. It is said: they push away shirk with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It is said: they push away sins with repentance and seeking forgiveness. ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, that is: they spend their wealth in acts of obedience and in what the Shariah has commanded.

Then He praised them, glorified is He, for turning away from vain talk, saying: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾, out of nobility, dignity, and adherence to the etiquette of the Shariah. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. Here, vain talk is what they hear from the polytheists, such as insults to them and their religion and mockery of them. ﴿And they say: "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds"﴾: the harm of your disbelief will not reach us, and the benefit of our faith will not reach you. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾: this peace is not the greeting of salutation; rather, what is meant is the peace of those who abandon (dispute), and its meaning is: security for you from us and safety; we will not join you or respond to you in what you are engaged in.

Al-Zajjaj said: This was before the command to fight. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾, that is: we do not seek their company. Muqatil said: We do not want to be among the people of ignorance and foolishness. Al-Kalbi said: We do not love your religion which you follow.

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ among people, and that is not up to you ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance ﴿and He knows best those who are guided﴾, that is: those who are receptive to guidance and prepared for it. This verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, and this has been mentioned earlier in Bara'a.

Al-Zajjaj said: The commentators agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. It has been established in the principles (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of jurisprudence) that the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specific cause of revelation, so Abu Talib enters into this ruling in the first place.

﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land"﴾, that is: the polytheists of Quraysh and those who followed them said: "If we enter your religion, O Muhammad, we will be snatched away from our land", that is: the Arabs will seize us from our land, meaning Makkah, and we have no power against them. This is among their false excuses and their empty pretexts. Al-takhattuf, in origin, is seizing quickly.

The majority read "natakhattaf" with a jazm (apocopate) as a response to the condition. Al-Minqari read it with a raf' (nominative) as a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

Then Allah refuted them with a refutation introduced by a question of reproach and rebuke, saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾, that is: did We not make for them a sanctuary with security?

Abu al-Baqa said: it takes its object directly because it has the meaning of "ja'ala" (to make), as is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a sanctuary?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 67]. Then He described this sanctuary with His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾, that is: the fruits are gathered to it from its various kinds, from different lands, and carried to it.

The majority read "yujbā" with the yaʾ (third person masculine), considering the masculine form of "kull shay'" (every thing) and the presence of a barrier between the verb and "thamarāt" (fruits), and also because the feminine form of "thamarāt" is not a true feminine. Abu Ubayd chose the majority reading for the reasons we mentioned. Nafi' read it with the taʾ (feminine), considering "thamarāt."

The majority also read "thamarāt" with two fathas. Aban read it with two dammas, the plural of "thumur" with two dammas. It was also read with a fatha on the thaʾ and sukun on the mim. ﴿A provision from Us﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "yujbā" is "We provide them." It may also be accusative as an object of a hidden verb, that is: "We bring it to them as a provision from Us." It may also be accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), that is: providing. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because of their extreme ignorance, their great heedlessness, their lack of reflection on the matter of their return and their right guidance, because they are among those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and placed a covering over their sight.

Al-Firyabi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (all together) narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, that he said: "They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I have answered you before you call upon Me."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another chain from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Asakir narrated it from him through another chain with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah, and al-Daylami narrated from Amr ibn Absah who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾: What was the calling? And what was the mercy?" He said: "Allah wrote it two thousand years before He created His creation, then He placed it upon His Throne, then He called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, My mercy has preceded My wrath. I have given you before you ask Me, and I have forgiven you before you seek My forgiveness. Whoever among you meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is My servant and My messenger, truthfully, I will admit him into Paradise." (p. 1106)

al-Khutalli in al-Dibaj narrated from Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, traced to the Prophet, something similar.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Hudhayfah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, traced to the Prophet: "He said: They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, you did not call upon Us when We answered you, nor did you ask Us when We gave you."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, traced to the Prophet: "Allah called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, respond to your Lord. He said: They responded while they were in the loins of their fathers and the wombs of their mothers until the Day of Resurrection, and they said: 'Labbayka, You are truly our Lord, and we are truly Your servants.' He said: 'You have spoken truly. I am your Lord and you are truly My servants. I have pardoned you before you call upon Me, and I have given you before you ask Me. Whoever meets Me among you with the testimony that there is no god but Allah will enter Paradise.'"

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who perishes in the fatrah (the gap between prophets) will say: 'My Lord, no book or messenger came to me.'" Then he recited this verse: ﴿Our Lord, if only You had sent to us a messenger...﴾ (the verse).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning His words: ﴿They said: "Two magics supporting each other"﴾ etc.

He said: They are the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). ﴿Indeed we are disbelievers in both﴾, meaning by the two books: the Torah and the Furqan.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, al-Mawardi, and Ibn Qani' (the three in the lexicons of the Companions, al-Ma'ajim al-Sahabah) and al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh with a good chain, narrated from Rifa'ah al-Qurazi who said: The verse ﴿And We have conveyed to them the word that perhaps they will remember﴾ down to His saying ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ was revealed concerning ten men, I being one of them.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ that he said: It means those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ).

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three will be given their reward twice: a man from the People of the Book who believed in the first Book and the last, a man who had a slave-girl whom he educated well, then freed and married her, and a servant who worshipped his Lord well and gave sincere counsel to his master."

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from the hadith of al-Musayyib, and Muslim and others from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that His saying ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Talib when he refused to accept Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas that some people of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If we follow you, the people will snatch us away," and then the verse ﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you"﴾ was revealed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ that he said: "The fruits of the earth."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 44–57 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾. This begins the explanation of the sending down of the Qur'an. That is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the western side of the mountain, so this is an instance of omitting the qualified noun and placing the adjective in its position. Al-Zajjaj chose this view.

Al-Kalbi said: "On the western side of the valley," that is, the place where Musa spoke with his Lord. ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾, that is, We entrusted him and firmly settled the matter with him concerning the message to Pharaoh and his people. ﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ to that, so that you would stand upon its reality and relate it from your own knowledge.

Since it has been established that knowledge of the details of those circumstances cannot be obtained by being present there, by our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) witnessing them, and since it has been established by sound evidences that he did not receive that from any other human being, nor did any human teacher instruct him, as we have already set out, it becomes clear that it is from Allah, the Exalted, by revelation from Him to His Messenger through the angel sent down with it. So this statement is in the manner of ﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to see] which of them would undertake the care of Maryam﴾ (Aal 'Imran 3:44). It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿When We decreed to Musa the command﴾ is: when We charged him and obligated him. And it has been said: We informed him that the nation of Muhammad is the best of nations. The negation of his being on the western side does not entail the negation of his being among the witnesses, because it is possible for him to be present without witnessing.

It has been said: the witnesses are the seventy whom Musa chose for the appointed time.

﴿But We brought into being generations﴾, that is, We created nations between your time, O Muhammad, and the time of Musa. ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾: the respite lengthened for them and the duration extended over them, so the laws and rulings changed, the religions were forgotten, and they abandoned the command of Allah and forgot His covenant. Similar to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So the term grew long for them and their hearts became hard﴾ (al-Hadid 57:16). This statement has been cited as evidence that Allah, the Exalted, had made covenants with Musa concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) and belief in him; then, when the lifetime grew long for them and generations passed after generations, they forgot those covenants and abandoned fulfilling them.

﴿Nor were you a dweller among the people of Madyan﴾, that is, residing among them as Musa resided, so that you would recite to the people of Makkah their news and relate it to them from your own knowledge. It is said: thawa yathwi thawa'an wa thuwiyyan, fa huwa thawin (he dwelt, so he is a dweller).

Dhu al-Rummah said:
"Indeed there was in a year of dwelling that I dwelt, its lubanat being decided, and the weary traveler grows weary."

And al-‘Ajjaj said:
"So he spent the night where the dweller enters,"
meaning the guest who stays. Another said:
"The dwelling was prolonged over the messenger of the abode."

﴿Reciting to them Our verses﴾, that is, reciting to the people of Madyan Our verses and learning from them. It has been said: reminding them of the promise and the threat. The clause is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial clause, or as a second predicate. It is also permissible that this clause be the predicate and "dweller" be a circumstantial state.

Al-Farra' made it a resumptive clause, as if it were said: "And here you are reciting to your nation." ﴿But We were ever sending [messengers]﴾, that is, We sent you to the people of Makkah and sent down upon you these reports, and had that not been so, you would not have known them.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We revealed them to you and related them to you.

﴿Nor were you on the side of the Tur when We called﴾, that is: and you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the mountain called the Tur when We called Musa, when he came to the appointed time together with the seventy.

It has been said: the one called was the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Wahb said: That is because when Allah mentioned to Musa the virtue of Muhammad and his nation, (p-1104) he said: "O Lord, show them to me." Allah said: "You will not reach them, but if you wish, I will call them and make you hear their voice." He said: "Yes, O Lord." So Allah said: "O nation of Muhammad!" and they answered from the loins of their fathers.

So the meaning of the verse according to this is: you were not, O Muhammad, on the side of the Tur when We spoke to Musa, and We called your nation. What indicates this and strengthens and supports it will come at the end of the discussion, if Allah wills. ﴿But it was a mercy from your Lord﴾, that is: but We did that as a mercy from Us to you. It has been said: We sent the Qur'an as a mercy to you. It has been said: We taught you. It has been said: We made you know.

Al-Akhfash said: it is in the accusative: meaning as a mercy, as an infinitive of the verb: "But We had mercy on you with a mercy."

Al-Zajjaj said: it is an object of purpose: that is, We did that for you for the sake of mercy.

Al-Nahhas said: that is, you did not witness the stories of the prophets, nor were they recited to you, but We sent you and revealed them to you as a mercy.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is the predicate of an implied kana: that is, "but that was a mercy." ‘Isa ibn ‘Umar and Abu Haywah read "rahmatun" with the nominative, on the estimate: "but you are a mercy." Al-Kisa'i said: the nominative is because it is the subject of an implied kana, but this is remote unless it is taken that kana is complete.

The lam in ﴿that you may warn a people to whom no warner had come before you﴾ is connected to the verb implied, according to the disagreement over its estimate. The people are the people of Makkah, for no warner had come to them before him (ﷺ). The clause "mā atāhum" is conjoined and is an attribute of "qawman" (a people). ﴿Perhaps they will remember﴾, that is: they will take warning by your warning.

﴿And [so] that they would not say, if disaster struck them for what their hands had sent forth: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so we would follow Your verses and be among the believers?"﴾ The "law" here is the one of prohibition, and "an" with what is in its scope is in the position of a nominative as the subject. Its response is omitted. Al-Zajjaj said: its estimate is: "We did not send messengers to them." That is, the motive for sending messengers is the removal of their excuses. This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that there will not be for the people any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:165). Ibn ‘Atiyyah estimated it as: "We would have hastened the punishment for them," and al-Wahidi agreed with him on this estimate, saying: the meaning is: had it not been that they would argue by the abandonment of sending to them, We would have hastened the punishment upon them for their disbelief. His saying "fa-yaqūlū" is conjoined to "tuṣībahum" and is among what is within the scope of "law": that is, "fa-yaqūlū, 'Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger...'" The second "law" here is the one of urging: that is, "Why did You not send to us a messenger from You?" Its response is ﴿so we would follow Your verses﴾, and it is in the accusative by the implied "an" because it is a response to the urging. The "verses" are the verses of revelation, manifest and clear. The reason the saying was conjoined to "tuṣībahum" is that it is the cause of the sending; but since the punishment was the cause of the saying, and its existence came with its existence, it is as if the punishment itself were the cause of sending the messengers through the saying. ﴿And [so] that we would be among the believers﴾ in these verses.

The meaning of the verse is: were We to punish them, they would say, "The time has been long since the messengers, and Allah did not send to us a messenger," and they would think that this is an excuse for them. But there is no excuse for them after the reports of the messengers reached them. Rather, We have completed the proof, removed the pretext, and perfected the clarification by sending you, O Muhammad, to them.

﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ That is: when the truth came to the people of Makkah from Allah, which is Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down upon him of the Qur'an, they said, out of obstinacy and contentious falsehood: "Why was this Messenger not given the like of what was given to Musa of the signs, among which is the Torah sent down to him all at once?" Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before?﴾ That is: before this saying, or before the appearance of Muhammad. The meaning: they had disbelieved in the signs of Musa just as they disbelieved in the signs of Muhammad. The clause ﴿They said: "Two sorceries supporting each other"﴾ is resumptive, brought to establish their disbelief and obstinacy. The intended meaning of their saying "two sorcerers" is Musa and Muhammad, and "tazahara" means they cooperated, that is: they cooperated in sorcery. The pronoun in His saying ﴿Did they not disbelieve﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh. It has been said: it refers to the Jews.

The first is preferable, for the Jews do not describe Musa as a sorcerer; this is said only by the disbelievers of Quraysh and their like, unless what is meant is one who denied the prophethood of Musa, like Pharaoh and his people, for they described Musa and Harun as sorcerers, but they were not Jews.

It is possible that the pronoun refers to those who disbelieved in Musa and those who disbelieved in Muhammad, for those who disbelieved in Musa described him as a sorcerer, and those who disbelieved in Muhammad also described him as a sorcerer.

It has been said: the meaning is: did the Jews of the age of Muhammad not disbelieve in what was given to Musa before him, by the good tidings of ‘Isa and Muhammad?

The majority of readers read "sāḥirān" (two sorcerers), but the Kufans read "siḥrān" (two sorceries), meaning the Torah and the Qur'an. It has been said: the Gospel and the Qur'an. Al-Farra' spoke in accordance with the first, and Abu Zayd spoke in accordance with the second.

It has been said: the pronoun in "awa lam yakfurū" refers to the Jews, and that by their saying "sāḥirān" they meant ‘Isa and Muhammad. ﴿And they said: "Indeed we are disbelievers in each of them"﴾, that is: in each of Musa and Muhammad, or in Musa and Harun, or in Musa and ‘Isa, according to the differing opinions. This is according to the reading of the majority. As for the second reading, what is meant is the Torah and the Qur'an, or the Gospel and the Qur'an.

In this clause there is a confirmation of what precedes it, of describing the two prophets as sorcerers, or of describing the two scriptures as such, and an emphasis of that.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet to say to them a statement by which their incapacity would become manifest, so He said: ﴿Say: "Then bring a Book from Allah that is better guidance than both of them, and I will follow it, if you are truthful."﴾ That is: say to them, O Muhammad: "Then bring a Book which is better guidance than the Torah and the Qur'an." "And I will follow it" is the response to the command, and the majority of readers have put it in the jussive for this reason.

Zayd ibn ‘Ali read "atabi‘uhu" in the nominative, as a resumption: that is, "then I follow it." Al-Farra' said: on this reading it is an attribute of "Book." In this statement there is a mockery of them.

It is also evidence that the reading of the Kufans is stronger than the reading of the majority, because the speech returns to the two books and not to the two messengers. The meaning of "if you are truthful" is: if you are truthful in what you have described the two messengers or the two books with.

﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾, that is: they do not do what you charged them with, of bringing a Book that is better guidance than the two books. The response of the condition is: ﴿then know that they only follow their own desires﴾, that is: their deviant opinions and their false preferences without any proof or evidence. It has been said: the meaning is: if they do not respond to you by believing in what you have brought. Construing "yastajībū" with "lām" is one of the two permissible usages. ﴿And who is more astray than one who follows his own desire without guidance from Allah?﴾ That is: no one is more astray than him; rather, he is the complete example of error. Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people, who wrong themselves by disbelief, denying the prophets and turning away from the signs of Allah.

﴿And We have certainly made the word continuous for them﴾ (p-1105) The majority read "waṣṣalnā" with a shaddah on the ṣād, and al-Hasan read it without the shaddah. The meaning of the verse: We made some of it follow others, and We sent messenger after messenger.

Abu ‘Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: its meaning is: We completed it.

Ibn ‘Uyaynah and al-Suddi said: We made it clear. Ibn Zayd said: We joined for them the good of this world with the good of the Hereafter, until it was as if they witnessed the Hereafter in this world. The first is preferable, and it is derived from joining ropes, one part to another. Among its usage is the saying of the poet:

"So say to the sons of Marwan: what is the matter with my covenant, bound by a weak rope that is never joined?"

And Imru' al-Qays said:
"Turning his two hands with a joined thread."

The pronoun in "lahum" refers to Quraysh, and it has been said: to the Jews, and it has been said: to all of them, "that perhaps they will remember," so that remembrance would be a cause of their belief, out of fear that what befell those before them might befall them.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾: that is, before the Qur'an. The relative pronoun is the subject and its predicate is "they believe in it." Allah, the Exalted, informed that a group of the Children of Israel believed in the Qur'an, such as ‘Abd Allah ibn Salam and the rest of the People of the Book who embraced Islam. It has been said: the pronoun in "min qablihi" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), but the first is preferable.

The pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an according to the first view, and to Muhammad according to the second view.

﴿When it is recited to them, they say: "We believe in it"﴾, that is: when the Qur'an is recited to them, they say, "We affirm it" ﴿Indeed it is the truth from our Lord﴾, that is: the truth that we recognize, sent down from our Lord ﴿Indeed we were Muslims before it﴾, that is: devoted to Allah in monotheism (tawhid), or believers in Muhammad and in what he brought, because of what we know of his mention in the Torah and the Gospel, its good tidings of him, and that he would be sent at the end of time and the Qur'an would be revealed to him.

The reference in His words ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾ is to those described with these qualities. The "bi" in ﴿bi-mā ṣabarū﴾ (because they endured) denotes causation, that is: because of their patience and steadfastness in faith in the first Book and the last Book, and in the first Prophet and the last Prophet. ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾. Al-darʾ (repelling) means pushing away: they push away, with forbearance and good speech, the harm they encounter.

It is said: they push away disobedience with obedience. It is said: they push away shirk with the testimony that there is no god but Allah. It is said: they push away sins with repentance and seeking forgiveness. ﴿And from what We have provided them, they spend﴾, that is: they spend their wealth in acts of obedience and in what the Shariah has commanded.

Then He praised them, glorified is He, for turning away from vain talk, saying: ﴿And when they hear vain talk, they turn away from it﴾, out of nobility, dignity, and adherence to the etiquette of the Shariah. Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And when they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72]. Here, vain talk is what they hear from the polytheists, such as insults to them and their religion and mockery of them. ﴿And they say: "For us are our deeds and for you are your deeds"﴾: the harm of your disbelief will not reach us, and the benefit of our faith will not reach you. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾: this peace is not the greeting of salutation; rather, what is meant is the peace of those who abandon (dispute), and its meaning is: security for you from us and safety; we will not join you or respond to you in what you are engaged in.

Al-Zajjaj said: This was before the command to fight. ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾, that is: we do not seek their company. Muqatil said: We do not want to be among the people of ignorance and foolishness. Al-Kalbi said: We do not love your religion which you follow.

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ among people, and that is not up to you ﴿but Allah guides whom He wills﴾ to His guidance ﴿and He knows best those who are guided﴾, that is: those who are receptive to guidance and prepared for it. This verse was revealed concerning Abu Talib, as is established in the two Sahihs and others, and this has been mentioned earlier in Bara'a.

Al-Zajjaj said: The commentators agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib. It has been established in the principles (usul al-fiqh, the foundations of jurisprudence) that the consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specific cause of revelation, so Abu Talib enters into this ruling in the first place.

﴿And they say: "If we follow the guidance with you, we will be snatched from our land"﴾, that is: the polytheists of Quraysh and those who followed them said: "If we enter your religion, O Muhammad, we will be snatched away from our land", that is: the Arabs will seize us from our land, meaning Makkah, and we have no power against them. This is among their false excuses and their empty pretexts. Al-takhattuf, in origin, is seizing quickly.

The majority read "natakhattaf" with a jazm (apocopate) as a response to the condition. Al-Minqari read it with a raf' (nominative) as a new sentence (istiʾnaf).

Then Allah refuted them with a refutation introduced by a question of reproach and rebuke, saying: ﴿Did We not establish for them a secure sanctuary?﴾, that is: did We not make for them a sanctuary with security?

Abu al-Baqa said: it takes its object directly because it has the meaning of "ja'ala" (to make), as is explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We have made a sanctuary?﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 67]. Then He described this sanctuary with His words: ﴿to which are brought the fruits of every thing﴾, that is: the fruits are gathered to it from its various kinds, from different lands, and carried to it.

The majority read "yujbā" with the yaʾ (third person masculine), considering the masculine form of "kull shay'" (every thing) and the presence of a barrier between the verb and "thamarāt" (fruits), and also because the feminine form of "thamarāt" is not a true feminine. Abu Ubayd chose the majority reading for the reasons we mentioned. Nafi' read it with the taʾ (feminine), considering "thamarāt."

The majority also read "thamarāt" with two fathas. Aban read it with two dammas, the plural of "thumur" with two dammas. It was also read with a fatha on the thaʾ and sukun on the mim. ﴿A provision from Us﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because the meaning of "yujbā" is "We provide them." It may also be accusative as an object of a hidden verb, that is: "We bring it to them as a provision from Us." It may also be accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), that is: providing. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, because of their extreme ignorance, their great heedlessness, their lack of reflection on the matter of their return and their right guidance, because they are among those whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and placed a covering over their sight.

Al-Firyabi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il (all together) narrated from Abu Hurayrah concerning His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾, that he said: "They were called: O Ummah of Muhammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I have answered you before you call upon Me."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another chain from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Asakir narrated it from him through another chain with similar wording.

Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah, and al-Daylami narrated from Amr ibn Absah who said: "I asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about His words: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called﴾: What was the calling? And what was the mercy?" He said: "Allah wrote it two thousand years before He created His creation, then He placed it upon His Throne, then He called out: O Ummah of Muhammad, My mercy has preceded My wrath. I have given you before you ask Me, and I have forgiven you before you seek My forgiveness. Whoever among you meets Me testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is My servant and My messenger, truthfully, I will admit him into Paradise." (p. 1106)
