Then He, glorified and exalted is He, praised Himself for His oneness and for His exclusive entitlement to praise, and said: **﴿He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾**: that is, in this world and the Hereafter, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. **﴿And to Him belongs the judgement﴾**: He judges among His servants as He wills, without any partner. **﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾**: by resurrection, so that He recompenses the doer of good according to his goodness and the wrongdoer according to his wrongdoing. You will not return to anyone else.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 58–70 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And We were not to destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾. He said: Allah said, "We did not destroy any town on account of faith, but He destroyed the towns on account of wrongdoing when their people did wrong. Had Makkah believed, they would not have perished along with those who perished. But they denied and did wrong, and for that they perished."

Muslim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me,'" and the hadith is given in full.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from ʿAbd ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection at their hungriest, their thirstiest, and their most naked. Whoever fed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will feed him; whoever clothed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will clothe him; whoever gave drink for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will give him drink; and whoever was in the pleasure of Allah, Allah will be in his pleasure."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿Then the information was obscured from them﴾ that he said: "The proofs," and regarding ﴿so they will not question one another﴾ that he said: "by lineages."

It has been firmly established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih the teaching of the istikharah (prayer for guidance) and the manner of its prayer and its supplication, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verses 58–70 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾**, meaning: from among the people of a town who were living in ease, comfort and plenty. Insolence (*baṭar*) then came upon them, and so they were destroyed.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-baṭar* is transgression at the time of blessing.

ʿAṭāʾ said: They lived in insolence, so they ate God's provision and worshipped idols.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mazini said: The meaning of ﴿بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَها﴾ (*baṭirat maʿīshatahā*, "its livelihood became insolent") is *baṭirat fī maʿīshatihā* ("it became insolent in its livelihood"). When the preposition was dropped, the verb became transitive, as in His saying: ﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("and Musa chose his people") [al-Aʿraf: 155]. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (*tafsīr*, an accusative of specification), as you say: *abṭaraka māluka* and *baṭirtahu* ("your wealth made you insolent" and "you were insolent in it"). A parallel to this is at His saying: ﴿إلّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("except one who makes a fool of himself") [al-Baqarah: 130]. However, the accusative of a definite noun as a specification is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the specification must be an indefinite noun that indicates a genus.

It was also said: *maʿīshatahā* is in the accusative governed by *baṭirat*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *jahilat* ("was ignorant of"). ﴿فَتِلْكَ مَساكِنُهم لَمْ تُسْكَنْ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited after them except a little"): that is, no one lived in them after them except for a short time, like a traveller who passes through and stays a day or part of a day. Or, no one remained to live in them except for a few days, because of the ill fate of the sins that had occurred in them.

It was also said: the exception refers to the dwellings, meaning that after the death of their people only a few of the dwellings were inhabited, and most of them were in ruins. Al-Farra' said this, but it is a weak view. ﴿وكُنّا نَحْنُ الوارِثِينَ﴾ ("and We were the inheritors"): that is, of them, because they did not leave any heir to inherit their homes and wealth. The clause ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَنِ﴾ (*lam tuskan*, "were not inhabited") may be in the nominative as a second predicate of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*), and it may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

**﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾**: that is, it was not valid nor proper that God should destroy the disbelieving towns, that is, towns whose people were disbelievers, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger who warns them and recites to them the verses of God that clearly state what God has made obligatory for them, the reward He has prepared for the obedient, and the punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿أُمِّها﴾ (*ummihā*, "their mother") is its largest and greatest town. He singled out the greatest of them for the sending of the messenger, because in it are the nobles of the people, the people of understanding and judgement, and the kings and great men. So by this consideration it became like a mother to the towns around it.

Al-Hasan said: the mother of the towns is its first. It was also said: what is meant by "the mother of the towns" here is Makkah, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed, the first House established for mankind") [Aal ʿImran: 96]. The explanation of what this verse contains has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. (p-1107) The clause ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آياتِنا﴾ ("reciting to them Our verses") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, reciting to them and informing them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

**﴿And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾**: this clause is coordinated with the clause before it. The exception is an exceptive clause with a missing antecedent (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the most general of states. That is: We would never destroy the people of the towns after We send to their mother-town a messenger calling them to the truth, except when they are in the state of being wrongdoers who have deserved destruction because of their persistence in disbelief after the proof has been established against them and their argument has been made firm, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ رَبُّكَ لِيُهْلِكَ القُرى بِظُلْمٍ وأهْلُها مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ ("Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers") [Hud: 117].

Then He, glorified is He, said: **﴿But whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾**. The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah. That is: whatever thing you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life, which you enjoy for the duration of your life or part of your life, after which you will depart from it or it will depart from you. In any case, that is headed to extinction and termination. **﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾**: that is, His reward and recompense are better than that which passes away and perishes, because it is a pure pleasure free from the admixture of turbidity, and more lasting because it endures forever, whereas this worldly life ends quickly. **﴿Then will you not reason?﴾**: will you not understand that the lasting is better than the perishing, and that what contains pure pleasure with no admixture is better than pleasures mixed with turbidity and spoiled by the afflictions of body and heart?

It was read with the accusative *matāʿ* (مَتاعَ), as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*): that is, "so you will be given enjoyment (*tumattaʿūn*) of the life." Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (*yaʿqilūn*, "they reason") with the third-person prefix (*taḥtiyyah*), while the rest read it with the second-person prefix (*fawqiyyah*) as address. Their reading is preferred because of His saying: ﴿وما أُوتِيتُمْ﴾ ("what you have been given").

**﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and he is to meet it, like one We have given enjoyment of the life of this world and then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth?﴾**: that is, We have promised him Paradise and the blessings in it that cannot be counted, so he is to meet it, that is, to attain it without doubt, since God does not break His promise. **﴿Like one We have given enjoyment of the worldly life﴾**: so he was given some of it as he desired, together with its quick passing away and its disturbance. **﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth﴾**: this is coordinated with His saying ﴿متعناه﴾ (*matteʿnāhu*, "We have given him enjoyment"), and it falls with it within the scope of the relative clause. It emphasises the denial of equivalence and establishes it. The meaning is: then this one whom We have given enjoyment is, on the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth to the Fire. The specification of "those brought forth" to those who are brought forth for punishment was required by the context. The interrogation is for denial: that is, their condition is not equal. The one promised Paradise must surely attain what he was promised, together with the fact that his share of the worldly life is not lost to him. This is the state of the believer.

As for the state of the disbeliever, he has only the bare enjoyment of some of the worldly life, in which he and the believer are equal, and each of them obtains his portion of it, and he is headed to the Fire. So are the two equal? The majority read ﴿ثُمَّ هو﴾ (*thumma huwa*) with the *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ*. Al-Kisa'i and Qalun read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*, treating *thumma* like the conjunctions *wa* and *fa*.

The accusative of **﴿يَوْمَ﴾** in His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ يُنادِيهِمْ﴾ ("and the Day He calls to them") is either by coordination with "the Day of Resurrection" or by an implied verb *udhkur* ("remember"). That is: the Day when God, glorified is He, calls these polytheists and says to them: **﴿Where are My partners that you used to claim?﴾**, that they would help you and intercede for you. The two objects of *tazʿumūn* ("you claim") are omitted, meaning: "you claimed them to be My partners," since the context indicates them.

**﴿Those upon whom the word has come into effect will say﴾**: that is, the word of punishment has come into effect for them. They are the leaders of misguidance who took lords besides God, as al-Kalbi said. Qatada said: they are the devils. **﴿Our Lord, these are the ones we misguided﴾**: that is, we called them to error, meaning the followers. **﴿We misguided them as we ourselves were misguided﴾**: that is, we led them astray as we were led astray. **﴿We disassociate ourselves before You﴾** from them. The meaning is that the leaders of misguidance, or the devils, disowned those who obeyed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them disowned others and became enemies, as God, Most High, said: ﴿الأخِلّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("Intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another") [al-Zukhruf: 67]. Here ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is the subject, and ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾ ("whom we misguided") is its descriptive clause. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *aghwaynāhum* ("we misguided them"), and the predicate is *aghwaynāhum*. ﴿كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ ("as we were misguided") is an adjectival description of an omitted verbal noun.

It was also said: the predicate of *hāʾulāʾ* is ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾, while ﴿أغْوَيْناهم كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ is a resumed statement that establishes what came before it. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi preferred this view and objected to the first view, and Abu al-Baqa' answered his objection. **﴿They did not used to worship us﴾**: rather they used to worship their own desires. It was also said that *mā* in *mā kānū* is a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, meaning: "we disown to You their worship of us." The first view is more preferable.

**﴿And it will be said: "Call upon your partners."﴾**: that is, this is said to the disbelievers among the children of Adam. The meaning is: seek help from your gods that you used to worship besides God in the world, so that they may help you and ward off from you. **﴿So they will call them, but they will not respond to them﴾**, nor will they benefit them in any way of benefit. **﴿And they will see the punishment﴾**: that is, the followers and the followed, for it will have overtaken them. **﴿If only they had been guided!﴾** Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted, and the meaning is: "if only they had been guided, that would have saved them and they would not have seen the punishment."

It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided, they would not have called upon them." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided in the world, they would have known that the punishment is true." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they were guided to some way of tricks, they would have warded off the punishment by it." It was also said: "It is time for them to be guided, if only they were guided." It was also said other than this. The first view is the most preferable.

**﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾**: *yawm* here is coordinated with what came before it. That is: what was your answer to the prophets who were sent to you when they conveyed My messages to you?

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verses 58–70 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾**, meaning: from among the people of a town who were living in ease, comfort and plenty. Insolence (*baṭar*) then came upon them, and so they were destroyed.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-baṭar* is transgression at the time of blessing.

ʿAṭāʾ said: They lived in insolence, so they ate God's provision and worshipped idols.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mazini said: The meaning of ﴿بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَها﴾ (*baṭirat maʿīshatahā*, "its livelihood became insolent") is *baṭirat fī maʿīshatihā* ("it became insolent in its livelihood"). When the preposition was dropped, the verb became transitive, as in His saying: ﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("and Musa chose his people") [al-Aʿraf: 155]. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (*tafsīr*, an accusative of specification), as you say: *abṭaraka māluka* and *baṭirtahu* ("your wealth made you insolent" and "you were insolent in it"). A parallel to this is at His saying: ﴿إلّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("except one who makes a fool of himself") [al-Baqarah: 130]. However, the accusative of a definite noun as a specification is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the specification must be an indefinite noun that indicates a genus.

It was also said: *maʿīshatahā* is in the accusative governed by *baṭirat*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *jahilat* ("was ignorant of"). ﴿فَتِلْكَ مَساكِنُهم لَمْ تُسْكَنْ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited after them except a little"): that is, no one lived in them after them except for a short time, like a traveller who passes through and stays a day or part of a day. Or, no one remained to live in them except for a few days, because of the ill fate of the sins that had occurred in them.

It was also said: the exception refers to the dwellings, meaning that after the death of their people only a few of the dwellings were inhabited, and most of them were in ruins. Al-Farra' said this, but it is a weak view. ﴿وكُنّا نَحْنُ الوارِثِينَ﴾ ("and We were the inheritors"): that is, of them, because they did not leave any heir to inherit their homes and wealth. The clause ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَنِ﴾ (*lam tuskan*, "were not inhabited") may be in the nominative as a second predicate of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*), and it may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

**﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾**: that is, it was not valid nor proper that God should destroy the disbelieving towns, that is, towns whose people were disbelievers, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger who warns them and recites to them the verses of God that clearly state what God has made obligatory for them, the reward He has prepared for the obedient, and the punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿أُمِّها﴾ (*ummihā*, "their mother") is its largest and greatest town. He singled out the greatest of them for the sending of the messenger, because in it are the nobles of the people, the people of understanding and judgement, and the kings and great men. So by this consideration it became like a mother to the towns around it.

Al-Hasan said: the mother of the towns is its first. It was also said: what is meant by "the mother of the towns" here is Makkah, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed, the first House established for mankind") [Aal ʿImran: 96]. The explanation of what this verse contains has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. (p-1107) The clause ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آياتِنا﴾ ("reciting to them Our verses") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, reciting to them and informing them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

**﴿And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾**: this clause is coordinated with the clause before it. The exception is an exceptive clause with a missing antecedent (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the most general of states. That is: We would never destroy the people of the towns after We send to their mother-town a messenger calling them to the truth, except when they are in the state of being wrongdoers who have deserved destruction because of their persistence in disbelief after the proof has been established against them and their argument has been made firm, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ رَبُّكَ لِيُهْلِكَ القُرى بِظُلْمٍ وأهْلُها مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ ("Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers") [Hud: 117].

Then He, glorified is He, said: **﴿But whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾**. The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah. That is: whatever thing you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life, which you enjoy for the duration of your life or part of your life, after which you will depart from it or it will depart from you. In any case, that is headed to extinction and termination. **﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾**: that is, His reward and recompense are better than that which passes away and perishes, because it is a pure pleasure free from the admixture of turbidity, and more lasting because it endures forever, whereas this worldly life ends quickly. **﴿Then will you not reason?﴾**: will you not understand that the lasting is better than the perishing, and that what contains pure pleasure with no admixture is better than pleasures mixed with turbidity and spoiled by the afflictions of body and heart?

It was read with the accusative *matāʿ* (مَتاعَ), as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*): that is, "so you will be given enjoyment (*tumattaʿūn*) of the life." Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (*yaʿqilūn*, "they reason") with the third-person prefix (*taḥtiyyah*), while the rest read it with the second-person prefix (*fawqiyyah*) as address. Their reading is preferred because of His saying: ﴿وما أُوتِيتُمْ﴾ ("what you have been given").

**﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and he is to meet it, like one We have given enjoyment of the life of this world and then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth?﴾**: that is, We have promised him Paradise and the blessings in it that cannot be counted, so he is to meet it, that is, to attain it without doubt, since God does not break His promise. **﴿Like one We have given enjoyment of the worldly life﴾**: so he was given some of it as he desired, together with its quick passing away and its disturbance. **﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth﴾**: this is coordinated with His saying ﴿متعناه﴾ (*matteʿnāhu*, "We have given him enjoyment"), and it falls with it within the scope of the relative clause. It emphasises the denial of equivalence and establishes it. The meaning is: then this one whom We have given enjoyment is, on the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth to the Fire. The specification of "those brought forth" to those who are brought forth for punishment was required by the context. The interrogation is for denial: that is, their condition is not equal. The one promised Paradise must surely attain what he was promised, together with the fact that his share of the worldly life is not lost to him. This is the state of the believer.

As for the state of the disbeliever, he has only the bare enjoyment of some of the worldly life, in which he and the believer are equal, and each of them obtains his portion of it, and he is headed to the Fire. So are the two equal? The majority read ﴿ثُمَّ هو﴾ (*thumma huwa*) with the *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ*. Al-Kisa'i and Qalun read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*, treating *thumma* like the conjunctions *wa* and *fa*.

The accusative of **﴿يَوْمَ﴾** in His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ يُنادِيهِمْ﴾ ("and the Day He calls to them") is either by coordination with "the Day of Resurrection" or by an implied verb *udhkur* ("remember"). That is: the Day when God, glorified is He, calls these polytheists and says to them: **﴿Where are My partners that you used to claim?﴾**, that they would help you and intercede for you. The two objects of *tazʿumūn* ("you claim") are omitted, meaning: "you claimed them to be My partners," since the context indicates them.

**﴿Those upon whom the word has come into effect will say﴾**: that is, the word of punishment has come into effect for them. They are the leaders of misguidance who took lords besides God, as al-Kalbi said. Qatada said: they are the devils. **﴿Our Lord, these are the ones we misguided﴾**: that is, we called them to error, meaning the followers. **﴿We misguided them as we ourselves were misguided﴾**: that is, we led them astray as we were led astray. **﴿We disassociate ourselves before You﴾** from them. The meaning is that the leaders of misguidance, or the devils, disowned those who obeyed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them disowned others and became enemies, as God, Most High, said: ﴿الأخِلّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("Intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another") [al-Zukhruf: 67]. Here ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is the subject, and ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾ ("whom we misguided") is its descriptive clause. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *aghwaynāhum* ("we misguided them"), and the predicate is *aghwaynāhum*. ﴿كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ ("as we were misguided") is an adjectival description of an omitted verbal noun.

It was also said: the predicate of *hāʾulāʾ* is ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾, while ﴿أغْوَيْناهم كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ is a resumed statement that establishes what came before it. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi preferred this view and objected to the first view, and Abu al-Baqa' answered his objection. **﴿They did not used to worship us﴾**: rather they used to worship their own desires. It was also said that *mā* in *mā kānū* is a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, meaning: "we disown to You their worship of us." The first view is more preferable.

**﴿And it will be said: "Call upon your partners."﴾**: that is, this is said to the disbelievers among the children of Adam. The meaning is: seek help from your gods that you used to worship besides God in the world, so that they may help you and ward off from you. **﴿So they will call them, but they will not respond to them﴾**, nor will they benefit them in any way of benefit. **﴿And they will see the punishment﴾**: that is, the followers and the followed, for it will have overtaken them. **﴿If only they had been guided!﴾** Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted, and the meaning is: "if only they had been guided, that would have saved them and they would not have seen the punishment."

It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided, they would not have called upon them." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided in the world, they would have known that the punishment is true." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they were guided to some way of tricks, they would have warded off the punishment by it." It was also said: "It is time for them to be guided, if only they were guided." It was also said other than this. The first view is the most preferable.

**﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾**: *yawm* here is coordinated with what came before it. That is: what was your answer to the prophets who were sent to you when they conveyed My messages to you?

**﴿Then the information will be obscure to them that Day﴾**: that is, their proofs will be hidden from them until they become like the blind who are not guided. The original would have been *ʿamū ʿan al-anbāʾ* ("they became blind to the news"), but the wording was reversed for emphasis. *Al-anbāʾ* means the reports, and their proofs were called "reports" only because they had no real proof in them; they were merely tales and stories. **﴿So they will not question one another﴾**: they will not ask one another, nor will they speak with any proof, nor will they know what to answer, because God has already given them a clear excuse in the world, so they will have no excuse or argument on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿عَمِيَتْ﴾ (*ʿamiyat*) with a *fatḥah* on the *ʿayn* and a light *mīm*. Al-Aʿmash and Janah ibn Hubaysh read it with a *ḍammah* on the *ʿayn* and a doubled *mīm* (*ʿummiyat*).

**﴿As for one who repents and believes and does righteousness, it is expected that he will be among the successful﴾**: that is, if he repents from polytheism, affirms what the messengers brought, performs the obligatory duties, and avoids sins, then it is expected that he will be among the successful, that is, those who attain their aims of the happiness of both abodes. Although *ʿasā* ("it is expected") originally indicates hope, it is from God a certainty, as is the custom of the noble.

It was also said: the expectation is from the repentant person mentioned, not from God, glorified is He.

**﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾**: that is, He creates whatever He wills, and chooses whatever He wills to choose. **﴿There is not for them any choice. Exalted is Allah above what they associate.﴾** [al-Qasas: 68] Here the statement is connected to the mention of the partners whom they worshipped and chose, meaning that choice belongs to God. **﴿Nor for them is any choice﴾**: that is, the power of choosing (*takhayyur*). It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that no one among God's creation has the right to choose, but choice belongs to God, mighty and majestic.

It was also said that this verse is an answer to their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from one of the two towns?") [al-Zukhruf: 31]. It was also said that this verse is an answer to the Jews, who said: "If the messenger to Muhammad were other than Jibril, we would have believed in him."

Al-Zajjaj said: the pause at ﴿ويَخْتارُ﴾ ("and chooses") is complete, with *mā* being a negation. He said: it is also permissible for *mā* to be in the accusative position governed by *yakhtāru* ("chooses"), and the meaning would be: "and He chooses that in which they have a choice." The correct view is the first, because of the consensus on the pause.

Ibn Jarir said: the implied sense of the verse is "and He chooses for His guardianship the best of His creation." This is extremely weak.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted that *kāna* be complete (*tāmmah*), so that *lahumu al-khiyarah* is a new independent clause. This too is very far-fetched.

It was also said that *mā* is a verbal particle, meaning: "He chooses their choice," and the verbal noun stands in the position of the object, meaning: "He chooses their chosen." This is like an explanation of Ibn Jarir's statement.

The preferable of these explanations is the first. Similar to it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ ولا مُؤْمِنَةٍ إذا قَضى اللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أمْرًا أنْ يَكُونَ لَهُمُ الخِيَرَةُ﴾ ("It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair") [al-Ahzab: 36]. *Al-khiyarah* means choosing, like *al-ṭiyarah*, which means divining by omens; they are two nouns used in the manner of verbal nouns.

Then He, glorified is He, declared His own transcendence and said: **﴿Glory be to Allah﴾**: that is, He is exalted with an exaltation specific to Him, without anyone disputing with Him or sharing with Him. **﴿And high is He above what they associate﴾**: that is, above those they make partners with Him, or above their association.

**﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare﴾**: that is, what they conceal of polytheism, or of enmity toward the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, or of everything they hide that opposes the truth. **﴿And what they declare﴾**: that is, what they make apparent of that.

The majority read ﴿تُكِنُّ﴾ (*tukinnu*) with a *ḍammah* on the initial *tāʾ* and a *kasrah* on the *kāf*. Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read it with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* and a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*.

Then He, glorified and exalted is He, praised Himself for His oneness and for His exclusive entitlement to praise, and said: **﴿He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾**: that is, in this world and the Hereafter, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. **﴿And to Him belongs the judgement﴾**: He judges among His servants as He wills, without any partner. **﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾**: by resurrection, so that He recompenses the doer of good according to his goodness and the wrongdoer according to his wrongdoing. You will not return to anyone else.

**﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and he is to meet it, like one We have given enjoyment of the life of this world and then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth?﴾**: that is, We have promised him Paradise and the blessings in it that cannot be counted, so he is to meet it, that is, to attain it without doubt, since God does not break His promise. **﴿Like one We have given enjoyment of the worldly life﴾**: so he was given some of it as he desired, together with its quick passing away and its disturbance. **﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth﴾**: this is coordinated with His saying ﴿متعناه﴾ (*matteʿnāhu*, "We have given him enjoyment"), and it falls with it within the scope of the relative clause. It emphasises the denial of equivalence and establishes it. The meaning is: then this one whom We have given enjoyment is, on the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth to the Fire. The specification of "those brought forth" to those who are brought forth for punishment was required by the context. The interrogation is for denial: that is, their condition is not equal. The one promised Paradise must surely attain what he was promised, together with the fact that his share of the worldly life is not lost to him. This is the state of the believer.

As for the state of the disbeliever, he has only the bare enjoyment of some of the worldly life, in which he and the believer are equal, and each of them obtains his portion of it, and he is headed to the Fire. So are the two equal? The majority read ﴿ثُمَّ هو﴾ (*thumma huwa*) with the *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ*. Al-Kisa'i and Qalun read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*, treating *thumma* like the conjunctions *wa* and *fa*.

The accusative of **﴿يَوْمَ﴾** in His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ يُنادِيهِمْ﴾ ("and the Day He calls to them") is either by coordination with "the Day of Resurrection" or by an implied verb *udhkur* ("remember"). That is: the Day when God, glorified is He, calls these polytheists and says to them: **﴿Where are My partners that you used to claim?﴾**, that they would help you and intercede for you. The two objects of *tazʿumūn* ("you claim") are omitted, meaning: "you claimed them to be My partners," since the context indicates them.

**﴿Those upon whom the word has come into effect will say﴾**: that is, the word of punishment has come into effect for them. They are the leaders of misguidance who took lords besides God, as al-Kalbi said. Qatada said: they are the devils. **﴿Our Lord, these are the ones we misguided﴾**: that is, we called them to error, meaning the followers. **﴿We misguided them as we ourselves were misguided﴾**: that is, we led them astray as we were led astray. **﴿We disassociate ourselves before You﴾** from them. The meaning is that the leaders of misguidance, or the devils, disowned those who obeyed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them disowned others and became enemies, as God, Most High, said: ﴿الأخِلّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("Intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another") [al-Zukhruf: 67]. Here ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is the subject, and ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾ ("whom we misguided") is its descriptive clause. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *aghwaynāhum* ("we misguided them"), and the predicate is *aghwaynāhum*. ﴿كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ ("as we were misguided") is an adjectival description of an omitted verbal noun.

It was also said: the predicate of *hāʾulāʾ* is ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾, while ﴿أغْوَيْناهم كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ is a resumed statement that establishes what came before it. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi preferred this view and objected to the first view, and Abu al-Baqa' answered his objection. **﴿They did not used to worship us﴾**: rather they used to worship their own desires. It was also said that *mā* in *mā kānū* is a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, meaning: "we disown to You their worship of us." The first view is more preferable.

**﴿And it will be said: "Call upon your partners."﴾**: that is, this is said to the disbelievers among the children of Adam. The meaning is: seek help from your gods that you used to worship besides God in the world, so that they may help you and ward off from you. **﴿So they will call them, but they will not respond to them﴾**, nor will they benefit them in any way of benefit. **﴿And they will see the punishment﴾**: that is, the followers and the followed, for it will have overtaken them. **﴿If only they had been guided!﴾** Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted, and the meaning is: "if only they had been guided, that would have saved them and they would not have seen the punishment."

It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided, they would not have called upon them." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided in the world, they would have known that the punishment is true." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they were guided to some way of tricks, they would have warded off the punishment by it." It was also said: "It is time for them to be guided, if only they were guided." It was also said other than this. The first view is the most preferable.

**﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾**: *yawm* here is coordinated with what came before it. That is: what was your answer to the prophets who were sent to you when they conveyed My messages to you?

**﴿Then the information will be obscure to them that Day﴾**: that is, their proofs will be hidden from them until they become like the blind who are not guided. The original would have been *ʿamū ʿan al-anbāʾ* ("they became blind to the news"), but the wording was reversed for emphasis. *Al-anbāʾ* means the reports, and their proofs were called "reports" only because they had no real proof in them; they were merely tales and stories. **﴿So they will not question one another﴾**: they will not ask one another, nor will they speak with any proof, nor will they know what to answer, because God has already given them a clear excuse in the world, so they will have no excuse or argument on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿عَمِيَتْ﴾ (*ʿamiyat*) with a *fatḥah* on the *ʿayn* and a light *mīm*. Al-Aʿmash and Janah ibn Hubaysh read it with a *ḍammah* on the *ʿayn* and a doubled *mīm* (*ʿummiyat*).

**﴿As for one who repents and believes and does righteousness, it is expected that he will be among the successful﴾**: that is, if he repents from polytheism, affirms what the messengers brought, performs the obligatory duties, and avoids sins, then it is expected that he will be among the successful, that is, those who attain their aims of the happiness of both abodes. Although *ʿasā* ("it is expected") originally indicates hope, it is from God a certainty, as is the custom of the noble.

It was also said: the expectation is from the repentant person mentioned, not from God, glorified is He.

**﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾**: that is, He creates whatever He wills, and chooses whatever He wills to choose. **﴿There is not for them any choice. Exalted is Allah above what they associate.﴾** [al-Qasas: 68] Here the statement is connected to the mention of the partners whom they worshipped and chose, meaning that choice belongs to God. **﴿Nor for them is any choice﴾**: that is, the power of choosing (*takhayyur*). It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that no one among God's creation has the right to choose, but choice belongs to God, mighty and majestic.

It was also said that this verse is an answer to their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from one of the two towns?") [al-Zukhruf: 31]. It was also said that this verse is an answer to the Jews, who said: "If the messenger to Muhammad were other than Jibril, we would have believed in him."

Al-Zajjaj said: the pause at ﴿ويَخْتارُ﴾ ("and chooses") is complete, with *mā* being a negation. He said: it is also permissible for *mā* to be in the accusative position governed by *yakhtāru* ("chooses"), and the meaning would be: "and He chooses that in which they have a choice." The correct view is the first, because of the consensus on the pause.

Ibn Jarir said: the implied sense of the verse is "and He chooses for His guardianship the best of His creation." This is extremely weak.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted that *kāna* be complete (*tāmmah*), so that *lahumu al-khiyarah* is a new independent clause. This too is very far-fetched.

It was also said that *mā* is a verbal particle, meaning: "He chooses their choice," and the verbal noun stands in the position of the object, meaning: "He chooses their chosen." This is like an explanation of Ibn Jarir's statement.

The preferable of these explanations is the first. Similar to it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ ولا مُؤْمِنَةٍ إذا قَضى اللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أمْرًا أنْ يَكُونَ لَهُمُ الخِيَرَةُ﴾ ("It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair") [al-Ahzab: 36]. *Al-khiyarah* means choosing, like *al-ṭiyarah*, which means divining by omens; they are two nouns used in the manner of verbal nouns.

Then He, glorified is He, declared His own transcendence and said: **﴿Glory be to Allah﴾**: that is, He is exalted with an exaltation specific to Him, without anyone disputing with Him or sharing with Him. **﴿And high is He above what they associate﴾**: that is, above those they make partners with Him, or above their association.

**﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare﴾**: that is, what they conceal of polytheism, or of enmity toward the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, or of everything they hide that opposes the truth. **﴿And what they declare﴾**: that is, what they make apparent of that.

The majority read ﴿تُكِنُّ﴾ (*tukinnu*) with a *ḍammah* on the initial *tāʾ* and a *kasrah* on the *kāf*. Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read it with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* and a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*.

Then He, glorified and exalted is He, praised Himself for His oneness and for His exclusive entitlement to praise, and said: **﴿He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾**: that is, in this world and the Hereafter, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. **﴿And to Him belongs the judgement﴾**: He judges among His servants as He wills, without any partner. **﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾**: by resurrection, so that He recompenses the doer of good according to his goodness and the wrongdoer according to his wrongdoing. You will not return to anyone else.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 58–70 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And We were not to destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾. He said: Allah said, "We did not destroy any town on account of faith, but He destroyed the towns on account of wrongdoing when their people did wrong. Had Makkah believed, they would not have perished along with those who perished. But they denied and did wrong, and for that they perished."

Muslim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me,'" and the hadith is given in full.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from ʿAbd ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection at their hungriest, their thirstiest, and their most naked. Whoever fed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will feed him; whoever clothed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will clothe him; whoever gave drink for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will give him drink; and whoever was in the pleasure of Allah, Allah will be in his pleasure."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿Then the information was obscured from them﴾ that he said: "The proofs," and regarding ﴿so they will not question one another﴾ that he said: "by lineages."

It has been firmly established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih the teaching of the istikharah (prayer for guidance) and the manner of its prayer and its supplication, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verses 58–70 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾**, meaning: from among the people of a town who were living in ease, comfort and plenty. Insolence (*baṭar*) then came upon them, and so they were destroyed.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-baṭar* is transgression at the time of blessing.

ʿAṭāʾ said: They lived in insolence, so they ate God's provision and worshipped idols.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mazini said: The meaning of ﴿بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَها﴾ (*baṭirat maʿīshatahā*, "its livelihood became insolent") is *baṭirat fī maʿīshatihā* ("it became insolent in its livelihood"). When the preposition was dropped, the verb became transitive, as in His saying: ﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("and Musa chose his people") [al-Aʿraf: 155]. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (*tafsīr*, an accusative of specification), as you say: *abṭaraka māluka* and *baṭirtahu* ("your wealth made you insolent" and "you were insolent in it"). A parallel to this is at His saying: ﴿إلّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("except one who makes a fool of himself") [al-Baqarah: 130]. However, the accusative of a definite noun as a specification is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the specification must be an indefinite noun that indicates a genus.

It was also said: *maʿīshatahā* is in the accusative governed by *baṭirat*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *jahilat* ("was ignorant of"). ﴿فَتِلْكَ مَساكِنُهم لَمْ تُسْكَنْ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited after them except a little"): that is, no one lived in them after them except for a short time, like a traveller who passes through and stays a day or part of a day. Or, no one remained to live in them except for a few days, because of the ill fate of the sins that had occurred in them.

It was also said: the exception refers to the dwellings, meaning that after the death of their people only a few of the dwellings were inhabited, and most of them were in ruins. Al-Farra' said this, but it is a weak view. ﴿وكُنّا نَحْنُ الوارِثِينَ﴾ ("and We were the inheritors"): that is, of them, because they did not leave any heir to inherit their homes and wealth. The clause ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَنِ﴾ (*lam tuskan*, "were not inhabited") may be in the nominative as a second predicate of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*), and it may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

**﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾**: that is, it was not valid nor proper that God should destroy the disbelieving towns, that is, towns whose people were disbelievers, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger who warns them and recites to them the verses of God that clearly state what God has made obligatory for them, the reward He has prepared for the obedient, and the punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿أُمِّها﴾ (*ummihā*, "their mother") is its largest and greatest town. He singled out the greatest of them for the sending of the messenger, because in it are the nobles of the people, the people of understanding and judgement, and the kings and great men. So by this consideration it became like a mother to the towns around it.

Al-Hasan said: the mother of the towns is its first. It was also said: what is meant by "the mother of the towns" here is Makkah, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed, the first House established for mankind") [Aal ʿImran: 96]. The explanation of what this verse contains has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. (p-1107) The clause ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آياتِنا﴾ ("reciting to them Our verses") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, reciting to them and informing them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

**﴿And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾**: this clause is coordinated with the clause before it. The exception is an exceptive clause with a missing antecedent (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the most general of states. That is: We would never destroy the people of the towns after We send to their mother-town a messenger calling them to the truth, except when they are in the state of being wrongdoers who have deserved destruction because of their persistence in disbelief after the proof has been established against them and their argument has been made firm, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ رَبُّكَ لِيُهْلِكَ القُرى بِظُلْمٍ وأهْلُها مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ ("Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers") [Hud: 117].

Then He, glorified is He, said: **﴿But whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾**. The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah. That is: whatever thing you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life, which you enjoy for the duration of your life or part of your life, after which you will depart from it or it will depart from you. In any case, that is headed to extinction and termination. **﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾**: that is, His reward and recompense are better than that which passes away and perishes, because it is a pure pleasure free from the admixture of turbidity, and more lasting because it endures forever, whereas this worldly life ends quickly. **﴿Then will you not reason?﴾**: will you not understand that the lasting is better than the perishing, and that what contains pure pleasure with no admixture is better than pleasures mixed with turbidity and spoiled by the afflictions of body and heart?

**﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾**: that is, He creates whatever He wills, and chooses whatever He wills to choose. **﴿There is not for them any choice. Exalted is Allah above what they associate.﴾** [al-Qasas: 68] Here the statement is connected to the mention of the partners whom they worshipped and chose, meaning that choice belongs to God. **﴿Nor for them is any choice﴾**: that is, the power of choosing (*takhayyur*). It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that no one among God's creation has the right to choose, but choice belongs to God, mighty and majestic.

It was also said that this verse is an answer to their saying: ﴿لَوْلا نُزِّلَ هَذا القُرْآنُ عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنَ القَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from one of the two towns?") [al-Zukhruf: 31]. It was also said that this verse is an answer to the Jews, who said: "If the messenger to Muhammad were other than Jibril, we would have believed in him."

Al-Zajjaj said: the pause at ﴿ويَخْتارُ﴾ ("and chooses") is complete, with *mā* being a negation. He said: it is also permissible for *mā* to be in the accusative position governed by *yakhtāru* ("chooses"), and the meaning would be: "and He chooses that in which they have a choice." The correct view is the first, because of the consensus on the pause.

Ibn Jarir said: the implied sense of the verse is "and He chooses for His guardianship the best of His creation." This is extremely weak.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah permitted that *kāna* be complete (*tāmmah*), so that *lahumu al-khiyarah* is a new independent clause. This too is very far-fetched.

It was also said that *mā* is a verbal particle, meaning: "He chooses their choice," and the verbal noun stands in the position of the object, meaning: "He chooses their chosen." This is like an explanation of Ibn Jarir's statement.

The preferable of these explanations is the first. Similar to it is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ لِمُؤْمِنٍ ولا مُؤْمِنَةٍ إذا قَضى اللَّهُ ورَسُولُهُ أمْرًا أنْ يَكُونَ لَهُمُ الخِيَرَةُ﴾ ("It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when God and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair") [al-Ahzab: 36]. *Al-khiyarah* means choosing, like *al-ṭiyarah*, which means divining by omens; they are two nouns used in the manner of verbal nouns.

Then He, glorified is He, declared His own transcendence and said: **﴿Glory be to Allah﴾**: that is, He is exalted with an exaltation specific to Him, without anyone disputing with Him or sharing with Him. **﴿And high is He above what they associate﴾**: that is, above those they make partners with Him, or above their association.

**﴿And your Lord knows what their breasts conceal and what they declare﴾**: that is, what they conceal of polytheism, or of enmity toward the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, or of everything they hide that opposes the truth. **﴿And what they declare﴾**: that is, what they make apparent of that.

The majority read ﴿تُكِنُّ﴾ (*tukinnu*) with a *ḍammah* on the initial *tāʾ* and a *kasrah* on the *kāf*. Ibn Muhaysin and Humayd read it with a *fatḥah* on the *tāʾ* and a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*.

Then He, glorified and exalted is He, praised Himself for His oneness and for His exclusive entitlement to praise, and said: **﴿He is Allah; there is no deity except Him. To Him belongs praise in the first and the last﴾**: that is, in this world and the Hereafter, that is, in the abode of the Hereafter. **﴿And to Him belongs the judgement﴾**: He judges among His servants as He wills, without any partner. **﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾**: by resurrection, so that He recompenses the doer of good according to his goodness and the wrongdoer according to his wrongdoing. You will not return to anyone else.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verse 58–70 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And We were not to destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾. He said: Allah said, "We did not destroy any town on account of faith, but He destroyed the towns on account of wrongdoing when their people did wrong. Had Makkah believed, they would not have perished along with those who perished. But they denied and did wrong, and for that they perished."

Muslim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'O son of Adam, I was ill and you did not visit Me,'" and the hadith is given in full.

ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad narrated in Zawa'id al-Zuhd from ʿAbd ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, who said: "People will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection at their hungriest, their thirstiest, and their most naked. Whoever fed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will feed him; whoever clothed someone for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will clothe him; whoever gave drink for the sake of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Allah will give him drink; and whoever was in the pleasure of Allah, Allah will be in his pleasure."

al-Firyabi, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿Then the information was obscured from them﴾ that he said: "The proofs," and regarding ﴿so they will not question one another﴾ that he said: "by lineages."

It has been firmly established from him (ﷺ) in the Sahih the teaching of the istikharah (prayer for guidance) and the manner of its prayer and its supplication, so we will not lengthen by mentioning it.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 28, verses 58–70 (part 1 of 2)**

**His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾**, meaning: from among the people of a town who were living in ease, comfort and plenty. Insolence (*baṭar*) then came upon them, and so they were destroyed.

Al-Zajjaj said: *al-baṭar* is transgression at the time of blessing.

ʿAṭāʾ said: They lived in insolence, so they ate God's provision and worshipped idols.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mazini said: The meaning of ﴿بَطِرَتْ مَعِيشَتَها﴾ (*baṭirat maʿīshatahā*, "its livelihood became insolent") is *baṭirat fī maʿīshatihā* ("it became insolent in its livelihood"). When the preposition was dropped, the verb became transitive, as in His saying: ﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾ ("and Musa chose his people") [al-Aʿraf: 155]. Al-Farra' said: it is in the accusative as a specification (*tafsīr*, an accusative of specification), as you say: *abṭaraka māluka* and *baṭirtahu* ("your wealth made you insolent" and "you were insolent in it"). A parallel to this is at His saying: ﴿إلّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("except one who makes a fool of himself") [al-Baqarah: 130]. However, the accusative of a definite noun as a specification is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the specification must be an indefinite noun that indicates a genus.

It was also said: *maʿīshatahā* is in the accusative governed by *baṭirat*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *jahilat* ("was ignorant of"). ﴿فَتِلْكَ مَساكِنُهم لَمْ تُسْكَنْ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited after them except a little"): that is, no one lived in them after them except for a short time, like a traveller who passes through and stays a day or part of a day. Or, no one remained to live in them except for a few days, because of the ill fate of the sins that had occurred in them.

It was also said: the exception refers to the dwellings, meaning that after the death of their people only a few of the dwellings were inhabited, and most of them were in ruins. Al-Farra' said this, but it is a weak view. ﴿وكُنّا نَحْنُ الوارِثِينَ﴾ ("and We were the inheritors"): that is, of them, because they did not leave any heir to inherit their homes and wealth. The clause ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَنِ﴾ (*lam tuskan*, "were not inhabited") may be in the nominative as a second predicate of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*), and it may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

**﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾**: that is, it was not valid nor proper that God should destroy the disbelieving towns, that is, towns whose people were disbelievers, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger who warns them and recites to them the verses of God that clearly state what God has made obligatory for them, the reward He has prepared for the obedient, and the punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿أُمِّها﴾ (*ummihā*, "their mother") is its largest and greatest town. He singled out the greatest of them for the sending of the messenger, because in it are the nobles of the people, the people of understanding and judgement, and the kings and great men. So by this consideration it became like a mother to the towns around it.

Al-Hasan said: the mother of the towns is its first. It was also said: what is meant by "the mother of the towns" here is Makkah, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed, the first House established for mankind") [Aal ʿImran: 96]. The explanation of what this verse contains has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf. (p-1107) The clause ﴿يَتْلُو عَلَيْهِمْ آياتِنا﴾ ("reciting to them Our verses") is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause: that is, reciting to them and informing them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

**﴿And We would never destroy the towns unless their people were wrongdoers﴾**: this clause is coordinated with the clause before it. The exception is an exceptive clause with a missing antecedent (*istithnāʾ mufarragh*) from the most general of states. That is: We would never destroy the people of the towns after We send to their mother-town a messenger calling them to the truth, except when they are in the state of being wrongdoers who have deserved destruction because of their persistence in disbelief after the proof has been established against them and their argument has been made firm, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿وما كانَ رَبُّكَ لِيُهْلِكَ القُرى بِظُلْمٍ وأهْلُها مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ ("Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reformers") [Hud: 117].

Then He, glorified is He, said: **﴿But whatever you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life and its adornment﴾**. The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah. That is: whatever thing you have been given is the enjoyment of the worldly life, which you enjoy for the duration of your life or part of your life, after which you will depart from it or it will depart from you. In any case, that is headed to extinction and termination. **﴿And what is with God is better and more lasting﴾**: that is, His reward and recompense are better than that which passes away and perishes, because it is a pure pleasure free from the admixture of turbidity, and more lasting because it endures forever, whereas this worldly life ends quickly. **﴿Then will you not reason?﴾**: will you not understand that the lasting is better than the perishing, and that what contains pure pleasure with no admixture is better than pleasures mixed with turbidity and spoiled by the afflictions of body and heart?

It was read with the accusative *matāʿ* (مَتاعَ), as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*): that is, "so you will be given enjoyment (*tumattaʿūn*) of the life." Abu ʿAmr read ﴿يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ (*yaʿqilūn*, "they reason") with the third-person prefix (*taḥtiyyah*), while the rest read it with the second-person prefix (*fawqiyyah*) as address. Their reading is preferred because of His saying: ﴿وما أُوتِيتُمْ﴾ ("what you have been given").

**﴿Is one to whom We have made a good promise, and he is to meet it, like one We have given enjoyment of the life of this world and then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth?﴾**: that is, We have promised him Paradise and the blessings in it that cannot be counted, so he is to meet it, that is, to attain it without doubt, since God does not break His promise. **﴿Like one We have given enjoyment of the worldly life﴾**: so he was given some of it as he desired, together with its quick passing away and its disturbance. **﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, he is of those brought forth﴾**: this is coordinated with His saying ﴿متعناه﴾ (*matteʿnāhu*, "We have given him enjoyment"), and it falls with it within the scope of the relative clause. It emphasises the denial of equivalence and establishes it. The meaning is: then this one whom We have given enjoyment is, on the Day of Resurrection, among those brought forth to the Fire. The specification of "those brought forth" to those who are brought forth for punishment was required by the context. The interrogation is for denial: that is, their condition is not equal. The one promised Paradise must surely attain what he was promised, together with the fact that his share of the worldly life is not lost to him. This is the state of the believer.

As for the state of the disbeliever, he has only the bare enjoyment of some of the worldly life, in which he and the believer are equal, and each of them obtains his portion of it, and he is headed to the Fire. So are the two equal? The majority read ﴿ثُمَّ هو﴾ (*thumma huwa*) with the *ḍamma* on the *hāʾ*. Al-Kisa'i and Qalun read it with a sukun on the *hāʾ*, treating *thumma* like the conjunctions *wa* and *fa*.

The accusative of **﴿يَوْمَ﴾** in His saying ﴿ويَوْمَ يُنادِيهِمْ﴾ ("and the Day He calls to them") is either by coordination with "the Day of Resurrection" or by an implied verb *udhkur* ("remember"). That is: the Day when God, glorified is He, calls these polytheists and says to them: **﴿Where are My partners that you used to claim?﴾**, that they would help you and intercede for you. The two objects of *tazʿumūn* ("you claim") are omitted, meaning: "you claimed them to be My partners," since the context indicates them.

**﴿Those upon whom the word has come into effect will say﴾**: that is, the word of punishment has come into effect for them. They are the leaders of misguidance who took lords besides God, as al-Kalbi said. Qatada said: they are the devils. **﴿Our Lord, these are the ones we misguided﴾**: that is, we called them to error, meaning the followers. **﴿We misguided them as we ourselves were misguided﴾**: that is, we led them astray as we were led astray. **﴿We disassociate ourselves before You﴾** from them. The meaning is that the leaders of misguidance, or the devils, disowned those who obeyed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: some of them disowned others and became enemies, as God, Most High, said: ﴿الأخِلّاءُ يَوْمَئِذٍ بَعْضُهم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ﴾ ("Intimate friends that Day will be enemies to one another") [al-Zukhruf: 67]. Here ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ (*hāʾulāʾ*, "these") is the subject, and ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾ ("whom we misguided") is its descriptive clause. The returning pronoun is omitted, meaning *aghwaynāhum* ("we misguided them"), and the predicate is *aghwaynāhum*. ﴿كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ ("as we were misguided") is an adjectival description of an omitted verbal noun.

It was also said: the predicate of *hāʾulāʾ* is ﴿الَّذِينَ أغْوَيْنا﴾, while ﴿أغْوَيْناهم كَما غَوَيْنا﴾ is a resumed statement that establishes what came before it. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi preferred this view and objected to the first view, and Abu al-Baqa' answered his objection. **﴿They did not used to worship us﴾**: rather they used to worship their own desires. It was also said that *mā* in *mā kānū* is a verbal (*maṣdariyyah*) particle, meaning: "we disown to You their worship of us." The first view is more preferable.

**﴿And it will be said: "Call upon your partners."﴾**: that is, this is said to the disbelievers among the children of Adam. The meaning is: seek help from your gods that you used to worship besides God in the world, so that they may help you and ward off from you. **﴿So they will call them, but they will not respond to them﴾**, nor will they benefit them in any way of benefit. **﴿And they will see the punishment﴾**: that is, the followers and the followed, for it will have overtaken them. **﴿If only they had been guided!﴾** Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to *law* ("if only") is omitted, and the meaning is: "if only they had been guided, that would have saved them and they would not have seen the punishment."

It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided, they would not have called upon them." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they had been guided in the world, they would have known that the punishment is true." It was also said: the meaning is "if only they were guided to some way of tricks, they would have warded off the punishment by it." It was also said: "It is time for them to be guided, if only they were guided." It was also said other than this. The first view is the most preferable.

**﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾**: *yawm* here is coordinated with what came before it. That is: what was your answer to the prophets who were sent to you when they conveyed My messages to you?

**﴿Then the information will be obscure to them that Day﴾**: that is, their proofs will be hidden from them until they become like the blind who are not guided. The original would have been *ʿamū ʿan al-anbāʾ* ("they became blind to the news"), but the wording was reversed for emphasis. *Al-anbāʾ* means the reports, and their proofs were called "reports" only because they had no real proof in them; they were merely tales and stories. **﴿So they will not question one another﴾**: they will not ask one another, nor will they speak with any proof, nor will they know what to answer, because God has already given them a clear excuse in the world, so they will have no excuse or argument on the Day of Resurrection.

The majority read ﴿عَمِيَتْ﴾ (*ʿamiyat*) with a *fatḥah* on the *ʿayn* and a light *mīm*. Al-Aʿmash and Janah ibn Hubaysh read it with a *ḍammah* on the *ʿayn* and a doubled *mīm* (*ʿummiyat*).

**﴿As for one who repents and believes and does righteousness, it is expected that he will be among the successful﴾**: that is, if he repents from polytheism, affirms what the messengers brought, performs the obligatory duties, and avoids sins, then it is expected that he will be among the successful, that is, those who attain their aims of the happiness of both abodes. Although *ʿasā* ("it is expected") originally indicates hope, it is from God a certainty, as is the custom of the noble.

It was also said: the expectation is from the repentant person mentioned, not from God, glorified is He.

**﴿And your Lord creates what He wills and chooses﴾**: that is, He creates whatever He wills, and chooses whatever He wills to choose. **﴿There is not for them any choice. Exalted is Allah above what they associate.﴾** [al-Qasas: 68] Here the statement is connected to the mention of the partners whom they worshipped and chose, meaning that choice belongs to God. **﴿Nor for them is any choice﴾**: that is, the power of choosing (*takhayyur*). A parallel to this is at His saying: ﴿إلّا مَن سَفِهَ نَفْسَهُ﴾ ("except one who makes a fool of himself") [al-Baqarah: 130]. However, the accusative of a definite noun as a specification is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians, because the specification must be an indefinite noun that indicates a genus.

It was also said: *maʿīshatahā* is in the accusative governed by *baṭirat*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *jahilat* ("was ignorant of"). ﴿فَتِلْكَ مَساكِنُهم لَمْ تُسْكَنْ مِن بَعْدِهِمْ إلّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("Those are their dwellings, which were not inhabited after them except a little"): that is, no one lived in them after them except for a short time, like a traveller who passes through and stays a day or part of a day. Or, no one remained to live in them except for a few days, because of the ill fate of the sins that had occurred in them.

It was also said: the exception refers to the dwellings, meaning that after the death of their people only a few of the dwellings were inhabited, and most of them were in ruins. Al-Farra' said this, but it is a weak view. ﴿وكُنّا نَحْنُ الوارِثِينَ﴾ ("and We were the inheritors"): that is, of them, because they did not leave any heir to inherit their homes and wealth. The clause ﴿لَمْ تُسْكَنِ﴾ (*lam tuskan*, "were not inhabited") may be in the nominative as a second predicate of the demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishārah*), and it may also be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

**﴿And your Lord would never destroy the towns until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger reciting to them Our verses﴾**: that is, it was not valid nor proper that God should destroy the disbelieving towns, that is, towns whose people were disbelievers, until He had sent to their mother-town a messenger who warns them and recites to them the verses of God that clearly state what God has made obligatory for them, the reward He has prepared for the obedient, and the punishment for the disobedient. The meaning of ﴿أُمِّها﴾ (*ummihā*, "their mother") is its largest and greatest town. He singled out the greatest of them for the sending of the messenger, because in it are the nobles of the people, the people of understanding and judgement, and the kings and great men. So by this consideration it became like a mother to the towns around it.

Al-Hasan said: the mother of the towns is its first. It was also said: what is meant by "the mother of the towns" here is Makkah, as in His saying: ﴿إنَّ أوَّلَ بَيْتٍ وُضِعَ لِلنّاسِ﴾ ("Indeed, the first House established for mankind") [Aal ʿImran: 96]. The explanation of what this verse contains has already been given at the end of Surah Yusuf.
